profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:38:18.533+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order
Later Student Tiāntāi
Song Annals, Part One
Beginning in the year Gēngshēn (the year of the Monkey),
ending in the year Guǐhài (the year of the Pig),
a total of four years.
The Liú clan had resided for generations in Péngchéng.
Péngchéng was part of the territory of the state of Sòng during the Spring and Autumn period,
therefore, when the Emperor first established the state, its name was Sòng (Song).
Emperor Wǔ, the High Ancestor
His personal name was Yù,
courtesy name Déyú,
childhood name Jìnú,
surname Liú,
a native of Suídélǐ, Péngchéng County,
and the twenty-first generation descendant of Liú Jiāo, King Yuán of Chǔ of the Hàn dynasty.
Péngchéng,
the capital of Chǔ,
thus his descendants made their home there.
When the Jìn house moved east,
the Liú clan relocated to Jīngkǒulǐ in Dāntú, Jìnlíng.
First year of Yǒngchū (Gēngshēn, 420)
The era name was changed in the sixth month of this year.
1 Spring,
first month,
Jǐhài,
the Wèi ruler returned to the palace.
When Jìn possessed the empire,
the Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government, regarding the Wèi ruler, consistently recorded his name;
this year,
Sòng received the abdication,
and for the first time changed the recording to use the format for the various states.
2 The Qín king Chìpán established his son Qǐfú
Mùmò as Crown Prince,
concurrently holding the titles of General Who Pacifies the Army and Commander of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad,
issued a general pardon,
and changed the era name to Jiànhóng.
3 The King of Sòng wished to receive the abdication but found it difficult to broach the subject,
so he gathered the court officials for a banquet,
these were the officials of the Sòng court.
Court,
pronounced zhāo.
"When Huán Xuán usurped the throne,
the Mandate of the tripod had already shifted.
I first advocated the great righteousness,
revived and restored the imperial house,
campaigning south and conquering north,
pacifying the four seas,
achieving merit and accomplishing the task,
I then received the Nine Bestowals.
This year I approach old age and decline,
having reached such a pinnacle of honor,
things abhor fullness and excess,
one cannot long remain secure;
now I wish to return my noble rank,
and retire to the capital in my old age."
The assembled officials only praised his merit and virtue profusely,
none comprehended his meaning.
As the day grew late,
the gathering dispersed.
The Secretariat Director Fù Liàng, upon returning outside,
then understood,
but the palace gates were already closed,
Liàng knocked on the gate requesting an audience,
the King immediately opened the gate and met him.
Liàng entered,
and merely said:
"I should temporarily return to the capital."
The King understood his meaning,
and without further words,
directly asked:
"How many men are needed to escort you?"
Liàng said:
"Several tens of men will suffice."
He then immediately took his leave.
Liàng went out,
it was already night,
he saw a long star spanning the sky,
slapped his thigh and sighed, saying:
"I have often not believed in celestial phenomena,
but now for the first time it is verified."
The long star signifies removing the old and establishing the new,
hence he spoke thus.
Summer,
fourth month,
summoned the King to enter and assist.
The King left his son Yìkāng as Commander of the Military Affairs of the Four Provinces of Yù, Sī, Yōng, and Bìng, and Governor of Yù Province,
to guard Shòuyáng.
Yù Province,
in the Later Hàn, its seat was at Qiáo;
in Wèi, its seat was at Rǔnán Ānchéng;
when Jìn pacified Wú,
its seat was at Chénguó;
after the move south of the Yangtze, its seat was at Shòuyáng, Wúhú, Zhūchéng, Niúzhǔ, Lìyáng, Mǎtóu, Shòuchūn, Gūshú,
not having a fixed location.
At the end of Ān Emperor's reign,
the Emperor wished to expand south of the river,
pacify and secure the land of Yù,
carved off the area west of the great river and north of Dàléi from Yáng Province,
and placed it all under Yù Province;
the foundation of Yù Province,
was thereby established.
After the Emperor pacified Guān and Luò,
he established the Governor of Sī Province,
with its seat at Hǔláo,
overseeing the three actual commanderies of Hénán, Xíngyáng, and Hóngnóng,
and the two émigré commanderies of Hénèi and Dōngjīngzhào,
while Yōng Province remained an émigré administration at Xiāngyáng.
The Qín and Bìng Province Governor guarded Púbǎn,
since Máo Dézǔ had already retreated from Púbǎn to station at Hǔláo,
then Bìng Province should have been temporarily administered at Hǔláo.
Yōng,
pronounced yòng.
Appointed the Army Advisor of the Counselor-in-Chief, Nányáng's Liú Zhàn, as Chief Clerk,
to decide matters of the headquarters and the province.
Headquarters and province,
refer to the Commander's headquarters and Yù Province.
He often compared himself to Guǎn and Zhūgě,
referring to Guǎn Zhòng and Zhūgě Liàng.
He did not write literary compositions,
nor did he enjoy discussions and debates.
The King held him in great esteem.
4 Fifth month,
Yǐyǒu,
Wèi changed the posthumous title of Emperor Xuānwǔ to Emperor Dàowǔ.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng of Wèi ruler Sì,
he posthumously titled his father Guī as Emperor Xuānwǔ.
Change,
pronounced gēng.
5 The Duke of Huáinán of Wèi, Sīmǎ Guófán, and the Viscount of Chíyáng, Sīmǎ Dàocì, plotted to rebel externally,
Sīmǎ Wénsī reported them.
Gēngxū,
the Wèi ruler killed Guófán and Dàocì,
and bestowed upon Wénsī the title of Duke of Yùlín.
Guófán and others' surrender to Wèi is seen in the previous volume, the thirteenth year of Yìxī of Jìn Ān Emperor.
Fán,
pronounced fú yuán.
Those implicated and executed along with their clans numbered several tens of people,
the son of the Marquis of Zhāng'ān, Fēng Yì, Xuánzhī, was among those implicated.
The Wèi ruler, considering Xuánzhī belonged to an old clan of the Yān court,
Mùróng Huī rose in Chānglí,
the Fēng clan attached themselves to him,
and thus served Yān for generations,
achieving nobility and prominence.
Xuánzhī said:
"My younger brother's son Mónú was orphaned early,
I beg to spare his life."
So he killed Xuánzhī's four sons but pardoned Mónú.
6 Sixth month,
Rénxū,
the King arrived at Jiànkāng.
Fù Liàng hinted to Jìn Gōng Emperor to abdicate the throne in favor of Sòng,
prepared the draft edict and presented it to the Emperor,
asking him to write it out.
The Emperor cheerfully took up the brush,
and said to his attendants:
"During Huán Xuán's time,
the Jìn house had already lost the empire,
it was again prolonged by Duke Liú,
for nearly twenty years;
in the third year of Yuánxīng of Jìn Ān Emperor, Yù campaigned against Huán Xuán,
up to now, a total of seventeen years.
Take up,
pronounced qiān gāo.
Again,
pronounced zhí lóng.
Year,
pronounced zǐ hài.
This is what I willingly accept."
He then wrote the edict on red paper.
Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor retired to his residence in Lángyá,
the hundred officials bowed in farewell,
the Director of the Palace Library Xú Guǎng shed tears in sorrow and anguish.
In the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔ Emperor receiving the abdication,
the year was Yǐyǒu;
the fourth year of Jiànxīng,
Cháng'ān fell,
the year was Bǐngzǐ;
a total of fifty-two years.
The following year,
Yuán Emperor established his reign title east of the Yangtze,
changed the era name to Jiànwǔ,
up to this year, the year being Gēngshēn,
a total of one hundred and three years.
Western and Eastern Jìn together enjoyed the state for one hundred and fifty-seven years before perishing.
In the dīngmǎo year,
the ruler held a ceremony at the southern suburb,
and ascended to the throne as Emperor.
After the ceremony,
he proceeded from Shítou with the imperial carriage into Jiànkāng Palace.
Xú Guǎng was moved to tears,
and the attendant-in-waiting Xiè Huì said to him:
“Mister Xú, is it not a minor offense?”
Guǎng said:
“You are an assistant to the Sòng dynasty,
but I am a relic of the Jìn dynasty.
Matters of sorrow and joy
naturally cannot be the same.”
Guǎng
was the younger brother of Miǎo.
Xú Miǎo was esteemed by Jìn Xiàowǔ.
The Emperor sat in the Tàijí Palace,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
For those who offended the reputation and public opinion,
all were cleansed,
and given a new beginning.
Those who offended the reputation and public opinion,
were those who insulted Confucian teachings.
“New,”
pronounced as gōng héng fān.
Péi Zǐyě commented: In the past, when Chónghuá received the end,
the four evil ones were exiled;
the record states: Yáo made Shùn his successor,
on the first day of the first month,
he received the end from Wénzǔ;
he exiled Gònggōng to Yōuzhōu,
banished Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
expelled Sānmáo to Sānwēi,
and executed Gǔn at Yǔshān;
four punishments and the world was pacified.
Chóng,
pronounced as zhí lóng fān.
The stubborn people were moved to Luò.
Wǔ Wáng conquered Yīn,
and moved the stubborn people to Luòyì.
The reputation and public opinion,
removing them was
an excess!
Jìn Gōng Emperor was made King of Línglíng;
honored with grand ceremonies,
all modeled after the initial practices of Jìn,
and he resided at the old Mòlǐng county.
Shěn Yuē said: the Mòlǐng county's original administration was sixty lǐ from the capital,
now the old administrative village.
In Jìn Ān Emperor's ninth year of Yìxī,
the administration moved to the capital,
located at the fighting ground.
In Gōng Emperor's first year of Yuánxī,
the Jīng Province ban on defense assistant officer was abolished,
and the county administration moved there.
The Empress was demoted to Queen.
The Emperor posthumously honored his father as Xiàomù Emperor,
and his mother, Zhào, as Xiàomù Empress;
honored Queen Mother Xiāo as Empress Dowager.
The Emperor's father Qiáo married Zhào,
and passed away after birthing the Emperor,
then married Xiāo.
Upon ascending to the throne,
his age was advanced,
and he attended the Empress Dowager every morning,
never missing the scheduled time.
An edict was issued regarding the Jìn family's titles,
stating they should change according to destiny,
leaving only the five dukes of Shǐxìng, Lúlíng, Shǐ'ān, Chángshā, Kānglè,
lowering their ranks to county duke and county marquis.
Shǐxìng, Lúlíng, Shǐ'ān, and Chángshā were all prefectural dukes,
only Kānglè
was merely a county duke.
According to the Southern History,
Shǐxìng Prefectural Duke was lowered to Huáróng County Duke,
Lúlíng Duke to Cháisāng County Duke,
Shǐ'ān Duke to Lìpǔ County Marquis,
Chángshā Duke to Lìlíng County Marquis.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
Those who exerted themselves during Yìxī and shared the hardships,
retained their original ranks.
On the gēngwǔ day,
Minister of Works Dàolián was made Grand Marshal,
and enfeoffed as King of Chángshā.
The late Minister of Works Dàoguī was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Línchuān,
and Dàolián's son Yìqìng inherited the title.
The other meritorious officials like Xú Xiànzhī,
had their ranks and titles increased accordingly.
Liú Mùzhī was posthumously enfeoffed as Duke of Nánkāng Prefecture,
and Wáng Zhèn'è as Marquis of Lóngyáng County.
The Emperor would often sigh and remember Mùzhī,
saying:
“If Mùzhī had not died,
he would have helped me govern the world.
It can be said, 'When men are gone,
the state is in distress!'”
This is a line from the poem 'Zhān Yáng'.
Distress,
pronounced as qín zuì fān.
“After Mùzhī's death,
people underestimated me.”
The Emperor's son, Guìyáng Duke Yìzhēn, was made King of Lúlíng;
Péngchéng Duke Yìlóng was made King of Yídōu;
Yìkāng was made King of Péngchéng.
On the jǐmǎo day,
the Tàishǐ Calendar was changed to the Yǒngchū Calendar.
Using the new era to change the calendar.
The Wèi ruler journeyed to Yìdú Mountain,
and then proceeded to Fénglǔ Pool.
According to the Northern History,
Yìdú Mountain is west of Píngchéng,
east of Wǔyuán.
Fénglǔ Pool is actually the Wǔyuán Salt Pool,
in the Tang dynasty, within the Yánzhōu boundary.
Lǔ,
pronounced lóng wǔ fān.
He summoned Cuī Hào via postal relay and said to him:
“Your words from previous years have proven true.”
Hào's words can be seen in the previous volume, Jìn Ān Emperor's fourteenth year of Yìxī.
In autumn,
the month of July,
on the dīngyǒu day,
the Wèi ruler went to Wǔyuán.
On the jiǎchén day,
an edict was issued appointing Liáng Duke Xīn as Commander-in-Chief of the Seven Commanderies including Gāochāng, General Who Conquers the West, and Duke of Jiǔquán;
Qín King Chìpán as General Who Pacifies the West.
Jiāozhōu Inspector Dù Huìdù attacked Lín'ip,
greatly defeating it,
as Lín'ip had frequently invaded,
hence Huìdù attacked it.
Lín'ip sued for peace,
and those who had been captured were all sent back.
While Huìdù was at Jiāozhōu,
his governance was detailed and meticulous,
just like managing a family,
causing officials and people to fear and love him;
city gates opened at night,
and property was not stolen on roads.
On the jǐmǐ day,
the Wèi ruler went to Yúnzhōng.
Héxī King Mèngsùn planned to attack Liáng,
but first led his troops to attack Qín's Hào Měng;
once he arrived,
he secretly withdrew and stationed his forces at Chuān Yán.
Liáng Duke Xīn intended to take advantage of the empty situation to attack Zhāngyè;
Sòng Zhāo and Zhāng Tǐshùn earnestly admonished him,
but he did not listen.
Empress Dowager Yǐn said to Xīn:
“You have just established this nation,
with narrow territory and few people,
even self-defense is barely sufficient,
how can you have the leisure to attack others!
The late king, before passing away,
when Lǐ Gāo passed, refer to Jin Ān Emperor's thirteenth year of Yìxī.
advised careful use of arms,
preserving the territory and bringing peace to the people,
while waiting for the right timing.
His words still echo in my ears,
how can you disregard them!
Mèngsùn is skilled in warfare,
and is not your match,
for several years,
he has constantly harbored ambitions of annexation.
Your state, though small,
can establish good governance,
cultivate virtue and nurture the people,
and quietly wait.
If he is foolish and tyrannical,
the people will naturally turn to you;
if he is fair and wise,
fair,
meaning good.
How could you act recklessly,
hoping for unrealistic gains!
In my view,
not only would you lose your army,
but it might also lead to national ruin!”
Yet he refused to listen.
Sòng Zhāo sighed and said:
“This time, the great affair is lost!”
Li Xīn led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry eastward.
Měngxùn heard of this and said:
"Xīn has already fallen into my trap;
however, upon hearing that I have turned my army back,
he will certainly not dare to advance."
He then posted a public proclamation in the western region,
claiming that he had already captured Hàomén,
and was about to attack Huánggǔ.
This public proclamation was not necessarily erected on a lacquered pole,
as was the custom for announcing victories in the Wei and Jin dynasties,
but rather a public notice spreading word of the matter.
Delighted,
Xīn advanced into Dūdújiàn.
Měngxùn led his troops to attack him,
and they fought at Huáichéng,
where Xīn was heavily defeated.
Someone urged Xīn to retreat and defend Jiǔquán.
Xīn said:
"I disobeyed my elderly mother's words and brought about this defeat.
If I do not kill this barbarian,
what face do I have to see my mother again!"
He then marshaled his troops and fought at Liǎoquán,
where he was killed by Měngxùn.
Xīn's younger brother, Jiǔquán Prefect Fān, Xīnchéng Prefect Yù, Commander of the Right Imperial Guard Mì, Left General Tiào, and Right General Liàng fled west to Dūnhuáng.
Měngxùn entered Jiǔquán.
In the fourth year of Emperor Ān of Jin's Lóng'ān era,
Lǐ Gǎo occupied Dūnhuáng.
In total, there were two rulers,
and it was destroyed after twenty-one years.
The officials and people remained undisturbed.
He appointed Sòng Yáo as Director of the Bureau of Personnel,
entrusting him with the selection of officials;
the old ministers of Liáng who were talented and reputable,
he all treated with courtesy and employed.
He appointed his son Mùjiān as Prefect of Jiǔquán.
Dūnhuáng Prefect Lǐ Xún,
was Fān's younger brother,
and together with Fān and others, he abandoned Dūnhuáng and fled to the Northern Mountains.
Měngxùn appointed Suǒ Sì's son Yuánxù as Acting Prefect of Dūnhuáng.
The matter of Suǒ Sì's death is recorded in the 111th volume of the Jin Annals, in the fourth year of Emperor Ān's Lóng'ān era.
Suǒ,
is pronounced as in ancient times.
Měngxùn returned to Gūzāng,
and upon meeting the Dowager of Liáng, Lady Yǐn, he consoled her.
Lady Yǐn said:
"The Lǐ family has been destroyed by barbarians,
what more is there to say!"
Měngxùn,
was a Lúshuǐ barbarian from Zhāngyè.
Consoled,
with effort.
Again,
as before;
the following is the same.
"Now the lives of mother and son are in the hands of others,
how can you be so arrogant!
Moreover, with the state destroyed and your son dead,
you show no sign of grief,
why is that?"
Lady Yǐn said:
"Survival and death,
are all determined by fate.
Why should I, like ordinary people,
grieve like a child!
I am an old woman,
with the state destroyed and family ruined,
how could I cling to my remaining life,
to become a subject or concubine of others!
Only a swift death would be fortunate."
Měngxùn admired her and pardoned her,
marrying her daughter to Mùjiān as his wife.
14 In the eighth month,
on Xīnwèi,
Lady Zāng was posthumously honored as Empress Jìng.
On Guǐyǒu,
the Crown Prince Yìfú was established as the Crown Prince.
15 In the intercalary month,
on Rénwǔ,
an edict was issued to place guards at all the imperial tombs of the Jin emperors.
16 In the ninth month,
the Qín General of Inspiring Might Wáng Jī and others attacked the Húyuán garrison of the King of Héxī, Měngxùn,
capturing over two thousand people and returning.
17 Lǐ Xún in Dūnhuáng had benevolent governance;
Suǒ Yuánxù was crude, treacherous, and fond of killing,
greatly losing the support of the people.
The commandery people Sòng Chéng and Zhāng Hóng secretly sent a letter to summon Xún.
In winter,
Xún led several dozen cavalry into Dūnhuáng,
and Yuánxù fled east to Liángxīng.
Liángxīng Commandery was located within the boundaries of Chánglè County, Guā Prefecture in the Táng dynasty.
Led,
read as command.
He changed the era name to Yǒngjiàn.
The King of Héxī, Měngxùn, sent his heir Zhèngdé to attack Dūnhuáng,
and Xún closed the city and did not engage in battle.
18 In the twelfth month,
on Dīnghài,
the Qiāng chieftain Dí Wēnzǐ of Xìngchéng led over three thousand households to surrender to Wèi.
He defected from Xià and surrendered to Wèi.
Chieftain,
pronounced as in ancient times.
Led,
read as command.
Surrendered,
pronounced as in ancient times.
19 In this year,
Lady Yáo of Wèi passed away,
and was posthumously honored as Empress Zhāo'āi.
The matter of Lady Yáo returning to Wèi is recorded in the 117th volume of the Jin Annals, in the eleventh year of Emperor Ān's Yìxī era.
Second Year (Xīnyǒu, 421)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
and issued a general pardon.
Pei Zǐyě commented: The suburban sacrifice to Heaven and Earth,
is an annual ritual;
pardoning those who are guilty,
what is the purpose of that!
2 The Emperor appointed the Governor of Yáng Prefecture, Prince of Lúlíng Yìzhēn, as Minister over the Masses,
the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Xú Xiànzhī as Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Governor of Yáng Prefecture,
and the Director of the Central Secretariat Fù Liàng as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
3 On Xīnwèi,
the Wèi Emperor Sì traveled to Gōngyáng.
4 The King of Héxī, Měngxùn, led twenty thousand troops to attack Lǐ Xún at Dūnhuáng.
5 The King of Qín, Chìpán, sent the General Who Conquers the North Mù Yìgān and the General Who Supports the State Yuán Jī to attack Shàngguī,
but they encountered continuous rain and returned.
6 In the third month,
on Jiǎzǐ,
the Wèi Prince of Yángpíng, Xī, passed away.
7 The Wèi Emperor mobilized six thousand people from Dàidū to build a park,
extending east to Báidēng,
with a circumference of over thirty lǐ.
8 The King of Héxī, Měngxùn, built a dam to block water and flood Dūnhuáng;
Lǐ Xún begged to surrender,
but was refused.
Xún's general Sòng Chéng and others surrendered the city,
and Xún committed suicide.
Měngxùn slaughtered the city,
captured Xún's nephew Bǎo,
and imprisoned him in Gūzāng.
The Lǐ family was destroyed.
Lǐ Bǎo eventually laid the foundation for the Táng dynasty from this.
Whom Heaven enlightens,
who can overthrow!
He submitted as a subject and offered tribute.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jǐmáo, the first day,
an edict was issued:
"All illicit shrines from Jiǎng Zǐwén downward are to be abolished;
those established for former worthies or for merit and virtue,
are not included in this order."
10 The King of Tǔyùhún, Āchái, sent an envoy to surrender to Qín,
and the King of Qín, Chìpán, appointed Āchái as Grand General Who Conquers the West,
with the honors of Opening the Establishment, Equal to the Three Ministers, Governor of Ān Prefecture, and King of Báilán.
Qín likely established Ān Prefecture in the territory of Tǔyùhún.
11 In the sixth month,
on Yǐyǒu,
the Wèi Emperor traveled north to Pányáng Mountain;
Pányáng Mountain is east of Cānhépō.
In the seventh month,
he traveled west to the river.
12 The King of Héxī, Měngxùn, sent the Right Guard General Jùqú Shànshàn and the General Who Establishes Integrity Jùqú Gǒushēng to lead seven thousand troops to attack Qín.
The King of Qín, Chìpán, sent the General Who Conquers the North Mù Yìgān and others to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry to resist them,
defeating Shànshàn and others at Wǔjiàn,
Wǔjiàn is north of Hóngchí Ridge.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic: Wǔjiàn Water emerges east of Gūzāng City and flows west,
then north into Mǎchéng River.
Defeated,
pronounced as in ancient times.
They beheaded two thousand and returned.
13. Earlier,
the Emperor had given a jug of poisoned wine
to the former Langyé Chief Clerk Zhāng Wěi,
ordering him to poison the Prince of Línglíng.
Wěi sighed and said:
"To poison one's lord in order to survive—
better to die!"
He then drank it himself on the road and died.
Wěi
was the elder brother of Zhào.
Earlier,
when the Emperor was in charge of Yángzhōu,
he recruited Zhào as a subordinate official.
They were both elder brothers of the Prince.
Whenever the Prince had a son,
the Emperor would order the Xiùzhī brothers to find an opportune way to kill him.
"Opportune way" means
to handle it as appropriate,
not letting the matter become exposed.
Fearing deeply that disaster would reach them,
they shared a single room with Chǔ,
cooking their own food in front of the bed.
All provisions for food and drink
came from Chǔ,
so the men of Sòng could find no opening to spy on them.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor ordered Dànzhī and his elder brother, the General of the Right Guard Shūdù, to go and see them,
and they came out to meet in a separate room.
Soldiers climbed over the wall and entered,
presenting medicine to the Prince.
The Prince refused to drink it,
saying:
"According to Buddhist teachings,
those who commit suicide will not obtain a human body again."
The soldiers smothered and killed him with a blanket.
The Emperor led the officials to mourn at the court hall for three days.
From this time onward,
rulers who abdicated the throne
rarely managed to survive intact.
(Note: "Shuài"
is read as "lǜ."
"Lín"
is pronounced "lì zhèn fān."
"Cháo"
is pronounced "zhí yáo fān.")
14. On Gēngxū,
the Wèi sovereign returned to the palace.
15. In winter,
the tenth month,
on Jǐhài,
an edict appointed the King of Héxī, Méngxùn, as General Who Guards the Army, Excellency of the Three Departments with Equal Rank, and Governor of Liángzhōu.
16. On Jǐhài,
the Wèi sovereign went to Dài.
17. In the eleventh month,
on Xīnhài,
the Jìn Emperor Gōng was buried at Chōngpíng Tomb,
and the Emperor led the officials to pay their respects and see him off.
18. In the twelfth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
the Wèi sovereign toured westward,
reaching Yúnzhōng.
19. The Qín king Chìpán sent General Who Conquers the West Kǒngzǐ and others, leading twenty thousand cavalry, to attack Qìhàn Tūzhēn at Luōchuān.
20. The Jìnchāng Grand Administrator Táng Qì, appointed by the King of Héxī Méngxùn, rebelled and held the commandery.
Méngxùn sent his heir, Zhèngdé, to attack him.
Qì
was the son of Yáo.
(Táng Yáo appears in the 111th scroll, in the fourth year of Lóng'ān of the Jìn Emperor Ān.)
21. When the Emperor was still the Duke of Sòng,
Xiè Zhān served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat in the Sòng administration,
and his younger brother Huì served as General of the Right Guard.
At that time, Huì's power and favor were already great.
When he returned to the capital from Péngchéng to fetch his family,
the Emperor, as Duke of Sòng,
had established the Sòng administration at Péngchéng.
The lanes and gates were packed and choked.
Zhān, at home, was shocked and alarmed.
He said to Huì:
"Your fame and position are not yet extensive,
yet people flock to you like this!
Our family has always made quiet retirement its way,
unwilling to meddle in current affairs.
Our social interactions have never extended beyond relatives and friends.
But now you have gained influence that overwhelms both court and countryside.
How can this be a blessing for our family!"
He then put up a fence to separate the courtyards, saying:
"I cannot bear to see this."
When he returned to Péngchéng,
he said to the Duke of Sòng:
"I am originally a man of simple background.
My father and grandfather held positions no higher than two thousand piculs.
Zhān and Huì
are the great-great-grandsons of Xiè Póu, the Grand Ceremonialist of Jìn,
and are collateral grandsons of Xiè Ān.
This means their high ancestors and Xiè Ān share the same origin,
but their fame and position are not comparable.
My aspirations and abilities are ordinary and limited,
yet I have been honored to head the administration,
holding a prominent and confidential position.
When blessings exceed, disaster arises;
its response is not far off.
I specifically beg to be demoted and dismissed,
to preserve our declining family."
He repeatedly presented this request.
Sometimes Huì would tell Zhān confidential court matters,
so Zhān would deliberately mention them to relatives and old friends,
using them as jokes,
to cut off such talk.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Huì, due to his merit in assisting the mandate,
saw his position and responsibilities grow even greater,
and Zhān became increasingly worried and fearful.
That year,
Zhān was appointed Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
He fell ill and did not seek treatment.
On his deathbed,
he left a letter for Huì, saying:
"I am fortunate to have kept my body intact,
what regrets could I have!
I hope you, my brother, will strive to encourage yourself,
for the state and for the family."
To dwell in favor yet think of danger—
Xiè Zhān exemplified this.
(This sets the stage for Xiè Huì's later killing and the destruction of his family.)
(Note: "Wéi"
is pronounced "yú wèi fān.")
Third Year (Rénxū, 422)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on Jiǎchén, the first day,
the Wèi sovereign toured westward from Yúnzhōng,
reaching Wūdòu City.
According to the History of the Northern Dynasties,
Wūdòu City is east of Xuēlín Mountain.
2. On Guǐchǒu,
Xú Xiànzhī was appointed as Minister of Works and Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
retaining his post as Regional Inspector.
The Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Wáng Hóng, was appointed as General of the Guard and Excellency of the Three Departments with Equal Rank.
General of the Central Army Xiè Huì was appointed as General of the Army of the Center and concurrently Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
entering to serve in the palace departments,
commanding the palace guards.
(Note: "Sàn"
is pronounced "xī dǎn fān."
"Qí"
is pronounced "qí jì fān.")
Xú Xiànzhī had served as Army Advisor to the General Who Pacifies the Army Huán Xiū,
and was in the same administration as the Emperor,
forming a deep bond.
When the righteous army was raised,
he became even more trusted and relied upon.
Simply due to his determination, capability, and bearing,
he suddenly found himself in the court,
and both court and countryside admired and submitted to him,
all saying he had the promise of a chief minister.
He was reserved and taciturn,
not showing joy or worry on his face.
He was quite skilled at chess and watching games,
yet often acted as if he did not understand,
and contemporaries especially admired him for this.
Fù Liàng and Cài Kuò often said:
"Lord Xú understands all matters,
and pacifies differences."
Once, when feasting with Fù Liàng and Xiè Huì,
Liàng and Huì were talented, learned, and eloquent,
while Xiànzhī was dignified and composed in demeanor,
speaking only at the appropriate time.
Zhèng Xiānzhī sighed and said:
"Listening to the discussions of Xú and Fù,
one no longer considers learning their strong point."
3. The Qín General Who Conquers the West Kǒngzǐ and others greatly defeated Qìhàn Tūzhēn,
capturing twenty thousand men and women,
and over five hundred thousand head of cattle and sheep.
Tūzhēn led several thousand cavalry fleeing westward,
and his separate tribe, Shùxī, leading five thousand households, surrendered to Qín.
4. In the second month,
on Dīngchǒu,
an edict divided Yùzhōu, with the area east of the Huái River, to form Nán Yùzhōu,
with its seat at Lìyáng,
appointing the Prince of Péngchéng, Yìkāng, as Regional Inspector.
At the beginning of the Yìxī era,
the Emperor wished to expand south of the Yellow River,
to pacify and secure the lands of Yù.
By the ninth year,
the area west of the Great River and north of Dàléi in Yángzhōu was all assigned to Yùzhōu.
By this time,
the lands west of the Huái were made Běi Yùzhōu,
with its seat at Rǔnán.
According to Shěn Yuē's Records,

Nán Yùzhōu administered nineteen commanderies: Lìyáng, Nán Qiáo, Lújiāng, Nán Rǔyīn, Nán Liáng, Jìn Xī, Yìyáng, Ānfēng, Nán Rǔnán, Xīncài, Dōngjùn, Nán Yǐng, Yǐngchuān, Xī Rǔyīn, Rǔyáng, Chénliú, Nán Chén Left Commandery, Biānchéng Left Commandery, and Guāngchéng Left Commandery.
According to Xú's Records and the Records of Commanderies and States of the Yǒngchū era, it only administered thirteen commanderies.
This is likely because Shěn's Records include commanderies established after the Jǐngpíng era among them.
The seat was at Línxiāng.
In the thirteenth year of Yìxī of the Jìn Emperor Ān, Xiāngzhōu was abolished,
but now it was re-established.
Línxiāng
is an old Hàn county,
which in Táng times became Chángshā County of Tánzhōu.
5. On Bǐngxū,
the Wèi sovereign returned to the palace.
6 In the third month,
the Emperor fell ill.

The Grand Commandant, the Prince of Chángshā, Liú Dàolián; the Minister of Works, Xú Xiànzhī; the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Fù Liàng; the General of the Central Army, Xiè Huì; and the General of the Guards, Tán Dàojì, all entered the palace to attend to his medical care.
The court officials requested to pray to the gods and spirits,
but the Emperor would not allow it,
only ordering the Palace Attendant Xiè Fāngmíng to report his illness to the ancestral temple.
The Emperor was by nature skeptical of the strange and supernatural.
In his humble days, there were many auspicious omens,
but after he became noble,
when the historians carefully inquired about what they had heard,
the Emperor refused to answer.
Tán Dàojì was sent out to serve as General Who Guards the North and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
stationed at Guǎnglíng,
overseeing all military affairs in Huáinán.
Emperor Chéng of Jìn established Yǎnzhōu,
with its seat at Jīngkǒu.
From this time onward, its seat was moved to Guǎnglíng,
administering the commanderies of Guǎnglíng, Hǎilíng, Shānyáng,
Xūyí, Qínjùn, and Nánpèi, among others.
"Oversee"
is pronounced with the meaning of supervision.
The Crown Prince often associated with petty individuals.
Xiè Huì spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty's years are already advanced.
You should consider preserving the dynasty for ten thousand generations.
The imperial throne is of utmost importance,
and it must not be entrusted to someone lacking in talent."
With these words, Xiè Huì
already harbored the intention of deposing the incompetent and establishing a wise ruler.
"Entrust"
is pronounced with the falling tone,
or also with its usual pronunciation.
"What about the Prince of Lúlǐng?"
Xiè Huì said:
"I request to observe him."
He went to visit the Prince of Lúlǐng, Liú Yìzhēn.
Yìzhēn eagerly wished to converse with him,
but Huì did not respond much.
Upon returning, he said:
"His virtue is lighter than his talent;
he is not fit to be a ruler."
On the day Dīngwèi,

Yìzhēn was sent out as Commander of the military affairs of the six provinces of Nán Yù, Yù, Yōng, Sī, Qín, and Bìng; General of Chariots and Cavalry; and Inspector of Nán Yùzhōu, with authority equal to the Three Excellencies.
This laid the groundwork for Huì and others to kill Yìzhēn.
"Yōng"
is pronounced yòng.
"Cavalry"
is pronounced jì.
Large provinces were generally given the title of Commander,
some overseeing as many as fifty provinces,
which cannot all be recorded in detail.
By the end of the Sòng dynasty,
the territory comprised only twenty-two provinces.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
provinces were established along the borders,
and there began to be fifty provinces.
"Again"
is pronounced fù.
7 The Emperor recovered from his illness.
On the day Jǐwèi,
a great amnesty was declared.
8 Refugees from Qín and Yōng entered Liángzhōu from the south.
On the day Gēngshēn,
an envoy was sent to deliver ten thousand bolts of silk,
and grain from Jīng and Yōng was transported by water to provide relief.
The "Yōng" in Qín and Yōng
refers to the ancient Yōngzhōu,
the region of Guānzhōng.
The "Yōng" in Jīng and Yōng
refers to the Nán Yōngzhōu established in the late Jìn period,
with its seat at Xiāngyáng.
"Envoy"
is pronounced shǐ.
"Relief"
is pronounced zhèn.
9 After Diāo Kuí was executed,
as recorded in the 113th year of the Yuánxīng era of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Dī Mí led several dozen men into Jīngkǒu,
and the Major of the Grand Commandant's Retained Headquarters, Lù Zhòngyuán, attacked and killed him.
At that time, the Prince of Chángshā, Liú Dàolián, as Grand Commandant, was stationed at Jīngkǒu,
but he had entered the palace to attend to the Emperor's medical care,
hence there was a retained headquarters.
10 On the day Yǐchǒu,
the King of Hénán of Wèi, Tuòbá Yào, died.
11 In the summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
the Wèi established the imperial son Tuòbá Tāo as Prince of Tàipíng,
appointed him Chancellor,
and granted him the title of Grand General;
Tuòbá Pī as Prince of Lèpíng,
Tuòbá Mí as Prince of Āndìng,
Tuòbá Fàn as Prince of Lè'ān,
Tuòbá Jiàn as Prince of Yǒngchāng,
Tuòbá Chóng as Prince of Jiànníng,
and Tuòbá Jùn as Prince of Xīnxīng.
12 On the day Yǐhài,
an edict was issued enfeoffing the Duke of Chóuchí, Yáng Shèng, as King of Wǔdū.
13 The King of Qín, Qǐfú Chìpán, appointed the General Who Breaks Through Enemy Lines, Qǐfú Shìchén, as Colonel of the Western Hú,
and built the city of Lièhún at Zhīluó to garrison it.
Zhīluó is likely the area of Luōchuān.
14 In the fifth month,
the Emperor's illness became severe.
He summoned the Crown Prince and admonished him, saying:
"Although Tán Dàojì has ability and strategy,
he lacks great ambition,
unlike his elder brother Shào, who has an ungovernable spirit.
Xú Xiànzhī and Fù Liàng
should harbor no treacherous intentions.
Xiè Huì has followed me on many campaigns,
and is quite adept at recognizing opportunities and adapting to change.
If there is anyone who will act differently,
it must be this man."
The Emperor already harbored suspicions about Huì.
"Many"
is pronounced shuò.
"If in later generations there is a young ruler,
all court affairs should be entrusted to the Chancellor.
The Empress Dowager should not trouble herself with attending court."
The Minister of Works Xú Xiànzhī, the Palace Secretary Fù Liàng, the General of the Central Army Xiè Huì, and the General Who Guards the North Tán Dàojì jointly received the final edict.
On the day Guǐhài,
the Emperor passed away in the Western Hall.
He was sixty years old.
From this time onward,
the deaths of rulers in the Northern and Southern Dynasties were all referred to as "passed away."
"Received"
is pronounced bèi.
"Final"
is pronounced gù.
He was strict, orderly, and governed by laws and regulations.
In his clothing and residence,
he was frugal, living as simply as a commoner.
He rarely held feasts or outings,
and had very few consorts.
He once obtained a niece of the Later Qín Emperor Gāozǔ.
The Later Qín Emperor Yáo Xīng
was given the temple name Gāozǔ.
"Niece"
is pronounced zòng.
She somewhat caused neglect of affairs;
Xiè Huì discreetly advised him,
and she was immediately sent away.
All wealth and silk were kept in the outer treasury;
there was no private hoard within the palace.
Once, Lǐngnán presented a bolt of extremely fine cloth, eight zhàng in length.
The Emperor disliked its exquisite beauty for causing hardship to the people.
Yáng Xióng's "Rhapsody on the Capital of Shǔ" says: The cloth is like spider silk,
so fine it cannot withstand the wind;
in the tube is yellow, moist cloth,
a single bolt worth several pieces of gold.
This describes its fineness.
"Disliked"
is pronounced wù.
He returned the cloth,
and issued an order prohibiting Lǐngnán from producing such cloth.
When a princess was married off,
the gifts sent did not exceed two hundred thousand coins,
and there were no brocade or embroidered items.
Inside and outside the palace, everyone observed the prohibitions,
and no one dared to be extravagant or wasteful.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne as Emperor,
at the age of seventeen.
A great amnesty was declared.
The Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
Sīmǎ Shi was established as Empress.
The Empress
was the Hǎiyán Princess, daughter of Emperor Gōng of Jìn.
The Wei ruler took the Cold-Food Powder,
causing recurrent drug effects for years,
and disasters and abnormalities frequently occurred,
causing him considerable anxiety.
He secretly sent an envoy to ask Cí Hào, Duke of White Horse, saying:
"Recently, solar eclipses have occurred in the regions of Zhào and Dài.
I fear that should something happen to me suddenly,
as my sons are all young,
what should be done?
Please consider a posthumous plan for me."
Hào replied:
"Your Majesty is in the prime of life,
and your health is improving;
if it becomes absolutely necessary,
allow me to offer my humble opinion.
Since the rise of our dynastic reign,
we have not emphasized establishing a second-in-command,
which is why at the beginning of the Yǒngxīng era,
the state was nearly endangered.
Select able ministers and officials to act as mentors and caretakers,
and have loyal subjects as friends;
let them handle government affairs internally,
and manage military affairs externally.
If this is done,
Your Majesty can leisurely maintain a state of inaction,
preserving health and longevity.
After a thousand years,
the state will have a competent ruler,
with the people having a figure to follow,
and treachery will have no place,
preventing disaster.
The imperial son Tāo is approaching the cycle of Jupiter,
to establish a son based on seniority is the fundamental principle,
if one must wait for maturity before selection,
it would disrupt natural order,
which would invite chaos."
He responded:
"To establish the eldest is orderly,
to position the competent is respected;
Tāo is both the eldest and competent,
ordained by heaven."
The emperor agreed,
establishing Prince of Tàipíng, Tāo, as the crown prince,
allowing him to preside over the court from the main hall,
acting as the deputy ruler.
Elder grandson Sōng and Sānyáng Duke Xī Jīn,
were seated on the east wing,
facing west;
Cí Hào and Grand Commander Mù Guān, courtier Qiū Duī from Dài, acted as right helpers,
facing east;
all the officials subordinated themselves to hear his commands.
Those seated in the east wing faced west,
those seated in the west wing faced east,
all respectfully bowing to the crown prince.
Observing discreetly,
he was greatly pleased,
and told his ministers:
"Sōng is an experienced and veteran minister,
serving four generations,
with contributions to state support;
Sōng served Emperor Zhāochéng, Emperors Dàowǔ, Míngyuán, and Crown Prince Tāo over four generations.
His reputation is widespread;
he understands popular sentiment,
is adept in matters;
Guān comprehends government essentials,
understands my policies;
Hào is well-versed and knowledgeable,
meticulous in understanding celestial and human affairs;
though Duī lacks significant use,
he is focused and diligent in official matters.
With these six aiding the crown prince,
I, with you, will patrol the four borders,
subjugate rebels and pacify territories,
and achieve our aspirations across the realm."
Sōng was originally surnamed Bábá,
Jīn was surnamed Dáxī,
Guān was surnamed Qiūmùlíng,
Duī was surnamed Qiūdūn.
At that time,
notable ministers from the north of Dài among the Wèi,
had often complex surnames,
and when moved to Luò by the emperor,
they all changed to simpler ones.
The old histories found
these intricacies troublesome,
thus they conformed to simplified surnames for convenience,
and now we follow this convention.
The Wèi ruler also ordered Liú Jié, who managed both Eastern and Western divisions, Gǔ Bì from Ménxìa,
and Tuóhélústráightránkofficer,
Tāobā shares ancestry with Mùróng and the Duàn clan, all descended from Xiānbēi,
which later grew strong,
calling the eastern branch Tuóhé.
They were assigned to attend to the Eastern Palace,
delegated important affairs,
delivering declarations.
The crown prince was intelligent,
and magnanimous;
ministers would report their doubts,
The emperor would say:
"This is not within my knowledge,
it should be resolved by you, the state leader."
In June,
on the Rénshēn day,
Fù Liàng, Minister of the Board of Military Affairs, was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat and Minister of the Board of Justice,
Xiè Huì, General of the Guards, was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat,
Xiè Fāngmíng, Imperial Attendant, was made prefect of Dānyáng.
Fāngmíng was skilled in governance,
acquiring a reputation for capability wherever he served;
succeeding previous administrations,
not altering their policies,
only changing what was necessary,
gradually adapting and transforming,
leaving no trace.
On the Wǔzǐ day,
the Duke of Chángshā, Dào Lián, passed away.
Wèi's General Jiànyì, Diāo Yōng, invaded Qīngzhōu,
but the provincial troops defeated him.
Yōng gathered scattered soldiers,
fled to defend Dàxiāng Mountain,
according to the Geographical Records of Wèi: Dàxiāng Castle was in Chéng County, Jìyīn Commandery.
In the autumn,
July,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
Emperor Wǔ was buried at Chūníng Mausoleum,
located at Jiàng Mountain in Jiànkāng County, Dānyáng.
The King of Héxī, Mèngsùn, dispatched General Qián, Jùqú Chéngdū, to lead ten thousand troops,
displaying military might south of the mountain,
and then stationed at Wǔjiàn.
The Qín King, Chìpán, sent Northern Expedition General Chūlián Qián and others, leading six thousand cavalry to attack them.
Early in the 21st year,
the Wèi ruler heard that Gāo Zǔ had conquered Cháng'ān,
see Volume 1, Jìn Ān Dì Yìxī 13th year.
He sent envoys to seek peace,
from then on, yearly interactions continued without interruption.
After Gāo Zǔ's death,
the palace general Shěn Fàn and others were at Wèi on a mission,
the Jìn established two guards,
still appointing palace generals.
Mission,
misleadingly interpreted;
the same below.
Upon reaching the river,
the Wèi ruler sent people to capture them,
planning to deploy troops to seize Luòyáng, Hǔláo, and Huátái.
Cuī Hào advised:
"Your Majesty did not suddenly rise against Liú Yù,
he received his envoys and tribute,
Yù also respected Your Majesty's authority.
Unluckily, he is now dead,
quickly attacking him in mourning,
even if successful, would not be admirable.
Moreover, the state today cannot capture Jiāngnán in one strike either,
and merely incurs the name of attacking during mourning,
propriety dictates one should not attack during mourning.
I suggest sending people to express condolences,
caring for orphans and the weak,
providing relief for their disasters,
spreading righteous fame in the world,
then Jiāngnán will submit without being attacked.
Moreover, since Yù recently died,
his faction has not yet disbanded,
if our troops press in at their borders,
they will certainly unite to resist,
success is not guaranteed.
It is better to delay,
wait for their strong ministers to vie for power,
internal strife will surely arise,
then send generals to dispatch the army,
achieving victory without exhausting the troops,
taking Huáiběi with ease."
The Wèi ruler said:
"Liú Yù took advantage of Yáo Xīng's death to extinguish him,
see Volume 117, Jìn Ān Dì Yìxī 12th year and Volume 1, Yìxī 13th year.
Why is it unacceptable?"
Hào said:
"Not so.
When Yáo Xīng died,
his sons quarreled amongst themselves,
so Yù took the opportunity to attack.
Now there is no internal strife in Jiāngnán,
it is not comparable."
The Wèi ruler did not heed,
granting Xi Jīn the temporary rank of Sīkōng,
adding commander-in-chief of the Jìn army and acting governor of Yángzhōu,
ordering him to command the Sòng army general and Jiāozhōu governor Zhōu Jǐ,
after Wèi Xiàowén used a descendant of Xiàn Dì's brother from the Pǔ clan for the Zhōu clan.
Jìn, Sòng, Wú, Zhèng, and Chǔ generals,
were all appointed by Wèi.
22 Yǐsì,
the Wèi ruler went to Lèinán Palace,
and then to Guǎngníng.
In the first year of Jiànxīng of Jìn Mǐn Dì,
Yīlú built New Píngchéng north of Lèi,
later building a palace south of Lèi.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Guǎngníng is fifty lǐ from Píngchéng.
Guǎngníng County,
was part of Shànggǔ Prefecture in Hàn,
established as a prefecture during Jìn Tàikāng.
Lèi,
pronounced lìqi,
23 Xīnhài,
the Wèi people built an outer wall at Píngchéng,
enclosing thirty-two lǐ.
24 The Wèi ruler went to Qiáoshān.
Wǔdài Zhì: Qiáoshān is located in Zhuō Prefecture Huáiróng County.
Liú Xù said: During the Táng, it was Huáiróng County in Guó Prefecture,
from Pān County of Shànggǔ in the Later Hàn.
Winter,
in the tenth month,
Jiǎxū,
the ruler returned to the palace.
25 The Wèi army was about to set out,
public officials gathered to discuss strategy before the regent,
whether to attack the city first or seize land first.
Xi Jīn wanted to attack the city first,
Cuī Hào said:
"The southern people excel at defending cities.
Formerly, the Fú clan attacked Xiāngyáng,
but could not capture it in a year.
See Volume 104, Jìn Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán 3rd and 4th years.
If we do not take it promptly,
it will demoralize the army,
and give the enemy time to prepare and approach us strongly,
while we grow weary as they gain strength,
this is a dangerous path.
It is better to split the army to seize territory,
up to the Huái River as a boundary,
appoint officials for governance,
collect taxes and grain,
then Luòyáng, Huátái, and Hǔláo would be north of the army,
severing hopes of southern rescue,
they must flee east along the river;
otherwise, they are like trapped prey,
why worry about not capturing them?"
Gōngsūn Biǎo persistently requested to attack the city,
the Wèi ruler agreed.
Thereupon, Xi Jīn and others led twenty thousand foot soldiers and cavalry,
crossed the river,
encamping east of Huátái.
At that time, the Sīstí captive Mào Dézǔ was garrisoned at Hǔláo,
East Prefecture governor Wáng Jǐngdù urgently reported to Dézǔ,
Wáng Jǐngdù was posted as East Prefecture governor at Huátái.
Prior to this,
Sīmǎ Chǔzhī gathered followers at the boundaries of Chénliú,
upon hearing Wèi troops crossed the river,
he sent emissaries to surrender.
Wèi appointed Chǔzhī as Southward Conqueror General, Jīngzhōu Governor,

the Wèi Minister Shì Huáiji led troops to ambush Cāngyán,

December,
Bǐngxū,

Xúzhōu covering Péngchéng, Péi, Xiàpī, Lánlíng, Dōnghǎi, Dōngguān, Dōng'ān, Lángyá, Huáiyáng, Yángpíng, Jìyīn, Běijìyīn, Zhōnglí, Mǎtóu and other prefectures.

The Wei ruler dispatched the Central Army Commander, the Dai person É Qīng, and the Qīsī Marquis, the Rourán person Lǘ Dàféi, to lead seven thousand troops to join Zhōu Jǐ and Shūsūn Jiàn in crossing the Yellow River southward.

The city of Què'áo overlooked the river crossing.
Later, during the Wei dynasty, it became the seat of Jì Prefecture.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* says: "The city was the former Chípíng County."
On the Guǐwèi day,
the Yǎn Prefecture Governor Xú Yǎn abandoned Yǐnmǎo and fled south.
The *Shuǐjīng* states: "The Jì River flows northwest from Xūchāng County past Yú Mountain,
then north past the west of Gǔchéng County."
The commentary says: "On the banks of the Jì River is the Yǐnmǎo fortress,
located over forty *lǐ* south of Yú Mountain."
This is within the boundaries of Gǔchéng County, the former Xiǎogǔ City of the Spring and Autumn period.
Jīnxiāng County,
belonged to Shānyáng Commandery during the Han,
and to Gāopíng Commandery during the Jin.
It seems a commandery was established by division towards the end of the Jin.
Sīmà Àizhī and Jìzhī had previously gathered followers east of the Jì River,

East of the Jì River was the boundary of Qīng Prefecture.
Jì,
read as *zǐlǐ*.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Wei troops advanced on Hǔláo.
The Qīng Prefecture Governor, Dōngguǎn's Zhú Kuí, defended Dōngyáng City.
Since Cáo Yí's time, Qīng Prefecture had been administered from Guǎnggù.
After Emperor Wǔ defeated Mùróng Chāo,
he razed that city,

located southwest of Guǎng County.
Sòng Bái said: "The present Qīng Prefecture administers Yìdū County,
and the prefecture's eastern city is Dōngyáng City."
In the early Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jin,
Dōngguǎn Commandery was established from a division of Lángyá.
Qīng Prefecture governed the commanderies of Qí, Jǐnán, Gāomì, Lè'ān, Píngchāng, Běihǎi, Dōnglái, Tàiyuán, Chángguǎng, and others.
Guǎn,
read as *guān*.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
an edict appointed the Nányǎn Prefecture Governor Tán Dàojì as Supervisor of Military Affairs for the Campaign,
to join Wáng Zhòngdé in rescuing them.
The Prince of Lúlíng, Liú Yìzhēn, sent the Dragon-Soaring General Shěn Shūlí with three thousand men to join Liú Cuì,
to proceed as appropriate to provide aid.
Yìzhēn was then stationed at Shòuyáng,
and Liú Cuì at Xuánhù.
Xiāng,
read as *sījiāng*.
Liàng, read as *liáng*.
28. The Qín King Chìpán summoned the Qín Prefecture Governor Tán Dá to serve as Left Chancellor and General Who Conquers the East.
The Prince of Yíngyáng
was named Yìfú,
his childhood name was Chēbīng,
and he was the eldest son of Emperor Wǔ.
*Kǎoyì* says: The Song Basic Annals
and Gāo's *Xiǎoshǐ* both record
"Yíngyáng";
the biographies of Empress Zāng, Xiè Huì, and Cài Kuò record
"Yíngyáng".
Yíngyáng
is a commandery name in the south,
so we follow that.
First year of Jǐngpíng (Guǐhài, 423)
1. Spring,
first month,
Jǐhài, first day of the month.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
2. On the Xīnchǒu day,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven.
3. Yú Lìdī of Wei attacked Jīnyōng.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Hénán Grand Administrator Wáng Juānzhī abandoned the city and fled.
The Wei ruler appointed Lìdī as Yù Prefecture Governor,
to defend Luòyáng.
4. The Wei ruler made an inspection tour south to Héng Mountain.
On the Bǐngchén day,
he reached Yè.
Last year in the twelfth month it was recorded that the Wei ruler reached Jì Prefecture,
now it records an inspection tour south to Héng Mountain.
One of these must be an error.
5. On the Jǐwèi day,
an edict summoned the Yùzhāng Grand Administrator Cài Kuò to serve as Minister of Personnel.
Since the Jin dynasty,
the Minister of Personnel has been called the Grand Minister,
because he ranked above the other Ministers,
and his authority and responsibilities were crucial.
"If all selection matters are entrusted to me,
I have no objection;
'no objection' means
I will not further discuss acceptance or refusal.
Otherwise, I cannot accept the post."
Fù Liàng relayed this to the Recorder of the Masters of Writing Xú Xiànzhī.
Xiànzhī said:
"For positions of Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and below, we can entrust them all to Cài;
we need not concern ourselves.
'Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and below' refers to
the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and the Regular and Assistant Cavalier Attendants-in-Ordinary.
Fù,
read as *fúyòu*.
But for higher positions, we should jointly deliberate on differences."
Kuò said:
"I cannot sign at the bottom of the paper for Xú Gànmù!"
Thus he did not accept the post.
Gànmù
was Xiànzhī's childhood name.
Selection documents were on yellow paper,
with the Recorder of the Masters of Writing and the Minister of Personnel signing jointly.
'Selection documents' refers to
the paperwork of the Selection Bureau.
Hóng Mài said: Yè Shílín stated that the use of yellow paper for imperial decrees began during the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
but this is incorrect.
During the time of Emperor Gōng of Jin,
when Wáng Shàozhī was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
all imperial edicts on yellow paper
were composed by him.
Thus, yellow paper was already used for writing edicts in the Eastern Jin.
Also,
during the time of Emperor Míng of Song,
the Minister of Personnel Chǔ Yuān conducted selections at Zhěqí.
For that campaign,
appointments were all made after battles,
and wooden tablets and proclamations were not supplied,
hence yellow paper slips were used.
Thus, in the Song period, appointments and rewards for military merit made in the field
often used yellow paper.
Also,
when Xú Xiànzhī summoned Cài Kuò to be Minister of Personnel,
Kuò said:
"I cannot sign at the bottom of the paper for Xú Gànmù,"
which shows that in the Song period, yellow paper was used for official documents.
By the Qi period,
a system was established for the Left and Right Assistants to sign documents:
For white documents,
the Right Assistant signed above,
the Left Assistant below;
for yellow documents,
the Left Assistant signed above,
the Right Assistant below.
Although it is distant and we cannot know precisely which were yellow documents and which were white,
what is known
is that the paper was already decisively divided into yellow and white.
By the time of the Marquis of Dōng Hūn,
eunuchs would wrap fish and meat in paper to take home,
and these were all yellow documents from the Five Departments.
Thus, the use of yellow paper for documents
has a long history.
During Emperor Gāozōng's time,
it was only for copying edicts and decrees to be sent down to prefectures and counties that yellow paper began to be used exclusively;
to say generally that the use of yellow paper for imperial edicts began with Emperor Gāozōng
is inaccurate.
Xuǎn,
read as *xūjuàn*.
Shěn Yuē commented: Cài Kuò firmly declined the responsibility of personnel evaluation,

The Ministry of Personnel managed selections;
the Recorder of the Masters of Writing oversaw the affairs of all the Ministers.
Duàn,
read as *dīngluàn*.
He did not wish to hold a position controlling advancement and obstruction.
The responsibility of personnel evaluation:
with the right person in charge, the path for the worthy is open;
with the wrong person, it is blocked.
Sè,
read as *xīzé*.
6. On the Gēngshēn day,
Tán Dàojì's army was at Péngchéng.
The Wei commander Shūsūn Jiàn entered Línzī,

*Kǎoyì* says: The *Suǒlǔ Zhuàn* states:

According to the *Hòu Wèi Shū*, there are no names such as Shèguī, etc.,

referring to Shūsūn Jiàn and others.
Those who did not enter cities
had people rely on mountainous terrain,
cutting down crops,
so when the Wei army arrived,
they could obtain no food.
The Jǐnán Grand Administrator Yuán Miáo led his followers to join Kuí.
Yuán Miáo abandoned Lìchéng to join Kuí.
Jì,
read as *zǐlǐ*.
Shuài,
read as *lǜ*;
same below.
Diāo Yōng met the Wei ruler in Yè.
The Wei ruler said:
"Shūsūn Jiàn and others entered Qīngzhōu,
but the people all hid and avoided them,
so they could not capture the city by assault.
They have long respected your prestige and trustworthiness.
Yōng first gathered troops between the Hé and Jì rivers.
Yōng,
read as Yōng.
Therefore, he appointed Yōng as the Governor of Qīngzhōu,
provided Yōng with cavalry,
and sent him to recruit soldiers to take Qīngzhōu.
The Wei troops crossing the river toward Qīngzhōu totaled sixty thousand cavalry.
Diāo Yōng recruited five thousand men,
pacified and comforted the soldiers and people,
and all sent taxes to supply the army.
7 The Rúrǎn invaded the Wei borders.
In the second month,
on Wùchén,
Wei built a long wall,
from Chìchéng west to Wǔyuán,
stretching over two thousand lǐ,
garrisoning it with soldiers,
to defend against the Rúrǎn.
8 On Dīngchǒu,
the Grand Empress Dowager Xiāo passed away.
9 The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, and the King of Tǔyùhún, Āchái, both sent envoys to present tribute.
On Gēngchén,
an edict appointed Méngxùn as Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of the four provinces Liáng, Qín, Hé, and Shā, General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Liángzhōu, and King of Héxī;
and appointed Āchái as Commander of the military affairs beyond the frontier, General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Shāzhōu, and Duke of Jiāohé.
Tǔyùhún occupied the sandy Qiáng lands beyond the frontier,
hence he was ordered to command the military affairs beyond the frontier.
Jiāo,
read as Jiāo.
10 In the third month,
on Rénzǐ,
Empress Xiàoyì was buried at Xīngnínglíng,
Xīngnínglíng is located at Yúshān in Jiànbì Village, Dāntú County, Jìnlíng.
11 Wei's Xī Jīn, Gōngsūn Biǎo, and others jointly attacked Hǔláo,
and the Wei ruler sent troops from Yè to assist them.
Máo Dézǔ dug a tunnel inside the city extending seventy zhàng,
divided into six passages,
emerging outside the Wei encirclement;
he recruited four hundred daring soldiers,
and had Adjutant Fàn Dàojī and others lead them,
emerging from the tunnel,
to launch a surprise attack on the enemy's rear.
The Wei army was alarmed and thrown into confusion,
several hundred heads were taken,
and they burned the enemy's siege equipment before returning.
Although the Wei troops retreated and scattered,
they soon regrouped,
and attacked even more fiercely.
Xī Jīn led three thousand infantry and cavalry from Hǔláo to attack Xǔchāng, where the Administrator of Yǐngchuān, Lǐ Yuándé, and others were stationed.
Yuándé and others were defeated and fled.
Wei appointed the man from Yǐngchuān, Yǔ Lóng, as Administrator of Yǐngchuān,
and garrisoned Xǔchāng.
Máo Dézǔ led troops out and engaged Gōngsūn Biǎo in a major battle,
from morning until evening,
killing several hundred Wei soldiers.
Meanwhile, Xī Jīn returned from Xǔchāng,
and together they attacked Dézǔ,
defeating him severely,
with over a thousand armored soldiers lost,
and he again shut himself within the city to defend.
The Wei ruler also sent over ten thousand men to cross the river from Báishā,
and encamped south of Púyáng.
Púyáng is opposite Dùnqiū's territory,
Báishā should be within the boundaries of present-day Chánzhōu.
The court discussion held that Xiàngchéng was not far from Wei,
and not something a light force could resist,
so they ordered Liú Cuì to recall Gāo Dàojǐn back to Shòuyáng;
if Shěn Shūlí had already advanced,
he should also be recalled.
Cuì memorialized:
"The barbarians are attacking Hǔláo,
and have not yet turned southward.
If we hastily withdraw our troops and abandon Xiàngchéng,
then the various commanderies west of the Huái will have nothing to rely on;
Shěn Shūlí has already stationed at Féikǒu,
Féikǒu,
is the mouth where the Féi River enters the Huái.
At that time, Lǐ Yuándé led two hundred scattered soldiers to Xiàng,
Liú Cuì had him assist Gāo Dàojǐn in defending the garrison,
and requested pardon for his crime of fleeing defeat,
which the court discussion approved.
On Yǐsì,
the Wei ruler hunted at Hánlíng Mountain,
Hánlíng Mountain is in Yè County of Wèi Commandery.
He reached Fāngtóu.
Earlier,
when Máo Dézǔ was in the north,
Máo Dézǔ was originally from Xíngyáng.
Before Emperor Wǔ captured Guān and Luò,
Dézǔ came from the north to submit.
Biǎo was resourceful and strategic,
which troubled Dézǔ,
so he established communication and exchanged messages with him;
secretly sending someone to persuade Xī Jīn,
saying that Biǎo was conspiring with him.
Every time he replied to Biǎo's letters,
he made many alterations;
this was the same stratagem Cáo Cāo used to sow discord between Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo.
Persuade,
read as shuì.
Alter,
read as zhì.
Jīn became suspicious,
and reported it to the Wei ruler.
Previously,
Biǎo and the Grand Astrologer Wáng Liàng had served together in the same camp when young,
and Biǎo enjoyed belittling and insulting Liàng;
Liàng memorialized
"Biǎo stationed his army east of Hǔláo,
not in an advantageous position,
thus preventing the bandits from being eliminated promptly."
The Wei ruler had always been fond of numerology,
and believed it,
accumulating previous grievances,
he had someone go to Biǎo's tent at night and strangle him to death.
On Yǐmǎo,
the Wei ruler crossed from Língchāng Ford,
Língchāng Ford,
is the ancient Yánjīn;
when Shí Lè attacked Liú Yào,
he passed through here,
and because the river ice provided divine assistance,
it was renamed Língchāng Ford.
Shūsūn Jiàn led thirty thousand cavalry to press upon Dōngyáng City,
where the civil and military officials inside the city numbered only fifteen hundred,
Zhú Kuí and Yuán Miáo exerted all efforts to defend firmly,
occasionally sending surprise troops to attack the Wei forces,
and defeated them.
The Wei infantry and cavalry formed a battle array over ten lǐ around the city,
and extensively prepared siege equipment;
Kuí constructed four layers of moats,
the Wei men filled three of them,
and used catapult carts to attack the city,
Kuí sent men out through tunnels,
using large hemp ropes to pull and break them.
The Wei men again built a long encirclement,
and attacked even more fiercely.
As time passed,
the city walls gradually crumbled and deteriorated,
many soldiers died or were wounded,
the remaining troops were exhausted,
and the city was about to fall day or night.
Tán Dàojì arrived at Péngchéng,
and because both Sī and Qīng provinces were in crisis,
and the troops under his command were few,
insufficient to divide and send to both;
Qīngzhōu was closer,
and Zhú Kuí's troops were weak,
so he and Wáng Zhòngdé hastened together to rescue it first.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Liú Cuì sent Lǐ Yuándé to attack Xǔchāng,
and beheaded Yǔ Lóng.
Yuándé then remained to pacify and comfort,
and also submitted taxes and grain.
The Wei ruler reached Méngjīn.
Yú Lìdī built a pontoon bridge at Yěbǎn Ford.
Guō Yuánshēng's Account of Campaigns says: Jiàntǔ,
is present-day Yěbǎn City.
The Commentary on the Water Classic says: the old city of Héyáng County is northwest of Yěbǎn.
The Wei Geographical Records say: Yěbǎn City,
formerly called Hànzǔ Crossing,
the city is strategically secure and solid,
facing Méngjīn to the south,
forty-two lǐ northwest of Luòyáng.
Méng,
read as Mèng.
On Yǐchǒu,
the Wei ruler led his troops north across the river,
heading west toward Hénèi.
É Qīng, Zhōu Jī, and Lǘ Dàféi campaigned through the territory to Húlù,
where the people of Gāopíng gathered and shot at them.
Qīng and others attacked and destroyed all the counties of Gāopíng,
exterminating several thousand families,
and capturing over ten thousand people;
the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Zhèng Shùnzhī, garrisoned Húlù,
but dared not come out due to having few troops.
The Wei ruler also sent the Governor of Bìngzhōu, Yīlóu Bá, to assist Xī Jīn in attacking Hǔláo;
Yīlóu,
is a barbarian compound surname.
Lóu,
is the same as Lóu.
They killed quite a few Wei soldiers,
but their own generals and soldiers gradually diminished.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on Dīngmǎo,
the Wei ruler went to Chénggāo,
cutting off the water-drawing route from the Yellow River at Hǔláo.
The Northern History states: Hǔláo lacked water,
and within the city, ropes were suspended to draw water from the river.
The Wei ruler ordered ships to be linked together and covered with fényūn (siege shelters),
cutting off their water-drawing route.
He personally supervised the troops in attacking the city,
but ultimately could not capture it,
so he went to Luòyáng to view the Stone Classics.
The Stone Classics
were those inscribed by Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn,
with detailed annotations found in the fifty-seventh scroll, under the fourth year of the Xīpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn.
Shūsūn Jiàn attacked Dōngyáng,
breaching its northern wall for about thirty paces;
Diāo Yōng requested to quickly enter,
but Jiàn did not permit it,
and thus they did not succeed.
When they heard that Tán Dàojì and others were about to arrive,
Yōng again said to Jiàn:
"The enemy fears the sudden cavalry of our government troops,
so they link carts with chains to form a box formation.
A box formation
is a square formation.
Chén
is read as zhèn (formation).
The terrain is narrow and confined everywhere,
and carts cannot travel side by side.
I, Yōng, request to lead the five thousand recruited troops I have to occupy strategic positions and intercept them;
defeating them is certain."
At that time, the weather was hot,
and many in the Wei army fell ill.
Jiàn said:
"More than half of the soldiers are ill.
If we continue to hold out without rest,
the troops will die off on their own;
what need is there to fight again!
Now, to return with the entire army intact
is the best strategy."
On Jǐsì,
Dàojì stationed his army at Línqú.
On Rénshēn,
Jiàn and others burned their camp and equipment and fled;
Dàojì reached Dōngyáng,
but his provisions were exhausted,
and he could not pursue.
Zhú Kuí, because the walls of Dōngyáng were damaged
and could not be defended,
moved the garrison to Bùjī City.
Bùjī County
belonged to Lángyá Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to Dōnglái Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and to Chángguǎng Commandery in the Jìn.
Rú Chún said: Jī
is pronounced jī.
Xián said: The old city of Bùjī
is located southwest of Jímò County in modern Láizhōu.
Shūsūn Jiàn went from Dōngyáng to Huátái,
and Dàojì dispatched Wáng Zhòngdé separately toward Yǐnmǎo.
Dàojì halted his army at Húlù,
and before Zhòngdé reached Yǐnmǎo,
hearing that the Wei troops were already far away,
he returned to join Dàojì.
Diāo Yōng then stayed to garrison Yǐnmǎo,
gathering over five thousand households from the people of Qiáo, Liáng, Péng, and Pèi,
and established twenty-seven camps to lead them.
12 The Man chieftain Méi Ān led several dozen tribal leaders to present tribute to Wei.
Initially,
these Man peoples originally lived between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
but later their tribes multiplied and spread,
distributed across several provinces,
connecting to Shòuchūn in the east,
linking to Bā and Shǔ in the west,
and bordering Rǔ and Yǐng in the north,
often found there.
During the Wei period, they were not much of a problem;
but by the Jìn,
they gradually became more prosperous,
and slowly turned to banditry and violence.
When Liú and Shí threw the Central Plains into chaos,
these Man peoples had nothing to fear,
and gradually moved north again,
so that south of Yīquē,
they filled the mountains and valleys.
According to history,
these Man peoples are descendants of Pánhù.
