he invited Tán Dàojì to stay together,
Huì was so agitated he could not sleep,
but Dàojì fell asleep as soon as he lay down,
and Huì admired him for this.
He admired that he could face major events without changing his usual demeanor.
At that time, the emperor set up market stalls in the Huálín Garden,
personally selling goods;
he also enjoyed boating with his attendants,
and in the evening,
he roamed the Tiānyuān Pond,
and slept on the dragon boat.
Early in the morning on Yǐyǒu,
Dàojì led troops at the front,
Xiànzhī and others followed behind,
entering through the Yúnlóng Gate;
Āntài and others had previously warned the palace guards,
so no one resisted.
The emperor had not yet risen,
soldiers entered and killed two attendants,
injured the emperor's finger,
supported him out of the eastern pavilion,
seized the imperial seal and ribbons,
the assembled ministers bowed in farewell,
and escorted him to the former Crown Prince's Palace.
Palace Attendant Chéng Dàohuì advised Xiànzhī and others to establish the emperor's younger brother, Yìgōng, Governor of Nányùzhōu.
Xiànzhī and others believed that Yìlóng, Prince of Yídū, had long enjoyed a good reputation,
and there were many auspicious signs.
At the beginning of the Jǐngpíng era,
a black dragon appeared in the west,
followed by five-colored clouds.
In the second year,
purple clouds appeared over the Jiānglíng city walls,
and those who observed the qi believed it to be an omen of an emperor,
which should come from the west.
Also, from west of Jiānglíng to Shàngmíng,
east to Jiāngjīn,
there were ninety-nine islets.
A Chǔ proverb said:
"When the islets reach one hundred,
a king will emerge."
At that time, suddenly an islet naturally formed,
created by the swirling of the river currents.
All were seen as responses to the dragon's flight above.
They enumerated the emperor's faults and evils,
deposed him as Prince of Yíngyáng,
and had Yìlóng, Prince of Yídū, succeed to the great lineage,
pardoning crimes punishable by death and below.
They also proclaimed an order from the Empress Dowager,
returning the imperial seal and ribbons;
and also deposed the empress as Princess of Yíngyáng,
and moved the Prince of Yíngyáng to Wú.
They sent Tán Dàojì to guard the court hall.
The prince arrived in Wú,
staying at the Jīnchāng Pavilion;
in the sixth month,
on Guǐchǒu,
Xiànzhī and others sent Xíng Āntài to assassinate him.
The prince was very strong,
and broke out through the Chāng Gate.
The Jīnchāng Pavilion was inside the Chāng Gate.
Sūn Quán's records note: The Chāng Gate,
the western outer gate of Wú,
was built by Fūchāi;
because it connected to the heavenly gate Chānghé,
it was thus named.
Later, Lord Chūnshēn changed it to Chāng Gate.
The Jīnchāng Pavilion,
because it was inside the western gate,
was called Jīnchāng.
Péi Zǐyě commented: In ancient times, when a ruler raised his sons,
as soon as they could speak, tutors were appointed to teach them proper speech,
and as soon as they could walk, masters were appointed to instruct them in ritual.
The instruction and guidance in the Sòng dynasty
were vastly different from this.
At home, they were entrusted to servants and concubines;
outside, they were kept close to runners and attendants.
Crown Princes and Princes
had commanders
and attendants.
These two positions
were both filled by lowly officials.
*Zuǒzhuàn*: Shēn Wúyǔ said: "Officers serve the lowly officials,
servants serve the runners."
The methods taught to them
and the guidance on what is good and bad
all came from these people.
Their words did not touch upon ritual and righteousness;
their knowledge did not extend to ancient and modern affairs.
The cautious and strict ones could only encourage them to be stingy;
the wild and foolish ones might lead them into wickedness and evil.
Although there were tutors and masters,
they were mostly elderly senior officials;
although there were companions and literary scholars,
they were mostly young men from wealthy and noble families.
They merely occupied their positions
and did not associate with the princes.
The kings established one literary scholar, one tutor, and one companion each,
a system from the Jìn dynasty.
According to the rites,
at fifty, one is called 'ài' (venerable),
and can serve in official government;
at sixty, one is called 'qí' (aged),
and gives directions.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: 'Ài' means
reaching the age of fifty,
when one's vitality and strength have already declined,
and one's hair has turned as white as mugwort.
Hè Yáng said: 'Qí' means
reaching,
reaching the state of old age.
Shào (young),
is pronounced as in the *Shījīng*.
The Chief Administrators handled affairs,
proclaiming and transmitting orders;
'handling affairs'
means administering the affairs of the commandery or province.
They often acted arbitrarily and willfully,
secretly wielding power and authority.
The *History of the Southern Dynasties* says: According to precedent,
when discussing matters within the jurisdiction of a commandery or province,
a memorandum was first written stating the matter under discussion;
afterwards, it was written
"Respectfully submitted,"
and below the date, it was written
"Submitted by such-and-such an official."
Therefore, commanderies and provinces established the position of Diǎnqiān to oversee this.
Originally a fifth-rank clerk,
it was changed to a scholar-official position at the beginning of the Sòng.
By the end of the Sòng,
many young and juvenile princes were appointed as regional governors.
The rulers of the time had their close attendants serve as Diǎnqiān,
and their power and responsibilities thus became heavy.
The succeeding rulers were young and immature,
and successive generations produced treacherous and perverse individuals.
Although evil creatures and vile types
naturally emerged,
habit then became the norm,
and its influence spread far.
Descending to Tàizōng,
he abandoned the entire empire,
which was also due to his intimacy with such people.
Alas!
Those who possess states and families,
let them take this as a warning!
Péi Zǐyě exhaustively discussed the calamity of the Sòng dynasty's loss of the state.
The *Comprehensive Mirror* records it here
to make those who possess states and families cautious from the beginning.
7 Fù Liàng led the officials of the mobile secretariat with the imperial carriage to welcome the Prince of Yídū at Jiānglíng.
The Minister of Sacrifices, Cài Kuò
(After the Jìn crossed the river,
the position of Minister of Sacrifices was first established.
It often shared duties with the Vice Director of the Right,
was not permanently established,
and was filled by the Vice Director of the Right acting concurrently;
if the Vice Director of the Right was vacant,
then the Minister of Sacrifices acted in his place.)
fell ill and was unable to proceed;
Fù Liàng bid him farewell.
Cài Kuò said:
"The Prince of Yíngyáng is in Wú.
You should provide him with generous support.
If an unfortunate event occurs,
you gentlemen will bear the name of regicides.
Wishing to establish yourselves in the world,
will it be possible?"
At that time, Fù Liàng had already conspired with Xú Xiànzhī to harm the Prince of Yíngyáng.
He then sent a fast messenger to stop it,
but it was too late.
Xú Xiànzhī was furious and said:
"Having made plans together with others,
how can you turn around and immediately shift the blame onto others?"
'Turn around'
is like what people today say 'in the blink of an eye';
'bèi' (turn)
is pronounced as usual.
*Textual Analysis*: The Basic Annals of the *History of the Southern Dynasties* of the Sòng,
after stating that in February, Yìzhēn was deposed and exiled to Xīn'ān,
immediately says
"The regents sent an envoy to execute Yìzhēn at Xīn'ān."
The Biography of Sòng Yìzhēn says:
"On the guǐwèi day of the sixth month,
Xú Xiànzhī and others sent an envoy to kill Yìzhēn at the place of exile."
The Biography of Xú Xiànzhī also says:
"After deposing the Emperor,
he killed Yìzhēn at Xīn'ān,
and killed the Emperor at Wú County."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the sixth month began on gēngyín,
there was no guǐwèi day,
it was probably guǐchǒu.
Xú Xiànzhī, because the region of Jīngzhōu was important,
feared that when the Prince of Yídū arrived,
he might appoint other people,
so he urgently, by order of the Recorder, appointed the General of the Central Army, Xiè Huì, as Acting Commander-in-Chief of the seven provinces including Jīng and Xiāng and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
'Order of the Recorder'
means orders issued by the Recorder of the Secretariat himself.
Elite troops and veteran generals
were all assigned to him.
Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, and Xiè Huì made such plans for their own sake,
yet it did not save them from the punishment of deposition and regicide.
Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng acted with utmost impartiality and sincere loyalty,
yet the records in the *Chūnqiū* differ from the *Shūjīng*,
probably because they did not envy Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng, who could only protect themselves but not their clans.
This was a great upheaval of heaven and earth,
truly a difficult position for ministers to be in.
General,
is pronounced as 'jiàng'.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the mobile secretariat reached Jiānglíng.
They erected a temporary gate south of the city,
inscribed with the words
"Gate of the Grand Marshal."
Fù Liàng led the officials to the gate to present a memorial,
offering the imperial seal and ribbons,
with very elaborate ceremonial objects.
The Prince of Yídū was eighteen years old at the time.
He issued an instruction saying:
"Unworthily, lacking in virtue,
I have mistakenly received the great mandate.
Looking at myself, I am fearful and trembling.
How can I bear this!
I shall temporarily return to the court,
to pay my respects at the imperial tombs,
and also to express my thoughts to the worthy and talented.
I hope you will understand my heart,
and do not waste words in refusal."
The assistants and clerks of the commandery and province all addressed him as 'subject',
and requested to inscribe placards on the various gates,
exactly following the palace and capital protocol;
the Prince did not allow any of it.
He instructed the administrators of the province, commandery, and principality to pardon those under their jurisdiction who were currently punished,
and to forgive outstanding debts.
Province,
refers to Jīngzhōu;
Commandery,
refers to the headquarters of the Commander-in-Chief;
Principality,
refers to the Principality of Yídū;
Administrators,
refers to the senior assistants and subordinate officials.
'Xiàn' (currently)
is pronounced as 'xiàn'.
'Bū' (outstanding)
means owing,
being in debt.
'Zé' (debt)
is pronounced as usual,
also pronounced 'zhài'.
*History of the Hàn*, Annals of Gāozǔ: "The two families broke the tallies and abandoned the debts,"
with no pronunciation given.
Biography of the Prince of Huáiyáng: "Zhāng Bó was in debt,"
pronounced 'zhài'.
When the generals and aides heard of the deaths of the Prince of Yíngyáng and the Prince of Lúlín,
they all became suspicious,
and urged the Prince not to proceed eastward.
Simǎ Wáng Huá said:
"The late Emperor had great achievements under heaven,
and was revered throughout the land.
Although the successor ruler lacked proper governance,
the people's expectations have not changed.
Xú Xiànzhī is a man of mediocre talent from a humble background,
and Fù Liàng is a commoner scholar;
it is clear they do not harbor the ambitions of Jìn Xuāndì or the Great General Wáng.
The Great General Wáng
refers to Wáng Dūn.
They would not dare to suddenly turn against virtue.
They feared the Prince of Lúlín's stern and decisive nature,
and believed he would not tolerate them in the future.
Knowing Your Highness's broad-mindedness, wisdom, benevolence, and kindness,
which is known far and wide,
and having welcomed you out of proper order,
they hope to demonstrate their virtue;
they hope to establish their merit through supporting the new policy.
It is almost certainly not the case.
Moreover,
Xiànzhī and the other four,
who share equal merit and rank,
who among them would be willing to yield to the others?
The five men
refer to Xú Xiànzhī, Fù Liàng, Xiè Huì, Tán Dàojì, and Wáng Hóng.
It is bound to be impossible.
If the deposed ruler remained alive,
they feared they would suffer calamity in the future,
hence they carried out this killing.
It is likely due to excessive greed for life,
how would they dare to suddenly harbor rebellious intentions!
They merely wish to grasp power to secure themselves,
and rely on the young sovereign for support.
Your Highness should only press forward with determination,
to fulfill the hearts of heaven and men."
The Prince said:
"Do you wish to become another Sòng Chāng?"
Chief Clerk Wáng Tánshǒu and Southern Barbarian Commandant Dào Yànzhī both urged the Prince to proceed.
The genealogy of surnames states: The Dào clan originated from the Gāoyáng lineage.
They are descendants of Qū Dào, the Lingyǐn of Chǔ.
During the Later Hàn, there was Dōngpíng Prefect Dào Zhì.
Tán,
is pronounced as túhán.
The Prince then said:
"The various lords received the late Emperor's behest,
and cannot betray righteousness.
Moreover, the diligent ministers and veteran generals,
are abundant both inside and outside.
Now our military strength is sufficient to control affairs,
what is there to doubt!"
He then ordered Wáng Huá to take overall responsibility for rear affairs,
and remain to guard Jīngzhōu.
The Prince wanted to send Dào Yànzhī to lead troops as the vanguard.
Yànzhī said:
"If we are certain they are not rebellious,
certain,
means decisively knowing.
To lead troops,
is pronounced jíliàng.
If there are concerns,
this army is not sufficient to rely on,
and would only create the beginnings of suspicion and discord,
which is not the way to fulfill the expectations of far and near."
Yànzhī's words truly accord with great principle,
and he also knew his own talent was insufficient to control Tán Dàojì.
He then sent Yànzhī to temporarily guard Xiāngyáng.
On the jiǎxū day,
the Prince departed from Jiānglíng,
summoned Fù Liàng for an audience,
wept loudly,
moving all those around him to sorrow.
Afterwards, he inquired about the details of Yìzhēn and the young Emperor's deaths and deposal,
and cried mournfully,
so that none of the attendants could look up.
Liàng sweated profusely, drenching his back,
and could not reply.
He then confided his innermost thoughts to Dào Yànzhī, Wáng Huá, and others,
deeply seeking to win them over.
The Prince had the civil and military officials of his administration guard him with strict military precautions,
and the hundred officials sent by the court were not allowed to approach the troops.
Central Army Cānjūn Zhū Róngzǐ held a sword and stayed outside the door of the Prince's cabin on the boat,
not loosening his belt for several decades.
This was to guard against unexpected events.
To stay,
is pronounced chānglǚ.
8. The Wèi sovereign returned to the palace.
9. Qín King Chìpán sent Crown Prince Mùmò to lead General Zhēngběi Mù Yìgān and others with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry out of Diāoqú Valley,
attacking Héxī's Báicǎo Ridge and Línsōng Commandery,
and defeated them both.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Southeast of Xīpíng's Xiāngǔ Pass is Báicǎo Ridge.
To lead,
is read as shuài.
Cavalry,
is pronounced qíjì.
10. In the eighth month,
on the bǐngshēn day,
the Prince of Yídū arrived at Jiànkāng.
The ministers welcomed and bowed to him at Xīntíng.
Xú Xiànzhī asked Fù Liàng:
"To whom can the Prince be compared?"
Liàng said:
"He is above Jìn Wéngōng and Jǐnggōng."
Xiànzhī said:
"He will surely understand my loyal heart."
Liàng said:
"Not necessarily."
Liàng already knew he could not escape.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the Prince paid respects at Chūníng Tomb,
then returned,
and stopped at Zhōngtáng.
Jìn Xiàowǔ, because the Imperial Academy was south of the Qínhuái River,
far from the palace city,
temporarily used Zhōngtáng as the Imperial Academy,
and personally performed the Shìdiàn ceremony to the former sages.
Thus Zhōngtáng was also north of the Qínhuái River,
but outside the palace city.
The hundred officials presented the imperial seal and ribbons.
Ribbons,
pronounced shòu.
He then accepted them,
and ascended the imperial throne at Zhōngtáng.
With the full imperial procession, he entered the palace,
ascended the main hall of Tàijí Palace,
issued a general pardon,
changed the era name,
and granted two ranks of promotion to all civil and military officials.
On the wùxū day,
he paid respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
An edict was issued to restore the Prince of Lúlín's former title,
and to welcome his coffin, along with Sūn Xiūhuá and Xiè, back to Jiànkāng.
Sūn Xiūhuá
was Yìzhēn's mother;
Xiè
was Yìzhēn's consort.
The History of the Southern Dynasties states: Jìn Wǔdì adopted the systems of Hàn and Wèi,
establishing Shūfēi, Shūyuàn, Shūyí, Xiūhuá, Xiūróng, Xiūyí, Jiéyú, Rónghuá, and Chōnghuá,
these being the Nine Concubines,
with ranks equivalent to the Nine Ministers.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: Guìpín
was established by Wèi Wéndì;
Fūrén,
was established by Wèi Wǔ when he first founded the state of Wèi;
Guìrén,
was established by Hàn Guāngwǔ;
in Jìn, these became the Three Ladies,
with ranks equivalent to the Three Dukes.
Shūfēi,
was established by Wèi Míngdì;
Shūyuàn,
was established by Wèi Wéndì;
Shūyí and Xiūhuá,
were established by Jìn Wǔdì;
Xiūróng,
was established by Wèi Wéndì;
Xiūyí,
was established by Wèi Míngdì;
Jiéyú and Rónghuá,
are old titles from the Former Hàn;
Chōnghuá,
was established by Jìn Wǔdì;
Měirén,
was established by Hàn Guāngwǔ.
On the gēngzǐ day,
Acting Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiè Huì was made substantive.
Huì, about to depart,
bid farewell to Cài Kuò,
dismissed others and asked:
"Can I avoid disaster?"
Kuò said:
"You received the late Emperor's final command,
entrusted with the state's responsibility,
deposing the foolish and establishing the wise,
was righteous and not improper.
But having killed the two elder brothers and then serving as their subject,
wielding awe-inspiring power that shakes the sovereign,
holding a crucial position upstream,
judging from ancient to present times,
avoiding disaster is difficult."
Cài Kuò and his son were known for their uprightness in the Sòng court.
Observing his outspokenness without avoidance or compromise,
it seemed insufficient to preserve his life;
yet he ultimately maintained his life and reputation,
why?
Because his usual conduct had already gained people's trust,
and when discussing matters, he was not ambiguous,
which also allowed him to act with integrity.
As for the one who asked,
trembling with concern over advantages and disadvantages,
seeking a decision,
then hearing it surely resonated in his heart,
so how could he dare to consider it taboo!
After departing,
he looked back at Shítóu City and joyfully said:
"Now I have escaped!"
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Xú Xiànzhī was promoted to the rank of Minister over the Masses,
Wáng Hóng was promoted to the rank of Minister of Works,
Fù Liàng was granted the additional honor of Kāifǔ Yìtóng Sānsī,
Xiè Huì was advanced in title to General of the Guards,
and Tán Dàojì was advanced in title to General Who Conquers the North.
Xiè Huì was advanced in title from his previous position of General of the Central Army,
and Tán Dàojì was advanced in title from his previous position of General Who Guards the North.
The relevant officials submitted a proposal that the imperial carriage, following precedent, proceed to the Huálín Garden to hear legal cases.
An imperial edict stated:
"I am not yet fully versed in governance and punishments;
it may be done as before,
with the Two Dukes conducting the interrogations."
The Two Dukes
refer to Xú Xiànzhī and Wáng Hóng.
The Emperor appointed Wáng Tánshǒu and Wáng Huá as Palace Attendants,
with Tánshǒu concurrently holding the post of General of the Right Guard,
and Huá concurrently holding the post of General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry.
Zhū Róngzǐ was appointed General of the Right Army.
Emperor Míng of Wèi had a General of the Left Army;
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Generals of the Vanguard Army and the Right Army,
and also established a General of the Rear Army,
making the Four Armies.
The General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry and the General of Agile Cavalry,
were both miscellaneous general titles of the Hàn dynasty,
and the Wèi dynasty established them as the Central Army.
By the Jìn dynasty,

the positions of General of the Central Army, General Who Protects the Army, Generals of the Left and Right Guards, General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry, and General of Agile Cavalry formed the Six Armies.
For 驍 (xiāo),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 堅堯 (jiān yáo).
For 騎 (jì),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 奇寄 (qí jì).
On the 11th day, Jiǎchén,
the Emperor posthumously honored his mother, Consort Hú, as Empress Zhāng.
He enfeoffed his imperial younger brother, Yìgōng, as Prince of Jiāngxià,
Yìxuān as Prince of Jìnglíng,
and Yìjì as Prince of Héngyáng;
and further appointed Yìxuān as General of the Left,
to garrison Shítóu.
Xú Xiànzhī and others wished to immediately appoint Dào Yànzhī as Governor of Yōng Province,
but the Emperor did not permit it;
instead, he summoned Yànzhī to serve as General of the Central Army,
entrusting him with military affairs.
Yànzhī traveled south from Xiāngyáng,
and by the time he arrived, Xiè Huì had already taken up his post,
and Huì was concerned that Yànzhī might not be on his side.
When Yànzhī reached Yángkǒu,
he went on foot to Jiānglíng,
where he expressed his sincere loyalty in great detail;
Huì also warmly sought to establish ties with him.
Yànzhī left horses, sharp swords, and famous blades for Huì,
and from then on, Huì felt greatly at ease.
The Róurán Kèhán, Héshēnggài, hearing that Emperor Tàizōng of Wèi had died,
led 60,000 cavalry into Yúnzhōng,
killing and plundering officials and commoners,
and attacking and capturing the Shènglè Palace.
The Wèi ancestor, Shíyìjiān, first resided in the Shènglè Palace in Yúnzhōng,
and built Shènglè City eight lǐ south of the old city.
For 紇 (hé),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 戶骨 (hù gǔ).
For 可 (kě),
it follows the entering tone of 刊 (kān).
For 汗 (hán),
the pronunciation is hán.
For 將 (jiàng),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 即亮 (jí liàng).
For 騎 (jì),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 奇寄 (qí jì).
For 樂 (lè),
the pronunciation is luò.
After three days and two nights, they reached Yúnzhōng.
Héshēnggài led his cavalry to surround the Wèi sovereign in over fifty layers,
with the cavalry pressing close to the heads of his horses,
forming a continuous wall;
the officers and soldiers were greatly frightened,
but the Wèi sovereign's countenance remained as usual,
and only then did the multitude's feelings become calm.
Héshēnggài appointed his younger brother's son, Yúzhìjīn, as a senior general,
but the Wèi men shot and killed him;
Héshēnggài became afraid,
and fled.
The Imperial Secretary, Liú Jié, said to the Wèi sovereign:
"Dàtán relies on the size of his forces,
and will certainly come again.
I request that we wait until the harvest is completed,
then mobilize a large army in two divisions,
advancing simultaneously from east and west to attack him."
The Wèi sovereign agreed.
In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lady Yuán was established as Empress;
she was the great-granddaughter of Yuán Dān.
Yuán Dān appears in the 95th scroll, in the first year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng of Jìn.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Tǔyùhún King Wēi, Āchái, died.
Āchái had twenty sons.
When he fell ill,
he summoned his sons and younger brothers and said to them:
"The Former Lord, the Chariot and Horse General,
for the sake of the great enterprise,
passed over his own son, Shíqián, and entrusted the state to me.
How dare I act selfishly for Wěidài and forget the Former Lord's intention!
The Former Lord
refers to Shùluògān.
Shùluògān proclaimed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and handed the state over to Āchái,
as seen in the 118th scroll, in the 13th year of the Yìxī era of Emperor Ān of Jìn.
For 緯 (wěi),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 于貴 (yú guì).
You all should serve Mùguī as your lord."
Wěidài was
Āchái's eldest son;
Mùguī was
Āchái's maternal younger brother, the son of his uncle, Wūgētí.
When Wūgētí was established,
he took Shùluògān's mother as his wife,
and they had two sons,
Mùguī and Mùlìyán.
For 緯 (wěi),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 于貴 (yú guì).
For 璝 (guī),
the pronunciation is according to the fǎnqiè 姑回 (gū huí).
For 提 (tí),
it should be
堤 (dī).
Āchái also ordered each of his sons to present one arrow,
took one arrow and gave it to his younger brother Mùlìyán, telling him to break it.
Mùlìyán broke it.
He then took nineteen arrows and told him to break them,
but Mùlìyán could not break them.
Āchái then instructed them, saying:
"Do you understand?
A single arrow is easily broken,
but many together are hard to destroy.
You must join forces and be of one mind,
and only then can you protect the state and bring peace to the family."
Having spoken these words, he died.
Mùguī also had talent and strategy,
and he settled the displaced people from Qín and Liáng, as well as various Dī and Qiāng tribes, amounting to five or six hundred settlements,

"The Song people are making extensive preparations,
and are about to invade.
We request 30,000 troops
to strike them preemptively before they launch their attack,

They also requested the execution of all refugees from Hebei who were within the border regions to eliminate potential guides for the enemy.
The Wei sovereign ordered his ministers to deliberate on the matter,

"It is not feasible.
The southern regions are low-lying and damp.
By the nature of heaven and earth,
the northwest is high while the southeast is low,
hence the lands of the southeast are low-lying, damp, and swampy.
The rainy season is currently at its peak,
vegetation is dense and overgrown,
the air is stifling and humid,
and diseases are prone to arise,
making it unsuitable for military campaigns.
Moreover, since they are heavily fortified,
their city defenses are certainly robust.
If we station troops for a prolonged siege,

if we divide our forces to plunder in all directions,
our strength will be scattered and insufficient,
leaving us unable to respond to the enemy.
Attacking them now
shows no advantage.
If they indeed advance northward,
we should wait until they are weary and exhausted,
when the autumn weather is cool and the horses are sturdy,
and then rely on the enemy's resources for provisions,
advancing slowly to attack them.
This is a foolproof strategy.
The court ministers and northwestern garrison commanders
who followed Your Majesty on campaigns,
pacified Hèlián in the west,
and achieved great success,
have grown envious upon hearing of this.
They also wish to raid the south to seize wealth and resources.
They are all pursuing personal gains,
creating troubles for the state—this must not be heeded."
The Wei sovereign then halted the plan.
The generals submitted another memorial:
"The southern invaders have arrived,
and our troops are few.
We request the selection of elite troops from south of Yōuzhōu to reinforce our defenses,
and the construction of ships along the Zhāng River to prepare for resistance."
They intended to build ships along the Zhāng River
and deploy them at river crossings to defend against Song.
They also proposed appointing Sīmǎ Chǔzhī, Lǚ Guǐ, and Hán Yánzhī as commanders
to recruit and lure southerners.
Cuī Hào said:
"This is not a sound strategy.
Chǔzhī and others are precisely whom they fear and detest.
If they now hear that our state is mobilizing all elite troops from south of Yōuzhōu,
building numerous ships and vessels,
and supplementing them with light cavalry,
they will assume our state intends to restore the Sīmǎ clan
and exterminate the Liú lineage.
They will certainly be thrown into nationwide panic,
fearing annihilation,
and will mobilize all their elite forces,
uniting their hearts and exerting their utmost strength
to fight to the death.
In that case, our southern border generals will be unable to withstand them.
Now, the ministers wish to repel the enemy through might,
but this will only hasten their advance.
This is what is meant by 'raising a false alarm and inviting real disaster.'
Therefore, with individuals like Chǔzhī,
if they go, the enemy will come;
if they stop, the enemy will cease—such is the inevitable dynamic.
Moreover, Chǔzhī and others possess only petty talents for seizing minor advantages.
They can only gather frivolous and unscrupulous individuals but cannot achieve great accomplishments,
merely plunging the state into endless warfare and calamity.
In the past, Lǚ Guǐ advised Yáo Xīng to seize Jīngzhōu,
but upon arrival, they were defeated and scattered.
In the end, it brought disaster upon Yáo Hóng.
This is the proven outcome."
The Wei sovereign did not find this convincing.
Cuī Hào then elaborated on celestial timing,
arguing that raising troops in the south would surely be unfavorable.
He said:
"First, baleful qi currently resides in Yángzhōu.
Second, Gēngwǔ represents self-punishment—those who strike first will suffer harm.
Third, the constellation is aligned with Dǒu and Niú.
Fourth, Yínghuò (Mars) is concealed in Yì and Zhěn, presaging turmoil and loss.
Fifth, Tàibái (Venus) has not yet appeared—those who advance troops will face defeat.
Last year, on the first day of the eleventh month,
a solar eclipse occurred in the division of Xīngjì,
with the constellation aligned with Dǒu and Niú.
Yínghuò is the star of punishment;
the state corresponding to its residing constellation suffers calamity,
including death, loss, invasion, and turmoil.
Yì and Zhěn correspond to the division of Chǔ,
belonging to Jīngzhōu.
Tàibái not appearing
is unfavorable for advancing troops.
Tàibái is an omen of warfare.
One should first cultivate human affairs,
then exhaust geographical advantages,
and finally observe celestial timing—thus every action will be foolproof.
Now, Liú Yìlóng's state is newly established;
human affairs are not yet harmonious.
Disasters and anomalies have repeatedly appeared;
celestial timing is unpropitious.
Rivers are drying up, hindering naval travel;
geographical advantages are not fully utilized.
Not one of these three conditions is met,
yet Yìlóng proceeds with his campaign—
he will undoubtedly face defeat."
The Wei sovereign could not defy the majority opinion,
and thus issued an edict for the three provinces of Jì, Dìng, and Xiàng to construct 3,000 ships.

to attack Dào Yànzhī.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Yànzhī sent his deputy general, Yáosǒngfū of Wúxīng, to cross the river and attack Yěbǎn,
engaging Xié in battle;
Sǒngfū's troops were defeated,
with many dead.
On the Wùyín day,
the Wei ruler sent the Grand General Who Conquers the West, Chángsūn Dàoshēng, to join with Prince Dàpí of Dānyáng and station troops on the river to defend against Yànzhī.
The Yān Tàizǔ fell ill and took to his bed,
this was the Yān king, Féng Bá.
He entrusted the aftermath of affairs.
In the ninth month,
his illness became severe,
and he was carried in a palanquin to the palace hall,
ordering the Crown Prince Yì to act in charge of state affairs,
to command troops and administer governance,
to prepare for any unusual events.
Madame Sòng wished to establish her own son, Shòujū,
and disliked Yì administering governance,
so she said to Yì:
"The Emperor's illness is about to recover,
why do you hastily desire to replace your father in ruling the world!"
Yì's nature was benevolent and weak,
so he returned to the Eastern Palace,
and went three times daily to inquire after the illness.
Madame Sòng forged an edict cutting off inside and outside,
only sending eunuchs to transmit inquiries,
so that Yì and all the sons and ministers could not see him,
only the Palace Attendant Hú Fú alone could come and go,
exclusively in charge of the forbidden guards.
Fú feared that Madame Sòng would succeed in her scheme,
so he spoke to the Minister Over the Masses, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Zhōngshān Duke Hóng,
Hóng and several tens of strong warriors donned armor and entered the forbidden quarters,
the night guards all scattered without fighting.
Madame Sòng ordered the eastern gate to be closed,
Hóng's household servant Kùdǒutóu was vigorous, agile, and had courageous strength,
he leapt over the gate and entered,
reaching the imperial hall,
and shot and killed one of the female attendants.
Tàizǔ, startled and fearful, passed away,
and Hóng then ascended to the position of Heavenly King,
Hóng,
styled Wéntōng,
was the younger brother of Bá.
"Heaven has sent down a calamitous misfortune,
the Great Departed has collapsed and passed away,
the Crown Prince did not attend to the illness,
the Duke of Jì did not rush to the mourning,
I suspect there is a rebellious plot,
the altars of state are in danger.
I, as a close younger brother,
jiè,
means great.
All officials who knock on the gate and enter,
will be advanced two ranks."
Bì,
means steps;
meaning to advance in rank.
Crown Prince Yì led the Eastern Palace troops out to fight but was defeated,
the troops all scattered and fled,
Hóng sent an envoy to bestow death upon Yì.
Tàizǔ had over a hundred sons,
Hóng killed them all.
He posthumously honored Tàizǔ as Emperor Wénchéng,
and buried him at the Chánggǔ Mausoleum.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
the Xià ruler sent his younger brother Wèiyǐdài to attack the Wei city of Fūchéng,
the Wei Pingxi General, Shǐpíng Duke Kuí Guī and others attacked him,
killing over ten thousand people,
and Wèiyǐdài fled.
The Xià ruler personally led several tens of thousands of men to intercept and attack Kuí Guī east of Fūchéng,
leaving his younger brother Shànggǔ Duke Shègàn and Guǎngyáng Duke Dùluògū to guard Píngliàng,
and sent an envoy to come and seek peace,
agreeing to join forces to destroy Wei,
and remotely divide Héběi: east of Héngshān to belong to Sòng,
west to belong to Xià.
The Wei ruler heard of this,
and prepared troops to attack Xià,
all his ministers said:
"Liú Yìlóng's troops are still in the middle of the river,
meaning in the middle of the river.
The former enemy may not necessarily be conquerable,
and if Yìlóng takes advantage of the emptiness to cross the river,
then we will lose Shāndōng."
This Shāndōng refers to east of Tàiháng and Héngshān,
that is, the land of Héběi.
He replied:
"Yìlóng and Hèlián Dìng remotely attract each other,
echoing each other with empty sounds,
together they spy on the great state,
Yìlóng hopes Dìng will advance,
Dìng waits for Yìlóng to go forward,
neither dares to enter first;
they are like tethered chickens,
unable to fly together,
and can do no harm.
I originally thought that when Yìlóng's army came,
they would station in the middle of the river,
and advance north in two routes,
the eastern route heading toward Jìzhōu,
the western route charging toward Yè,
if so,
then Your Majesty should personally deal with them,
and could not proceed slowly.
Now it is not so.
They have deployed troops east and west over a distance of two thousand lǐ,
at each place no more than several thousand,
their formation divided and strength weak.
Looking at it this way,
the child's true situation is revealed,
this is nothing more than wanting to fortify the river and defend themselves,
with no intention of crossing north.
Hèlián Dìng's remnant roots are easily crushed,
if we attack him he will certainly fall.
After conquering Dìng,
we can go east out of Tóngguān,
roll forward like a mat,
then our might will shake the southern extreme,
and north of the Jiāng and Huái rivers not a blade of grass will stand.
Your sagely strategy is uniquely issued,
not something we foolish ones nearby can reach,
I hope Your Majesty does not doubt."
On the Jiǎchén day,
the Wei ruler went to Tǒngwàn,
then attacked Píngliàng,
and had the Guard General Wáng Jīn guard Púbǎn.
Jīn,
was the son of Jiàn.
Wáng Jiàn assisted the Wei ruler Guī in capturing the Central Plains.
In Qín, from the first month there was no rain,
until the ninth month,
many people fled and rebelled.
In winter,
the tenth month,
they appointed Jìnglíng Prince Yìxuān as the Governor of Nánxúzhōu,
still guarding Shítóu.
Yìxuān had previously guarded Shítóu,
while Nánxúzhōu was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu,
it seems he held the governorship but still guarded Shítóu.
On the Wùwǔ day,
they established the Coinage Office,
and cast four-zhū coins.
Dào Yànzhī and Wáng Zhòngdé set up defenses along the river,
and retreated to defend Dōngpíng.
The Dōngpíng commandery at that time governed Xūchāng.
In the year of Yǐhài,
Wèi Ānxié crossed the Hé River south from Weisu Jīn,
attacking Jīnyōng.
Jīnyōng had not been maintained for a long time,
and there was no grain;
Dù Jì wanted to abandon the city and flee,
fearing punishment.
Earlier,
when Gāozǔ destroyed Qín,
he moved its bells and chimes to the south of the Jiāng,
and a great bell sank into the Luò River.
The Emperor sent Yáo Sǒngfū with fifteen hundred men to retrieve it.
Jì deceived him, saying:
"Jīnyōng City has been fully repaired,
and there is sufficient grain;
the only shortage is in manpower.
Now that the enemy cavalry has crossed south,
we should unite our forces to resist them;
once we have achieved great merit,
it will not be too late to retrieve the bell."
Sǒngfū agreed to this.
Upon arriving,
he saw that the city was indefensible,
so he withdrew,
and Jì subsequently fled south.
In Bǐngzǐ,
Ānxié captured Luòyáng,
killing over five thousand officers and soldiers.
Dù Jì returned,
reporting to the Emperor:
"I originally intended to defend to the death,
but Yáo Sǒngfū fled with the city,
leading to demoralization and collapse,
which cannot be stopped."
The Emperor was furious,
and executed Sǒngfū at Shòuyáng.
Sǒngfū was brave and strong,
unmatched by any of the lieutenants.
The armies of Wèi north of the Hé River gathered at Qīnǚ Jīn.
Qīnǚ Jīn is located on the northwest bank of Dōngpíng.
Deputy General Wáng Pánlóng was sent upstream to seize their boats,
and Dù Chāo and others attacked and beheaded him.
Ānxié, together with Long Xiáng General Lù Hóu, advanced to attack Hǔláo,
according to the Běishǐ,
"Lù Hóu"
should be
"Lù Sì".
【In the Zhāng, the Jiǎshíliùhángběn version correctly records it as
"Sì";
the Yǐshíyīhángběn version is the same.
】 Xiáng,
pronounced sī jiāng fān.
In the Xīnsì,
they captured it;
Yǐn Chōng and Jǐngyáng Prefect Qīnghé Cuī Mó surrendered to Wèi.
Late in the reign of the Qín King Mùmò, with pressure from Héxī,
he sent his ministers Wáng Kǎi and Wūnètián to request succor from Wèi,
and the people of Wèi granted him Píngliáng and Āndìng in fief.
Mùmò then set the towns and villages on fire,
destroyed treasures and artifacts,
leading fifteen thousand households,
eastward to Shàngguī.
When he reached Gāotián Valley,
which should be in the south of Nán'ān County,
he had not yet reached Shàngguī.
His plans were discovered,
and Mùmò killed them.
The Xià ruler heard that Mùmò was on his way,
and dispatched forces to oppose him.
Mùmò stayed to defend Nán'ān,
while his former territory was absorbed into Tuògǔhún.
From Yùanchuān to Xīpíng and Fúhàn, all were former lands of the Qǐfú family.
In the eighth year of Jìn Emperor Xiàowǔ's Táiyuán era,
which was the year Guǐwèi,
Qǐfú Guórén held Longxi,
and Nán'ān was also his territory.
In November,
Yǐyǒu,
the ruler of Wèi arrived at Píngliáng,
and the Xià leader Gōng Shètián and others fortified the city for defense;
the ruler of Wèi sent Hèlian Chāng to persuade them,
but they did not yield,
so he sent General Gu Bì and others to lead troops toward Āndìng.
The Xià ruler returned from Fū City to Āndìng,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry north to aid Píngliáng,
meeting with Bì,
who feigned retreat to lure him;
the Xià ruler pursued,
and the ruler of Wèi sent Gaoche to gallop and attack him,
resulting in a great defeat for the Xià forces,
with thousands beheaded.
The Xià ruler fled back,
climbing Chúngūyuán,
Chúngū County,
belonging to Běidì in the Former Hàn,
later belonged to Āndìng during the Hòu Hàn and Jìn,
containing Chúngūyuán;
in the first year of Tang Tiānbǎo,
it was renamed Lingtái County,
under Jīngzhōu.
Chún,
pronounced shūlún.
Gū,
pronounced gū.
Wèi's forces surrounded it.
On Rénchén,
enlarged Zhēngnán General Tán Dàojì received command to oversee and pacify various military affairs,
leading troops on a campaign against Wèi.
On Jiǎwǔ,
Wèi's Shòuguāng Marquess Shūsūn Jiàn and Dynasty of Rǔyīn Gōng Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng crossed the Hé River south.
Dào Yànzhī learned that Luòyáng and Hǔláo were undefended,
and the armies were in defeat,
he wished to withdraw his troops.
Palace General Yuán Hùzhī wrote to dissuade him,
advising that Zhú Língxiù should assist Zhū Xiūzhī in defending Huátái,
while he himself led the main force north,
further stating:
"In the past, people fought and battled for years,
losing men and lacking grain,
still they boldly pressed forward,
unwilling to retreat lightly.
Now Qīngzhōu is bountiful,
the Jì and Cāo rivers are flowing,
soldiers and horses are well-fed,
with undiminished might.
If you abandon Huátái,
you will lose your achievement,
is this what the court intended when they entrusted you?"
"Entrust,"
should be
"grant."
Hùzhī,
was Miáo's son.
Yuán Miáo,
was a border general.
When Emperor Wǔ marched west to Cháng'ān,
he ordered Miáo to guard the confluence of the Hé and Jì Rivers,
commonly known as Yuán Miáo City,
and three generations earned fame and recognition on the borders.
Yànzhī wanted to burn his ships and march on foot,
but Wáng Zhōngdé said:
"Luòyáng has fallen,
Hǔláo is undefended,
it is a natural development.
Now the enemy is still a thousand miles away,
Huátái still has strong forces,
if you hastily abandon ships and march south,
the troops will surely disperse.
We should navigate the ships into the Jì,
and at the mouth of Mǎ'ěr Valley,
decide the best course of action."
Mǎ'ěr Valley is Mǎ'ěr Pass.
Reaching this point, he acted extensively;
additionally, the officers and soldiers were stricken with disease,
thus he led his army from Qīng into the Jì.
The Water Classic states: the Jì River flows northeast past the west border of Shòuzhāng County in Ānmíntíng south,
where the Wén River from the northeast flows into it.
Commentary states;
the Jì River flows north,
where the Wén River flows in,
what Dài Yánzhī called Qīngkǒu.
Guō Yuánshēng writes in the Expedition Records: Qīnghé receives the floodwaters,
flowing north into the Jì,
some claim Qīng is the same as the Jì.
The Yǔ Gong states: the Jì flows northeast to join the Wén.
Now dried-up channels pour into the Great Marsh,
north of the Great Marsh is where the Qīng River meets with the Wén.
Jīng Xiāngfán said: now in Jìběi, northeast of Dōng'ē, there is an old Qīng Pavilion,
referring to the Qīng mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Thus the Jì River can be considered with the name Qīng,
combining with its clear and deep waters,
utilizing both appellations.
Therefore, the King of Yān said:
"I have heard Qí has the clear Jì and the murky Hé for defense."
It is this water.
Burning ships and abandoning armor,
they marched toward Péngchéng.
Zhú Língxiù abandoned Xūchāng,
fleeing south to Húlù,
causing great turmoil in Qīng and Yǎn.
Chángshā King Yìxīn was in Péngchéng,
where officials feared the arrival of a large Wèi army,
urging Yìxīn to abandon his stronghold and return to the capital,
but Yìxīn refused to comply.
The Wei army attacked Jìnán.
The seat of Jìnán Commandery was Lìchéng.
In the second year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
Wǔjìn County was established from parts of Dāntú and Qū'ē,
and placed under Jìnlíng Commandery.
After the southward crossing of the court,
it was placed under Nán Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Present-day towns such as Bēnniú, Qīngchéng, and Wànsuì are all within its territory.
Chéngzhī ordered the troops to stand down,
and opened the city gates.
The multitude said:
"The enemy is numerous while we are few,
how can you treat the enemy so lightly!"
Chéngzhī said:
"Now we are isolated, defending a desperate city,
the situation is already critical;
if we further show weakness,
we will surely be slaughtered.
We must only show strength and await them."
The Wei men suspected there was an ambush,
and thus withdrew.
Chéngzhī
was the father of Xiāo Dàochéng.
27 The Wei army besieged the Xià ruler for several days,
cutting off his water and grass supplies,
causing his men and horses to suffer hunger and thirst.
On Dīngyǒu,
the Xià ruler led his multitude down from Chúngūyuán.
Wei's General of the Martial Guards, Qiū Juàn, attacked him,
and the Xià multitude was utterly routed,
with over ten thousand dead.
The Xià ruler was severely wounded,
fled alone on horseback,
gathered his remaining troops,
drove fifty thousand civilians,
and retreated west to defend Shàngguī.
The Wei men captured the Xià ruler's younger brother, Dānyáng Duke Wūshìbá, Wǔlíng Duke Tūgǔ, and over a hundred others from dukes and marquises downward.
On that day,
the Wei troops, riding the momentum of victory, attacked Āndìng.
The Xià's Dōngpíng Duke Yǐdǒu abandoned the city and fled to Cháng'ān,
driving and plundering several thousand households,
then fled west to Shàngguī.
28 On Wùxū,
Wei's Shūsūn Jiàn attacked Zhú Língxiù at Húlù,
and Língxiù was heavily defeated,
with over five thousand dead.
Jiàn returned and stationed his troops at Fànchéng.
This was the city of Fàn County in Dōngpíng Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Fàn County of Pú Prefecture
was the fief of the Jìn senior official Shì Kuài.
29 On Jǐhài,
the Wei ruler went to Āndìng;
on Gēngzǐ,
he returned,
arriving at Píngliáng,
where he dug moats and besieged it,
comforted those who had recently submitted,
pardoned the people of Qín and Yōng,
and granted them exemption from taxes and corvée for seven years.
The Xià's Lǒngxī defending general surrendered to Wei.
30 On Xīnchǒu,
Wei's Ān Xié supervised the various armies in attacking Huátái.
31 The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, sent his Secretary Lang, Zōng Shū, and others to present tribute to Wei.
The Wei ruler feasted with them,
and taking Cuī Hào's hand, showed it to Shū and the others, saying:
"The Cuī Gōng you have heard of,
this is he.
The excellence of his talent and strategy,
is unmatched today.
I consult him on all my actions,
he predicts success and failure in advance,
matching like tally and token,
never erring."
32 Wei appointed Shūsūn Jiàn as Commander-in-Chief of military affairs for the four provinces of Jì, Qīng, and others.
Wei had not yet obtained Qīng Province,
so they sent Jiàn to command the various armies to manage and plan for it.
33 Wei's Secretary Kù Jié led five thousand cavalry to welcome the Qín King Mùmò.
The Wèi Shū's Treatise on Officials and Clans states: Among the northern surnames,
the Kùnǚguān clan was later changed to the Kù clan.
Shuài (to lead)
is pronounced as shuài;
same below.
Qí (cavalry)
is pronounced jì;
same below.
Mùmò followed him,
and Kù Jié led the way back.
Over ten thousand Qiāng from various tribes in Nán'ān rebelled against Qín,
electing the General Pacifying the South, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs for eight commanderies, and Governor of Guǎngníng, Jiāo Yí, as their leader.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography states: Guǎngníng Commandery administered Lǒngxī Zhàng County.
"Níng"
should be
"níng".
Zhàng County
was established in the Later Hàn,
and in the Táng dynasty, it was within the territory of Lǒngxī County of Wèi Prefecture.
They then coerced Yí's nephew, the Great Wall Protector Liàng, to be their leader.
The Wǔ Dài Zhì states: Bǎiquán County of Píngliáng Commandery
was where the Later Wei established Chángchéng Commandery.
Mùmò requested aid from the Dí King Yáng Nándāng.
Nándāng sent General Fú Xiàn leading three thousand cavalry to rescue him,
and Mùmò joined forces with him to attack the various Qiāng.
The various Qiāng were routed,
Liàng fled back to Guǎngníng,
and Mùmò advanced his army to attack him.
He sent a handwritten order to Jiāo Yí to capture Liàng.
In the twelfth month,
Yí beheaded Liàng and emerged to surrender,
and Mùmò promoted Yí's title to General Who Guards the State.
Qín's Governor of Lüèyáng, Hóngnóng's Yáng Xiǎn, surrendered the commandery to Xià.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Lüèyáng Commandery from parts of Tiānshuǐ.
Xiáng (to surrender)
is pronounced xiáng;
same below.
34 On Xīnyǒu,
[the court] appointed Chángshā King Yìxīn as Governor of Yù Province,
stationed at Shòuyáng.
Shòuyáng's land was desolate and its people scattered,
its walls and moats were dilapidated,
and bandits operated openly;
Yìxīn managed affairs as appropriate,
bringing peace and livelihood within his jurisdiction,
to the point where lost items were not picked up on the road,
the city's government offices were intact and substantial,
and it thus became a prosperous frontier region.
The Quèbēi reservoir had long been abandoned;
Yìxīn repaired its dikes and embankments,
channeled river water into the reservoir,
irrigating over ten thousand qǐng of farmland,
eliminating further drought disasters.
This was channeling the water of the Féi River into Quèbēi.
Fù (again)
is pronounced fù.
35 On Dīngmǎo,
Xià's Shànggǔ Duke Shègàn and Guǎngyáng Duke Dùluògū emerged and surrendered,
and Wei captured Píngliáng.
The Marquis Within the Passes, Dòu Dàitián, captured Xī Jīn and É Qīng,
and presented them to the Wei ruler.
The Wei ruler bestowed the Xià ruler's empress upon Dàitián,
and ordered Jīn to kneel-walk and serve wine to Dàitián,
saying to Jīn:
"The one who spared your life
is Dàitián."
He enfeoffed Dàitián as Marquis of Jǐngxíng.
Cáo Wèi established the Marquis Within the Passes,
which had a noble rank but no fief,
similar to the Marquis Within the Passes of Qín and Hàn,
its rank below that of a full marquis.
Tuòbá rewarded Dòu Dàitián,
promoting him from Marquis Within the Passes to Marquis of Jǐngxíng,
which then came with a fief,
though it was not actual territory he ruled.
Xíng (陘)
is pronounced xíng.
He was appointed as the Capital Duànjiàng of the Interior.
One hundred men formed a duàn,
and a duàn had a commander;
this was the system of the Rúrán.
The Wei duànjiàng commanded the Three Lang Guards,
those on duty within the palace,
and had authority over all from Palace Attendants down to Mid-level Cavaliers and above.
Jiàng (general)
is pronounced jiàng;
same below.
The Xià defending generals of Cháng'ān, Línjìn, and Wǔgōng all fled,
and Guānzhōng entirely fell to Wei.
The Wei ruler left the Duke of Bādōng, Yán Pǔ, to guard Āndìng,
and appointed General Pacifying the West, Wáng Jīn, to guard Cháng'ān.
On Rénshēn,
the Wei ruler returned east,
appointing Xī Jīn as a Palace Provisioner,
making him carry wine and food to follow.
The Palace Provisioner managed food and drink.
Because Jīn had been defeated in battle and lost his dignity,
this was to humiliate him.
At that time, Wei had a Director of the Imperial Kitchen,
and the Palace Provisioner was likely his subordinate.
Cóng (to follow)
is pronounced cóng.
Wáng Jīn was arrogant and presumptuous, acting unlawfully,
trusting and employing his close attendants,
and imposing levies and corvée on the common people;
the people could not endure the demands,
and several thousand households fled south to Hànchuān.
The Wei ruler investigated and found the facts true,
and beheaded Jīn as a public warning.
36 The Right General, Dào Yànzhī, and the General Pacifying the North, Wáng Zhòngdé, were both imprisoned and dismissed from office,
and the Governor of Yǎn Province, Zhú Língxiù, was executed for abandoning his army.
The Emperor, having seen Yuán Hùzhī's letter, thought well of him,
and appointed him as Governor of Běi Gāopíng.
Nán Gāopíng Commandery
was an émigré commandery,
subordinate to Nán Yǎn Province.
Běi Gāopíng Commandery
was an ancient commandery,
subordinate to Yǎn Province,
administering Húlù.
When Yán Zhī went on the northern expedition,
his troops and supplies were extremely abundant;
but after his defeat and return,
everything was abandoned and completely lost,
leaving the government storehouses and armories empty.
On another day,
the Emperor was feasting with his ministers,
and there was a surrendered person from the outer wilderness present.
Since the division of rule between north and south,
each side considered the area beyond its own borders as the outer wilderness.
Surrendered,
read as hù jiāng fān.
Present,
read as cú wò fān.
"How many weapons are still left in the armory?"
Chēn deceitfully replied:
"There are weapons for a hundred thousand men."
The Cao Wei established twenty-three Directors of the Imperial Secretariat,
with the Armory Department being one of them,
in charge of military equipment, imperial processions, and ceremonial guards.
Chēn,
read as chǒu lín fān.
The Emperor, hearing Chēn's reply,
was very pleased.
Chēn
was the great-grandson of Hé.
For Gù Hé, see the first year of the Dàxīng era of Emperor Yuán of Jin in scroll ninety.
37 Prince Yìkāng of Péngchéng and Wáng Hóng both served as Directors of the Imperial Secretariat.
Yìkāng was still discontented in his heart,
wanting to obtain the governorship of Yángzhōu,
which was evident in his words and expressions;
and because Hóng's younger brother Tánshǒu held a central position,
favored and entrusted by the Emperor,
he became even more displeased.
Hóng, due to old age and illness,
repeatedly requested to retire,
and Tánshǒu himself sought the governorship of Wú Commandery,
but the Emperor did not permit either request.
Yìkāng said to others:
"Lord Wáng has been ill for a long time and cannot rise;
how can the Divine Land be governed from a sickbed!"
Tánshǒu advised Hóng to reduce the civil and military staff in his office by half and transfer them to Yìkāng.
The Emperor agreed to transfer two thousand men,
and only then was Yìkāng pleased.

Emperor Tàizǔ, the Literary Emperor, Part 1, Lower Section
Eighth Year of Yuánjiā (Xīnwèi, 431)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the first day of the month, Rénwǔ,
Yān proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Dàxīng.
2 On Bǐngshēn,
Tán Dàojì and others went from Qīngshuǐ to rescue Huátái,
and Wèi's Shūsūn Jiàn and Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng resisted them.
On Dīngyǒu,
Dàojì reached Shòuzhāng,
where he encountered Wèi's Duke Ānpíng, Yǐzhān Juàn.
The Wèi official clan records state: The Xian Emperor ordered the descendants of his paternal uncle to take the surname Yǐzhān.
He heavily defeated him;
and after fighting his way to Gāoliáng Pavilion,
he beheaded Wèi's Governor of Jìzhōu, Xīfán Kùjié.
In the eighth year of the Tàicháng era of Emperor Míngyuán of Wèi,
Jìzhōu was established,
with its seat at Qiāo'áo City.
Jì,
read as zǐ lǐ fān.
3 The Xià ruler attacked the Qín general Yáo Xiàn,
defeating him;
he then sent his paternal uncle, Duke Wéifá of Běipíng, to lead ten thousand troops to attack Nán'ān.
Last year, Mùmò defended Nán'ān.
People ate each other.
The Qín Palace Attendant,
General Chūlián Fǔzhèng for Subduing the Caitiffs, Palace Attendant and General of the Right Guard Qǐfú Yánzuò, and Minister of Personnel Qǐfú Bá Báyú fled over the city wall to Xià;
the Qín king Mùmò, in dire straits,
carried his coffin out and surrendered.
The Qǐfú clan had four rulers,
and perished after forty-nine years.
Coffin,
read as chū jìn fān.
Surrendered,
read as hù jiāng fān.
Xìngguó was captured by Qín,
see the sixth year in the previous scroll.
Jǔ,
read as zǐ yú fān.
The Director of the Crown Prince's Affairs,
was in charge of impeaching palace officials and commanding the troops of the Crown Prince's Guard.
The Jin records do not have this official,
likely established by the two Zhào, Yān, and Qín.
"You, sir, bear the nation's favor and grace,
and hold the important responsibility of a frontier command.
Now that our court has been overthrown,
how can you not lead the assembled people to raise the great cause and exterminate the enemy!"
Yí said:
"Now the sovereign has already fallen into the hands of the rebels,
it is not that I cherish life and forget righteousness,
but considering that if we pursue them with a large army,
it would hasten his death.
It would be better to select a worthy person from the royal clan,
support him as ruler and then attack,
then perhaps we can succeed."
Kǎi then built an altar and swore an oath to the people,
and within twenty days,
over ten thousand people joined him.
But then Yí fell ill and died,
and Kǎi could not carry out the plan alone,
so he fled to Héxī.
4 Second month,
on Wùwǔ,
appointed the Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Jiāng Yí as Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
5 Tán Dàojì and others advanced to the Jì River,
and within over twenty days,
fought more than thirty battles with Wèi,
with Dàojì winning most of them.
When the army reached Lìchéng,
Lìchéng County had belonged to Jǐnán Commandery since the Hàn,
and in Sòng it was the seat of the Governor of Jìzhōu.
They burned the grass and grain,
and Dàojì's army ran out of food,
so they could not advance;
thus, Ān Xié and Sīmǎ Chǔzhī were able to concentrate their forces on attacking Huátái,
and the Wèi ruler again sent General Chǔbīng Wáng Huìlóng to assist them.
Zhū Xiūzhī held out for several months,
until the food ran out,
and he and his soldiers smoked rats and ate them.
On Xīnyǒu,
Wèi captured Huátái,
seizing Xiūzhī and the Grand Administrator of Dōng Commandery, Shēn Mó.
Dōng Commandery had its seat at Báimǎ since the Hàn and Wèi;
Báimǎ
is the location of Huátái.
Mó,
was the great-grandson of Zhōng.
For Shēn Zhōng, see the ninth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng of Jin in scroll ninety-five.
6 On Guǐyǒu,
the Wèi ruler returned to Píngchéng,
held a great feast,
reported to the ancestral temple,
and the generals and all officials received rewards,
with the soldiers granted exemption from corvée for ten years.
This was to reward the achievements of the northern expedition against Róurán, the western expedition against Xià, and the southern defense against Sòng.
General,
read as jí liàng fān.
Commander,
read as suǒ lèi fān.
Exemption,
read as fāng mù fān,
meaning exemption from service;
the same for the exemption of the territory below.
At this time, there was a great flood in the southern regions of Wèi,
and many people starved to death.
The Imperial Secretariat Director Liú Jié said to the Wèi ruler:
"Recently, border invaders have encroached from within,
and war chariots have been frequently deployed;
Heaven has aided Your Sagely Brilliance,
and wherever you went, you achieved victory;
now that the difficulties have been pacified,
all have received generous rewards.
But the people of the commanderies and states,
though they did not go on campaigns,
diligently engaged in farming and sericulture,
to supply the army and the state,
which is truly the great foundation of governing the world,
and the source of the treasury's resources.
Now, from east of the mountains,
everywhere has suffered flood disasters,
we should show compassion,
to extend nurturing care."
The Wèi ruler followed this advice,
and exempted the territory from a year's land tax.
7 Tán Dàojì and others ran out of food,
and withdrew from Lìchéng,
and some soldiers deserted and surrendered to Wèi,
reporting everything.
The Wèi pursued them,
and the troops were terrified,
on the verge of collapse.
Dàojì, at night, chanted tallies and measured sand,
covering it with the little rice that remained.
At dawn,
the Wèi army saw this,
thought Dàojì had ample supplies and provisions,
and executed the deserters as liars.
At that time, Dàojì had few troops,
while the Wèi army was very numerous,
with cavalry surrounding them on all sides.
Dàojì ordered all soldiers to don armor,
while he himself, dressed in white, rode in a carriage,
and led the troops out slowly.
The Wèi thought there was an ambush,
and did not dare to press close,
gradually retreating,
and Dàojì returned with his entire army intact.
The Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Xiāo Sīhuà, heard that Dào Jì had returned south,
and wanted to abandon his garrison and retreat to a defensible position.
(The Sòng administration of Qīngzhōu was at Dōngyáng City.)
He did not follow through.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Sīhuà abandoned his garrison and fled to Píngchāng.
(Píngchāng County
belonged to Lángyá Commandery under the Former Hàn,
and to Běihǎi Commandery under the Later Hàn;
according to the Tàikāng-era geographical records of the Jìn, it belonged to Chéngyáng Commandery,
and during Emperor Huì's reign, Píngchāng Commandery was separately established.
According to the *Wǔdài Zhì*: the former name of Jiāoxī County in Mìzhōu was Qiánzōu,
where Píngchāng Commandery was established.)
Hearing this,
he also abandoned the city and fled.
The Wèi army in the end did not arrive,
but the accumulated supplies at Dōngyáng had already been burned by the common people.
Sīhuà was held accountable and summoned,
and imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
8 The King of Yān established his consort, Lady Mùróng, as Queen.
9 On the Gēngxū day,
Wèi generals Ān Xié and others returned to Píngchéng.
The Wèi sovereign praised Zhū Xiūzhī for maintaining his integrity,
and married him to a woman of the imperial clan.
(This sets the stage for Xiūzhī's eventual return from the north.)
To take as a wife,
read as zǐ xì fān.
Initially,
when the Emperor dispatched Dào Yànzhī,
he admonished him, saying:
"If the northern state's troops move,
before they arrive,
proceed directly into the [Yellow] River;
if they do not move,
remain at Péngchéng and do not advance."
When Ān Xié captured Sòng prisoners,
the Wèi sovereign first heard these words.
He said to his dukes and ministers:
"You all previously said that my use of Cuī Hào's plan was mistaken,
and were alarmed and firmly remonstrated.
Those of a constantly victorious house,
at first all consider themselves surpassing others,
but when it comes to the final outcome,
(the final outcome,
refers to the ultimate point of the situation's development.)
Sīmǎ Chǔzhī submitted a memorial,
believing that the various regions were already pacified,
and requested a major campaign to attack Sòng.
The Wèi sovereign, because the troops had long been wearied,
did not permit it.
He summoned Chǔzhī to be a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and appointed Wáng Huìlóng as the Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng.
(Although Wèi established a Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng,
in reality, they regarded Hǔláo as an important garrison.
According to the *Wèishū Guānshì Zhì*: in the third year of the Tài'ān era of Emperor Gāozōng,
they began to make the various tribal Protectorate Commandants each into Grand Administrators.
Probably at this time, only Wáng Huìlóng was appointed as Grand Administrator of Xíngyáng,
and by the third year of Tài'ān, they had all been changed.)
To guard,
read as shì yòu fān.
Huìlóng was in the commandery for ten years,
cultivating both agriculture and warfare,
greatly establishing his reputation and achievements,
with over ten thousand households submitting and attaching themselves to him.
The Emperor spread disinformation within Wèi,
saying
"Huìlóng, considering his achievements high but his position low,
wants to lead the Sòng people in an invasion,
and thereupon seize Sīmǎ Chǔzhī to rebel."
The Wèi sovereign heard this,
and bestowed upon Huìlóng an imperial edict, saying:
"Liú Yìlóng fears the General like a tiger,
and wants to harm you;
I know this myself.
Rumors borne on the wind and dust,
I imagine are not worth taking to heart."
The Emperor again sent an assassin, Lǚ Xuánbó, to assassinate him,
saying:
"If you obtain Huìlóng's head,
you will be enfeoffed as a Baron of two hundred households,
and rewarded with a thousand bolts of silk."
Xuánbó pretended to be a defector,
requesting that people be dismissed to discuss something;
Huìlóng was suspicious,
and had someone search his bosom,
finding a foot-long knife.
Xuánbó kowtowed and begged for death,
Huìlóng said:
"Each is acting for his own lord."
And released him.
His attendants admonished him, saying:
"The Sòng people's schemes are not yet exhausted,
if you do not kill Xuánbó,
there will be no way to control the future."
Huìlóng said:
"Life and death are fated,
how could he harm me!
I use benevolence and righteousness as my shield and barrier,
what is there to worry about!"
Thereupon he spared him.
(The historian here concludes the account of Huìlóng guarding Xíngyáng.)
10 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Gēngyín day,
the Wèi sovereign went to Yúnzhōng.
11 In the sixth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
a great amnesty was issued.
12 The Xià sovereign killed Qǐfú Mùmò and his clan of five hundred people.
13 The Xià sovereign, fearing pressure from the Wèi people,
gathered over a hundred thousand people of Qín,
(the people of Qín,
refers to the people obtained from the Qǐfú clan.)
built a city across the [Yellow] River,
wanting to attack the King of Héxī, Méngxùn, and seize his territory.
The King of Tǔyùhún, Mùguī, sent his Yìzhōu Governor, Mùlìyán, and Níngzhōu Governor, Shí Qián,
leading thirty thousand cavalry,
to attack them while they were halfway across,
intercepting and striking them,
capturing the Xià sovereign, Dìng, and returning with him.
(The Hèlián clan lasted through three sovereigns for twenty-six years before being destroyed.)
From this time, the Central Plains and the northwestern lands were all unified under Wèi.
To lead,
read as shuài.
Cavalry,
read as qí jì fān.
Shí Qián
was the son of Shù Luògān.
(Shù Luògān died in the thirteenth year of the Yìxī era of Jìn Emperor Ān.)
14 Wèi border officials captured over twenty scouts of Róurán,
the Wèi sovereign bestowed clothing upon them and sent them back.
Róurán was moved and pleased.
In the intercalary month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
the Róurán Chìlián Kèhán sent an envoy to Wèi,
and the Wèi sovereign treated him with great courtesy.
15 The Wèi sovereign sent the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Zhōu Shào, to come and offer greetings,
and also to seek a marriage alliance;
the Emperor gave an evasive reply.
16 The Governor of Jīngzhōu, the Prince of Jiāngxià, Liú Yìgōng,
as he gradually grew older,
wanted to monopolize governmental affairs.
The Chief Clerk, Liú Zhàn, often checked and restrained him,
and thus they developed a rift.
(Under Sòng regulations: when a young prince governs a province,
generally the Chief Clerk administers the affairs of the prefecture and province,
and all matters are decided by the Administrator. Yìgōng wanted to monopolize them, but Zhàn would not allow it,
hence the rift developed.)
To grow,
read as zhī liǎng fān.
He sent someone to reprimand Yìgōng,
and also to reconcile them.
At this time,
Wáng Huá and Wáng Tánshǒu had both died,
and the General of the Central Army, Yīn Jǐngrén, had always been on good terms with Zhàn.
He informed the Emperor that the worthy men of the time were dwindling,
and summoned Zhàn to be the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
adding the title of Gentleman Attendant at the Palace,
to jointly participate in governmental affairs.
He appointed the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Zhāng Shào, to replace Zhàn as Chief Clerk of the Pacifying Army and Commandant of the Southern Man.
After a short while,
Shào was charged with, while in Yōngzhōu, engaging in private hoarding and accumulation,
with corruption amounting to two million, four hundred and fifty thousand [coins],
and was handed over to the Commandant of Justice,
deserving death.
(In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
Shào governed Yōngzhōu.)
Yōng,
read as yú yòng fān.
Xiè Shù spoke of Shào's past merits from the previous dynasty,
(When Emperor Wǔ campaigned against Huán Xuán,
Shào, on behalf of his father Xiè Gǔ, submitted a memorial pledging loyalty,
and also did not attach himself to Liú Yì.)
The Emperor personally wrote an edict in response and accepted [the plea],
dismissed Shào from office,
and stripped him of his noble rank and fief.
Shù said to his son, Zōng:
"The Sovereign, taking pity on Shào's long-standing sincerity,
specially granted an exception and pardoned him.
What I said happened to coincide [with his intentions],
hence it was specially accepted in response.
If this matter is publicized,
then it would be encroaching upon and seizing the Sovereign's grace,
which is the greatest impropriety."
He had Zōng face forward and burn it.
The Emperor later said to Shào:
"That you were spared,
Xiè Shù had a hand in it."
17 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the Wèi sovereign went to Héxī.
18 In the eighth month,
on the Yǐyǒu day,
the King of Héxī, Méngxùn, sent his son, Ānzhōu, to enter service at Wèi.
19. Tǔyùhún King Mùguī sent his attendant minister Xiè Tàiníng to present a memorial to Wei,
requesting to send Hèlián Dìng.
On the jǐchǒu day,
Wei appointed Mùguī as Grand General and King of Western Qín.
20. Left Imperial Counselor Línchuān King Yìqìng firmly requested to be relieved of his duties;
on the jiǎchén day,
Yìqìng was appointed as Director of the Central Secretariat,
while retaining his position as Governor of Dānyáng.
21. In the ninth month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
the Wei ruler returned to the palace.
On the gēngshēn day,
Grand Commandant Zhǎngsūn Sōng was additionally appointed as Pillar of State Grand General,
marking the beginning of the title Pillar of State Grand General.
Conquest-Western Grand General Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng was appointed as Minister of Works.
Dàoshēng was by nature pure and frugal,
using a single bear-skin saddle flap
for several decades without changing it.
The "Lèi Piān" states: A horse's mud guard is called chàn.
Chàn,
pronounced chāng yàn fān.
The Shǔ commentary says: It shields against mud and mire.
"As wise as Cuī Hào,
as incorruptible as Dàoshēng."
22. The Wei ruler wished to select an envoy to go to Héxī,
Cuī Hào recommended the Secretary Lǐ Shùn,
and thus Shùn was appointed as Grand Master of Ceremonies,

and Héxī King Méngxùn was appointed as Palace Attendant, Commander of Military Affairs of Liángzhōu, the Western Regions, Qiāng, and Róng, Grand Tutor, Acting Conquest-Western Grand General, Governor of Liángzhōu, and King of Liáng,
ruling over the seven commanderies of Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, Xīhǎi, Jīnchéng, and Xīpíng;
the edict stated:
"Your prosperity and decline, survival and demise,
shall rise and fall with Wei.
To the north reaching the barren lands,
to the south extending to Yōng and Mín,
to the west bordering the Kūnlíng Mountains,
to the east reaching the Héqū bend,
the "Jīngdiǎn Shìwén" states: Sīmǎ says: Qióngfà,
refers to the land beneath the North Pole where there is no vegetation.
Note: Máo,
means grass.
Geographical texts say: Mountains regard grass and trees as their hair.
Yōng,
refers to the lands of Wèixīng and Shàngyōng.
Mín is a mountain.
Kūnlíng,
refers to the Kūnlún Mountains.
Héqū,
refers to the Héqū of Shuòfāng. Mín,
is the same as Mǐn.
Bordered by,
pí yì fān.
To assist the imperial house.
Establish generals, ministers, high officials, and all officers,
receiving authority to appoint them.
Erect the banners of the Son of Heaven,
with guards clearing the way when coming and going,
following the precedent of the feudal kings in the early Hàn."
23. On the rénshēn day,
the Wei ruler issued an edict stating:
"Now that the two enemies have been crushed and annihilated,
we shall lay down arms and cultivate culture,
restore neglected offices,
and promote reclusive talents.
Fànyáng Lú Xuán, Bólíng Cuī Chuò, Zhàojùn Lǐ Líng, Héjiān Xíng Yǐng, Bóhǎi Gāo Yǔn, Guǎngpíng Yóu Yǎ, Tàiyuán Zhāng Wěi, and others,
are all descendants of the worthy and outstanding,
the leading figures of their respective provinces.
"Zhōu",
should be
"zhōu".
[Chapter note: Line 11 of version A correctly reads
"zhōu";
line 11 of version B is the same;
the Kong edition is the same.
'I shall bind you with silken cords.'
This is the line from the second yang line of the Zhōngfú hexagram in the "Yì Jīng".
Order all provinces and commanderies to send them with due ceremony."
Thus, Xuán and others, along with several hundred recommended by the provinces and commanderies, were summoned,
and they were graded and appointed accordingly.
Cuī Chuò firmly declined due to his mother's old age.
Xuán and others were all appointed as Secretariat Erudites.
Xuán
was the great-grandson of Chén;
after the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
Lú Chén moved among the Shì clan,
and after Rǎn Mǐn's defeat,
he died in the fighting.
Chén,
shì rén fān.
He was the paternal cousin of Shùn.
Xuán's maternal uncle Cuī Hào,
whenever speaking with Xuán,
would sigh and say:
"Facing Zǐzhēn deepens my feelings of nostalgia for antiquity."
Lú Xuán,
styled Zǐzhēn.
He sought to clarify and distinguish clans and families.
Xuán stopped him, saying:
"The creation of institutions and establishment of affairs,
each has its own time;
those who would delight in this,
how many are there!
You should think it over thrice."
Hào did not listen,
and thus incurred the resentment of the multitude.
24. Initially,
Wèi Zhāochéng Emperor first established laws and decrees:
Shíyìjiān was posthumously titled Zhāochéng Emperor.
"Those who commit treason shall have their clans exterminated;
others deserving death may be permitted to redeem their crimes with gold and horses;
murderers may be permitted to compensate the victim's family with oxen, horses, and burial goods to settle the matter;
those who steal government property,
repay fivefold;
private property,
repay tenfold."
Bèi,
means to compensate,
nowadays many say péibèi.
There was no suffering from imprisonment, interrogation, or牵连,
and the realm was at peace.
When Tàizǔ entered the Central Plains,
Dàowǔ Emperor's temple name was Tàizǔ.
He ordered the Gentleman of the Three Dukes, Wáng Dé, to revise and codify them,
striving for simplicity and ease.
This matter is recorded in the 110th scroll, the second year of the Lóng'ān era of Jìn Āndì.
Yì,
yǐ chì fān.
Punishments became excessive and cruel;
this matter is recorded in the 111th scroll, the fourth year of the Lóng'ān era of Jìn Āndì.
Bèi,
pí yì fān.
The legal documents also became intricate.
Míngyuán Emperor's temple name was Tàizōng.
In the tenth month,
on the wùyín day,
Shìzǔ ordered Cuī Hào to revise the laws and decrees again,
abolishing the five-year and four-year punishments,
and adding a one-year punishment;
those practicing sorcery and witchcraft,
shall carry a black ram and a dog and be sunk in the deep.
For the first time, it was decreed that officials of the ninth rank and above could use their official titles and ranks to commute punishments.
Hàn officials were graded by stone rank,
Wèi and Jìn began to establish the order of rank grades.
Those who have recently given birth shall have their sentences decided only after one hundred days.
To the left of the palace gate, a drum for lodging appeals was hung to allow the wronged to reach the emperor.
Yǔ ordered those with legal disputes to shake a drum,
the "Zhōu Lǐ" states: To the left, the Jiā Stone was used to pacify the weary people.
These were all means to reach the obscure and wronged.
The drum for lodging appeals,
allows those bearing grievances to come to the palace gate and beat the drum,
so that their cases are immediately brought to the emperor's attention.
25. The Wei ruler went to the south of the desert.
In the eleventh month,
on the bǐngchén day,
the northern Chìlè chieftain Mòfú Kùruògān
The Gaochē chieftain is called Mòfú.
"Textual Analysis Notes": The "Later Wèi Shū" and "Běi Shǐ" basic annals both write
"Chìlè",
while the Dèng Yuān biography writes
"Gaochē".
Note: Gaochē is another name for Chìlè.
drove several million deer,
to the Wei ruler's temporary residence.
The Wei ruler held a great hunt to reward his accompanying officials.
On the dīngchǒu day of the twelfth month,
he returned to the palace.
26. This year,
the Liáng king changed his reign title to Yìhé.
27. Línyì King Fàn Yángmài invaded Jiǔdé,
and Jiāozhōu troops repelled him.
Jiǔdé commandery,
was the ancient state of Yuèshángshì,
in Suí and Táng times it became Huānzhōu.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the bǐngwǔ day,
the Wei ruler honored his foster mother, Empress Dowager Dòu, as Grand Empress Dowager,
honoring a foster mother as a mother,
is contrary to ritual.
His son Huǎng was made Crown Prince;
a great amnesty was declared;
the reign title was changed to Yánhé.
2. The Yān king made Wángrén, son of Empress Mùróng, Crown Prince.
3. In the third month,
on the gēngxū day,
General of the Guards Wáng Hóng was promoted to Grand Guardian,
and additionally appointed as Supervisor of the Central Secretariat.
On the dīngsì day,
Conquest-Southern Grand General Tán Dàojì was promoted to Minister of Works,
and returned to garrison Xúnyáng.
Dàojì had returned with his army from Lìchéng to Jiànkāng,
and was again sent back to garrison Xúnyáng.
4 On the Rénshēn day,
Tǔyùhún king Mùguī sent Hèlián Dìng to Wèi,
and the Wèi people killed him.
Mùguī submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject captured the usurping rebel,
and presented the victory to the royal court.
Although my rank and position have been elevated, my territory has not been expanded;
my chariots and banners have been adorned, yet wealth has not been fully bestowed as a reward.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this."
The Wèi ruler referred the matter for discussion.
The high officials believed:
"What Mùguī captured was only Dìng.
The people beyond the frontier are all under his control,
yet he is insatiably greedy in his demands.
This cannot be granted."
The Wèi ruler then issued an edict stating:
"The lands of Jīnchéng, Fúhǎn, and Lǒngxī that the Western Qín king obtained,
We have already granted to him.
This is the division of territory;
why must it be expanded further?
When tribute from Western Qín arrives,
silk and cloth will be sent according to the frequency of the envoys,
with temporary increases,
not as a single bestowal that ends there."
From then on, the tribute missions sent by Mùguī to Wèi gradually decreased.
5 The Wèi fangshì Qí Xiān proposed changing Dài to Wànnián,
making the Dài Governor the Wànnián Governor,
and the Dài Magistrate the Wànnián Magistrate.
Cuī Hào said:
"In the past, Tàizǔ responded to Heaven and received the mandate,
combining the names Dài and Wèi in imitation of the Yīn and Shāng.
Emperor Kù's capital was at Bó;
his son Xiè was enfeoffed at Shāng.
From Xiè to Tāng, there were eight relocations,
and Tāng finally made Bó his capital,
residing where his ancestors had lived.
It was called Bó Yīn,
hence the combined names Yīn and Shāng.
Our dynasty should enjoy ten thousand generations,
and does not need to rely on false names for benefit.
What Xiān has heard
is all incorrect and improper.
It is appropriate to restore the old names."
The Wèi ruler followed this advice.
6 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Huáróng Wénzhāo Gōng Wáng Hóng passed away.
