Now, if we strike unexpectedly,
with a large army arriving suddenly,
they will certainly panic and be thrown into confusion,
not knowing what to do,
and capturing him is assured."
The Wei sovereign said:
"Excellent!
My own thoughts are also thus."
Thereupon, he extensively gathered the high ministers and officials to deliberate in the Western Hall.
(The Tàijí Hall in Píngchéng, Wei, had Eastern and Western Halls.)
The Prince of Hóngnóng, Xī Jīn, and over thirty others all said:
"Mùjiān
is the ruler of a minor western border state.
Although his heart is not that of a pure vassal,
since succeeding his father's position,
his tribute and offerings have not been lacking.
The court treats him as a feudal vassal,
and married a princess to him.
Now his crimes and evil are not yet manifest;
he should be pardoned and forgiven.
Our state has recently campaigned against the Rúrú;
our soldiers and horses are weary and exhausted,
and we cannot undertake a major campaign.
Moreover, I have heard his land is saline and barren.
Salty land is called 'lǔ' (鹵),
and barren land is called 'jí' (瘠).
Once our large army arrives,
he will certainly fortify the city and defend it stubbornly.
If we attack and cannot take it,
and there is nothing to plunder in the countryside,
this would be a dangerous course."
Earlier,
Cuī Hào detested the Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Shùn.
During the campaign against Xià,
Hào and Shùn had a rift.
Shùn, because of his missions to Liáng, was favored and treated well by the Wei sovereign,
causing Hào to detest him even more.
"Detest" (惡)
is pronounced "wù lù."
The Wei sovereign considered him capable.
The Martial and Proclaiming King of Liáng (Liáng Wǔxuān Wáng) often went on outings and banquets with Shùn.
(Jǔqú Méngxùn was posthumously titled the Martial and Proclaiming King.)
"Often" (數)
is pronounced "suǒ jiǎo."
Fearing Shùn would reveal this,
he subsequently placed gold and treasures into Shùn's bosom,
and Shùn also concealed it for him.
Hào learned of this
and secretly reported it to the Wei sovereign,
but the Wei sovereign did not believe it.
When the discussion about attacking Liáng Province arose,
Shùn and the Minister of Personnel, Gǔ Bì, both said:
"From the Wēnyù River west to Gūzāng,
according to the History of the Northern Dynasties,
'Wēnyù River'
should be
'Wēnwéi.'
there is absolutely no water or grass.
The people there say,
'On the Tiāntī Mountain south of Gūzāng city,
in winter there is accumulated snow,
deep to over ten feet,
which melts in spring and summer,
flowing down to form streams,
which the inhabitants channel for irrigation.'
When they hear our army has arrived,
they will breach the openings of these channels,
and water will certainly become scarce and cut off.
'The people there'
refers to the people of Liáng.
The land produces no grass;
men and horses will hunger and thirst,
making it difficult to remain long.
Jīn and others' opinion is correct."
The Wei sovereign then ordered Hào and Jīn and others to debate and refute each other.
The assembly had no other arguments,
but only said
"There is no water or grass there."
Hào said:
"The Treatise on Geography in the Book of Hàn states, 'The livestock of Liáng Province are the richest in the world.'
If there were no water or grass,
how could livestock multiply?
Furthermore,
the Hàn people would certainly not have built walled cities
and established commanderies and counties in a place without water or grass.
Moreover, the melting snow
can only settle the dust;
how could it possibly supply channels for irrigation?!
These words are greatly deceptive and false."
"Deceptive" (欺)
means to deceive.
"False" (誣)
means fraudulent.
"Hearing is not as good as seeing;
I have personally seen it,
how can we debate it?"
Hào said:
"You have accepted their money,
and wish to lobby on their behalf.
Do you think just because I haven't seen it with my own eyes, you can deceive me?!"
The Emperor, listening in secret,
heard this.
He then came out to see Jīn and the others,
his words and expression severe and stern.
The ministers did not dare speak further,
only assenting meekly.
After the ministers had left,
the General Who Spreads Might, Yìbá of the Dài people, said to the Emperor:
"If Liáng Province truly had no water or grass,
how could they have established a state there?
The opinions of the assembly are all unusable;
we should follow Hào's words."
The Emperor approved of this.
In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the Dīngchǒu day,
the ruler of Wèi conducted military training in the western suburbs;
in the sixth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
he set out from Píngchéng.
He appointed the Shìzhōng, Prince Yìdū Mù Shòu, to assist the Crown Prince Huǎng in overseeing the state,
deciding matters of the remaining court,
with all internal and external affairs subject to his authority.
He also sent the Dàjiāngjūn, Prince Chánglè Jī Jìng,
"Jī Jìng,"
in the Běishǐ, it is written as
"Jī Jìng,"
which should be followed.
The Wèishū Guānshì Zhì states: among the northern surnames,
the Héxī clan was changed to the Jī clan.
He ordered the dukes and ministers to write a letter reprimanding the King of Héxī, Mùjiān,
enumerating his twelve crimes,
and saying:
"If you personally lead your ministers to present tribute and welcome us from afar,
bowing before the horse's head,
that is the best strategy.
Once the six armies arrive,
binding yourself and carrying a coffin,
that is the second-best strategy.
If you stubbornly defend your isolated city,
failing to repent in time,
you will die, and your clan will be exterminated,
becoming a great disgrace to the world.
You should consider the middle path,
and seek abundant blessings for yourself!"
8 On the Jǐyǒu day,
the King of Lǒngxī, Tǔyùhún Mùlìyán, was re-enfeoffed as the King of Hénán.
9 The ruler of Wèi crossed the river from Yúnzhōng;
in autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Jǐsì day,
he arrived at the Shǔguó city of Shàngjùn.
The Hàn dynasty established Shǔguó in border commanderies to settle surrendered Hú tribes;
this Shǔguó city
is an old Hàn city.
The Bānshū Dìlǐ Zhì states: in Qiūcí County of Shàngjùn,
the Shǔguó Dūwèi governed.
On the Rénwǔ day,
he left behind the heavy baggage,
divided the various armies,
and sent the Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn, Prince Yǒngchāng Jiàn, the Shàngshū Lìng Liú Jié, and Prince Chángshān Sù as the vanguard,
advancing along two routes simultaneously;
the Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Prince Lèpíng Pī, and the Tàizǎi, Prince Yángpíng Dù Chāo, followed as reinforcements;
he appointed the Píngxī Jiāngjūn Yuán Hè as the guide.
The ruler of Wèi asked Hè about the strategy for capturing Liángzhōu,
and he replied:
"Beside Gūzāng city, there are four Xiānbēi tribes,
all former subjects of my grandfather,
Tūfǎ Rùtán occupied Gūzāng,
but later it was taken by Jǔqú,
and the four Xiānbēi tribes remained living outside the city.
Hè
is the son of Rùtán.
If we proclaim the state's prestige and trustworthiness,
showing them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
they will surely follow and submit.
Once the external aid is subdued,
then taking their isolated city
will be as easy as turning over one's hand."
The ruler of Wèi said:
"Excellent!"
In the eighth month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
Prince Yǒngchāng Jiàn captured over two hundred thousand livestock from Héxī.
The King of Héxī, Mùjiān, heard that the Wèi army was coming,
and exclaimed in alarm:
"Why is this happening!"
Following the plan of his Zuǒchéng, Yáo Dìngguó,
he refused to go out to welcome them,
and sought help from Róurán.
He sent his younger brother, the Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Dǒng Lái, to lead over ten thousand troops to battle south of the city,
but they fled in panic at the sight of the enemy.
Liú Jié, following the words of a diviner,
believed the day and hour were inauspicious,
so he gathered his troops and did not pursue,
allowing Dǒng Lái to return to the city.
The ruler of Wèi was angered by this.
This laid the groundwork for Wèi to execute Liú Jié.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
the ruler of Wèi arrived at Gūzāng,
and sent an envoy to instruct Mùjiān to surrender.
Mùjiān heard that Róurán intended to invade Wèi's borders,
hoping that the ruler of Wèi would return east,
so he fortified the city and held firm;
his nephew Zǔ climbed over the city wall and surrendered.
The ruler of Wèi learned the full situation,
and then divided his army to besiege the city.
Yuán Hè led troops to recruit and pacify over thirty thousand households from various tribes,
so the ruler of Wèi could focus on attacking Gūzāng,
with no further external concerns.
The ruler of Wèi saw the abundant water and grass outside Gūzāng city,
and from this, he resented Lǐ Shùn,
saying to Cuī Hào:
"Your past words,
have now indeed come true."
From then on, the ruler of Wèi was determined to execute Lǐ Shùn.
"As your subject, I dare not speak untruthfully;
all my words are like this."
When the ruler of Wèi was about to attack Liángzhōu,
Crown Prince Huǎng also had doubts.
At this time,
the ruler of Wèi bestowed an edict upon the Crown Prince, saying:
"Outside the west gate of Gūzāng city,
a spring flows
and merges north of the city,
as large as a river.
The remaining canals flow into the desert,
and there is no dry land in between.
Therefore, I issue this decree
to resolve your doubts."
10 On the Gēngzǐ day,
he established his son Shuò as the Prince of Nánpíng.
11 In the ninth month,
on the Bǐngxū day,
Wànnián, the nephew of the King of Héxī, Mùjiān, led his followers and surrendered to Wèi.
Kǎoyì says: the Sòngshū Díhú Zhuàn states:
"Màoqián's nephew Wànnián acted as an internal agent for the enemy,
and Màoqián was captured."
Now, we follow the Hòu Wèishū.
Shuài
is read as lǜ.
Xiáng,
pronounced as hùjiāng fān;
the same below.
Mùjiān led his five thousand civil and military officials, bound himself, and requested surrender;
the ruler of Wèi released his bonds and treated him with courtesy.
He seized over two hundred thousand households within the city,
and the treasures in the warehouses were beyond count.
He appointed the King of Zhāngyè, Tūfǎ Bǎozhōu,
Bǎozhōu had fled to Wèi,
was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhāngyè,
and now was promoted to king.
Bǎozhōu
was the elder brother of Yuán Hè.
Shèng,
pronounced as shēng.
The Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn Yuán Hè separately pacified the various commanderies,
and miscellaneous Hú tribes surrendering numbered several hundred thousand more.
Initially,
Mùjiān appointed his younger brother Wúhuì as the Cìshǐ of Shāzhōu, Dūdū of military affairs west of Jiànkāng, and concurrently Tàishǒu of Jiǔquán,
Yídé as the Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu, Dūdū of military affairs west of Dānlǐng, and concurrently Tàishǒu of Zhāngyè,
Dānlǐng is west of Gūzāng,
which is Shāndānlǐng.
After Qìfú declined and perished,
Lèdū also came under Jǔqú's control.
Lè,
pronounced as luò.
Kǎoyì says: the Sòngshū
"Yídé"
is written as
"Yídé,"
"Ānzhōu"
is written as
"the nephew Fēngzhōu,"
now we follow the Hòu Wèishū.
When Gūzāng was captured,
the ruler of Wèi sent the Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, the Dàirén Xī Juàn, to attack Zhāngyè,
and the Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Fēng Tà to attack Lèdū;
Yídé burned the warehouses,
fled west to Jiǔquán,
Ānzhōu fled south to Tǔyùhún,
and Fēng Tà plundered several thousand households and returned.
Xī Juàn advanced to attack Jiǔquán,
Wúhuì and Yídé gathered the remaining people and fled to Jìnchāng,
then joined Táng'ér at Dūnhuáng.
The ruler of Wèi sent the Duke of Yìyáng, Yuán Jié, to guard Jiǔquán,
and stationed generals to guard both Wǔwēi and Zhāngyè.
The ruler of Wèi held a banquet in Gūzāng,
and said to his ministers:
"Cuī Gōng has abundant wisdom and strategy,
I no longer find it surprising.
Yī Bá is a man skilled in archery and horsemanship,
yet his insights are the same as Cuī Gōng's,
which is truly remarkable."
Bá was skilled in archery,
able to pull an ox backward while walking,
and could run as fast as a galloping horse,
and his nature was loyal and cautious,
so the ruler of Wèi particularly favored him.
When the Wei ruler embarked on his western campaign,
Mù Shòu escorted him to the river,
accompanying the Wei ruler from Píngchéng west to the river.
"Wútí and Mùjiān have long been deeply allied;
upon hearing that I am attacking Mùjiān,
Wútí is certain to invade our borders.
(Note: The Rouran Chìlián Khan is named Wútí.)
I entrust you with assisting the crown prince.
Once the harvest is completed,
immediately dispatch troops to the southern desert,
station them in ambush at key positions to await the enemy's arrival.
Lure them deep into our territory,
then strike them;
this will ensure victory.
Liángzhōu is far away,
and I will be unable to send reinforcements.
Do not disobey my orders!"
Shòu bowed his head and accepted the command.
Shòu deeply trusted the court academician Gōngsūn Zhì,
regarding him as his chief strategist.
Both Shòu and Zhì believed in divination,
convinced that the Rouran would certainly not come.
Thus, they made no preparations.
Zhì
was the younger brother of Guǐ.
(Gōngsūn Guǐ appears in scroll 120, year four.)
When the Rouran Chìlián Khan heard that the Wei ruler was heading toward Gūzāng,
he seized the opportunity to invade,
leaving his elder brother Qǐlièguī to confront Jī Jìng and Jiànníng Prince Chóng at the northern garrison.
The northern garrison,
refers to the six garrisons established by the Wei ruler after defeating and subjugating the Gāochē.
Because they were located north of Píngchéng,
they were called the northern garrisons.
Some say
the northern garrison was directly north of Dàidū,
namely Huáishuò Garrison.
When they reached Shànwú's Qījiè Mountain,
Píngchéng was thrown into great panic,
with people scrambling to flee into the inner city.
Mù Shòu was at a loss about what to do,
intending to seal the western outer gate
and urging the crown prince to take refuge in the southern mountains.
Empress Dowager Dòu refused to allow this, and the plan was abandoned.
Empress Dowager Dòu
was the same as Empress Dowager Bǎo.
At that time, Jī Jìng and Jiànníng Prince Chóng defeated Qǐlièguī north of Yīnshān,
capturing him,
along with his paternal uncle Tāwúwúlùhú and five hundred officers,
beheading over ten thousand.
When Chìlián heard this,
he fled,
and was pursued to the southern desert before the pursuers turned back.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Xīnyǒu,
the Wei ruler returned east,
leaving Yuèpíng Prince Pī and General Zhēngxī Hè Duōluó to garrison Liángzhōu,
and relocating Jǔqú Mùjiān's clan and thirty thousand households of officials and commoners to Píngchéng.
(Textual note: The *Sixteen Kingdoms Spring and Autumn Excerpt* says
"one hundred thousand households,"
but here we follow the *Book of Later Wei*.)
On Guǐhài,
Tūfǎ Bǎozhōu led various Xiānbēi tribes to occupy Zhāngyè and rebel against Wei.
In the twelfth month,
on Yǐhài,
Crown Prince Shào underwent the capping ceremony,
and a great amnesty was declared.
Shào had handsome eyebrows and beard,
enjoyed reading,
was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and delighted in hosting guests.
Whatever he desired,
the emperor would invariably comply.
The Eastern Palace was equipped with troops equal in number to the Yǔlín guards.
(Yán Shìgǔ notes: Yǔlín
are palace guards;
the name implies they are as swift as feathers
and as numerous as a forest.
This sets the stage for Shào's later use of Eastern Palace troops to commit regicide.)
On Rénwǔ,
the Wei ruler arrived at Píngchéng.
Because the Rouran invasion
had caused no major losses,
Mù Shòu and others escaped execution.
The Wei ruler still treated Jǔqú Mùjiān as a brother-in-law,
retaining his titles as General Zhēngxī and Prince of Héxī.
When Mùjiān's mother died,
she was buried with the rites of a grand empress dowager;
thirty households were assigned to guard the tomb of Wǔxuān Prince.
(This refers to establishing tomb guards for Jǔqú Méngxùn.)
Since the time of the Zhāng family,
Liángzhōu had been renowned for its many scholars.
During the turmoil of the Yǒngjiā era,
scholars from the Central Plains sought refuge in Héxī.
The Zhāng family treated them with respect and employed them,
and their descendants continued this tradition,
ensuring that scholarly culture did not decline.
Hence, Liángzhōu was known for its many scholars.
The Wei ruler appointed Dūnhuáng's Kàn Yīn as Governor of Gūzāng,
Zhāng Zhàn as Minister of War,
(Cáo Wèi established the position of Minister of the Five Armies.
Based on this,
the title "Ministry of War" originated in Héxī.)
Jīnchéng's Sòng Qīn as Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and Zhào Róu as Director of the Treasury.
(Cáo Wèi established twenty-three director positions,
with the Treasury being one of them,
responsible for managing wealth and supplies.)
After the Wei ruler conquered Liángzhōu,
he treated them all with respect and employed them,
appointing Kàn Yīn and Liú Bǐng as Advisers to Yuèpíng Prince Pī.
Hú Sǒu of Āndìng
displayed exceptional talent from a young age.
He went to serve Mùjiān,
but Mùjiān did not highly regard him.
Sǒu said to Chéng Hóng:
"Your ruler resides in a remote and backward state yet arrogantly assumes grand titles and usurps rituals.
While serving a greater power, his heart is not sincere.
Outwardly, he admires benevolence and righteousness, but in reality, he lacks virtue.
His downfall can be expected imminently.
I shall choose a different tree to perch on.
(From the *Zuǒzhuàn*: When Wèi's Kǒng Wénzǐ planned to attack Tàishū Jí,
he consulted Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
'Matters of warfare
I have not studied.'
He then withdrew,
ordered his carriage, and departed,
saying:
'A bird chooses its tree;
how can a tree choose a bird!')
I shall part from you for a while,
but it will not be a long separation."
He then went to Wei.
A little over a year later, Mùjiān was defeated.
The Wei ruler considered Sǒu prescient,
appointing him as General Hǔwēi,
and enfeoffing him as Baron of Shǐfù.
(Note: There is no place named Shǐfù.
According to the *Hànshū* *Treatise on Geography*,
Yuèxī Commandery had a Gūfù County.
Perhaps
the character "shǐ"
is an error for
the character "gū.")
Sǒu lived in Liángzhōu for generations,
refusing official appointments and honors.
The Wei ruler appointed him as General Xuānwēi.
Héxī's Right Minister Sòng Yáo accompanied the Wei ruler to Píngchéng and died there.
The Wei ruler appointed Suǒ Chǎng as a court academician.
At that time, the Wei court emphasized military achievements,
and the noble youths showed little interest in scholarly learning.
(Zhèng Xuán notes: Noble youths are the sons of princes and dukes;
'youth' refers to those without official duties.)
Chǎng diligently guided them,
being strict yet courteous.
The noble youths all held him in awe,
and many achieved success,
with dozens eventually rising to prominent positions such as ministers, governors, and prefects.
Cháng Shuǎng established an academy on the right bank of the Wēn River.
(The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* notes: Ten *lǐ* west of Sānggān City are hot springs.)
Shuǎng established clear rules for rewards and punishments,
and his students served him as they would a strict father.
From this, Confucian learning in Wei began to flourish.
Gāo Yǔn often praised Shuǎng for his effective methods of instruction and discipline,
saying:
"Wén Wēng achieved success through gentleness,
while you, sir, achieve it through firmness.
(During the late reign of Hàn Jǐngdì,
Wén Wēng served as Governor of Shǔ Commandery.
He was benevolent and devoted to education,
selecting bright and talented junior clerks from the commandery and counties to study with court academicians in the capital.
He also established schools,
recruiting youths from subordinate counties in Chéngdū to become students,
exempting them from corvée labor.
As a result, great transformation occurred.
To this day, Bā and Shǔ value Confucian elegance,
all due to Wén Wēng's teachings.
'Kè' also means to overcome;
this means Wén Wēng overcame through gentleness, while Cháng Shuǎng overcomes through firmness.)
But in nurturing people to maturity, the result is the same."
Jiāng Qiáng from Chénliú,
resided temporarily in Liángzhōu.
He presented over a thousand scrolls of classics, histories, and a variety of philosophical texts, along with calligraphy.
He was also appointed as a Doctor in the Secretariat.
In the third year of Wèi Yánchāng,
Qiáng's grandson Shì submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that Fúxī created the eight trigrams as a representation of forms,
while Xuānyuán revealed the patterns of the sacred tortoise.
In ancient times, Cāng Jié
observed the patterns of the trigrams,
examined the traces of birds and beasts,
and invented characters to replace knotting cords,
using writing to manage affairs.
By the time of the Three Dynasties,
the forms had varied considerably.
Although based on categories and fashioned accordingly,
they could not deviate from Cāng Jié's original designs.
Therefore, in the Zhōu rites, at eight years old, children entered elementary school,
where the Tutor would teach them the Six Writings,
which are the legacy of Scribe Jié.
During the era of King Xuān, Scribe Zhòu compiled fifteen volumes of Dàzhuàn.
With ancient script, some writings were similar, others different,
known at the time as Zhòu Script.
Confucius edited the Six Classics,
Zuǒ Qiūmíng compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals,
all using ancient script.
The meaning therein was clear and expressible.
Later, the seven states took divergent paths,
resulting in chaotic and inconsistent scripts.
When the Qín unified the land,
Chancellor Lǐ Sī proposed abolishing those not conforming to Qín script.
Sī wrote the 'Cāng Jié Collection',
Zhōngchē Official Gāo composed the 'Yuánlì Collection',
while Tàishǐ Official Húmǔ Jìng authored the 'Extensive Learning Collection'.
All adopted Zhòu's style,
with some simplifications and modifications,
known as Xiǎozhuàn.
That was when Qín burned the classics,
eliminating old practices.
With increasing official and judicial matters,
in pursuit of simplicity,
they first used the Clerical Script.
From that point, the ancient script ceased to exist.
The Clerical Script was
created at the behest of the First Emperor by Chéng Miǎo, a man of Xiàdù, based on Xiǎozhuàn;
since Miǎo was a convict,
it was thus called 'Liàn Script'.
Consequently, there were eight scripts in Qín: first, Dàzhuàn;
second, Xiǎozhuàn;
third, Symbol Script;
fourth, Insect Script;
fifth, Model Seal;
sixth, Draft Script;
seventh, Weapon Script;
eighth, Clerical Script.
With the rise of the Hàn,
there was an office of Wèi Lǜ,
reinstating the teaching of Zhòu Script.
Students learned and tested in all eight scripts,
achieving the highest ranks,
thus appointed in the Secretariat.
Improper simplifications in script led to indictments and punishments.
There also arose the Cursive Script,
though none knows its beginnings.
Its form was informal yet adaptable to the times.
During Emperor Xiàoxuān's reign,
interpreters of the 'Cāng Jié Collection' were summoned,
only Zhāng Chǎng was taught it.
Governor of Liángzhōu, Dù Yè, and scholar Yuán Lǐ, along with lecturer Qín Jìn, could also discuss it.
Under Emperor Xiàopíng,
Lǐ and others, more than a hundred individuals, were invited to the Wèiyāng Palace to explain script.
Lǐ was made the scholar of elementary studies;
Imperial Household Gentleman Yáng Xióng selected from this for composing the 'Instructional Collection'.
At the fall of Wángmáng's regime,
considering destiny aligned with creative endeavors,
Grand Marshal Zhēn Fēng was ordered to review script departments,
making refinements to ancient scripts.
At that time, there were six scripts: first, Ancient Script;
writings from Confucius's walls;
second, Extraordinary Characters;
differing from Ancient Script;
third, Zhòu Script, known as Xiǎozhuàn;
fourth, Assistant Script;
Qín's Clerical Script;
fifth, Trace Seal;
used in stamp carvings;
sixth, Bird and Insect Script;
used in banners and letters.
The Wall Writings
were tangible texts like the 'Rites', 'Documents', 'Spring and Autumn Annals', 'Analects', and 'Classic of Filial Piety' found in the ruins of Confucius's house.
Furthermore,
Northern Peace Marquis Zhāng Cāng presented the 'Spring and Autumn Annals' with Zuǒ's commentary;
its script similar to Confucius's,
hence regarded as previous generations' Ancient Script.
In Later Hàn, Cáo Xǐ of Fúfēng was renowned for skilled seal script writing,
slightly different from earlier techniques, yet exquisite;
subsequently, later learners
all followed his style.
Additionally, orders were given to Historian Jiǎ Kuí to edit the old scripts,
removing diversions and unusual methods,
emphasizing state education,
incorporating anything beneficial to the state,
gathering without exception.
Kuí was the tutor of classical studies for Xǔ Shèn of Rǔnán.
Later, Shèn lamented contemporaries' fascination with novelty and critique of shallow scholars,
thus composing the 'Explanation of Script and Elucidation of Characters' in fifteen volumes.
Beginning with Jiǎ, ending with Hài,

The Valiant Cavalry General Xú Zhànzhī,
was the son of Xú Dáizhī.
Xú Dáizhī
was Emperor Wǔ's beloved son-in-law,
who died in the troubles caused by Sīmǎ Chǔzhī and Lǔ Zōngzhī.
"Valiant"
is pronounced jiān yáo fān.
"Cavalry"
is pronounced qí jì fān.
The Emperor deeply resented him.
When Yìkāng fell,
Xú Zhànzhī was arrested,
and his crime warranted death.
His mother, Princess Kuàijī,
was the eldest legitimate daughter among her brothers,
and had always been respected by the Emperor.
All household matters, big or small,
were consulted with her before action was taken.
When Emperor Gāozǔ was still in humble circumstances,
he once cut reeds at Xīnzhōu himself,
and had a patched cloth jacket.
"Patched"
is the same as "nà."
After he became noble,
he gave it to the princess, saying:
"If future generations become arrogant, extravagant, and unrestrained,
you can show them this garment."
At this time,
the princess entered the palace to see the Emperor,
wailed loudly,
and did not observe the rituals of a subject or concubine.
She took the patched garment from a brocade bag and threw it on the ground,
saying:
"Your family was originally poor and lowly.
This was made by my mother for your father.
Now that you have a full meal,
you are suddenly trying to kill my son!"
The Emperor then pardoned him.
The Minister of Personnel, Wáng Qiú,
was the paternal uncle of Lǚ Zhī.
He was known for his simplicity and detachment and enjoyed a fine reputation,
being highly regarded by the Emperor.
Lǚ Zhī was ambitious and profit-seeking.
This means Lǚ Zhī pursued advancement and was fond of gain.
Qiú repeatedly admonished him,
but he did not comply.
On the evening when Zhàn Zhī was executed,
Lǚ Zhī, barefoot, went to inform Qiú.
Qiú ordered his attendants to fetch shoes for him,
first warming some wine and giving it to him,
then saying:
"What did I always tell you?"
Lǚ Zhī, terrified, could not answer.
Qiú said slowly:
"As long as your uncle is here,
what do you have to worry about!"
People south of the Yangtze called paternal uncles "āfù,"
and those who were uncles also referred to themselves this way.
Ā,
is pronounced wū gě.
Lǚ Zhī was spared from death,
but was dismissed and confined to his home.
According to the *History of the Southern Dynasties*,
when the Emperor was initially the Prince of Yídū,
he appointed Qiú as a close associate.
Qiú was valued for his simplicity and detachment,
likely because the Emperor had long known him.
Meanwhile, Yìkāng was in power,
and people vied to seek his favor and closeness.
Only the Registrar of the Minister of Education, Jiāng Zhàn, was able early on to distance himself,
requesting to be sent out as the Prefect of Wǔlíng.
Tán Dàojì once sought a marriage alliance for his son with Zhàn,
but Zhàn firmly declined.
Dàojì then made the request through Yìkāng,
but Zhàn refused even more resolutely.
Thus, he was not implicated in the troubles of these two lords.
The Emperor heard of this and praised him.
Zhàn
was the son of Yí.
Jiāng Yí was employed at the beginning of the Yuánjiā era.
The Prince of Péngchéng, Liú Yìkāng, remained in the capital for over ten days.
When he went to bid farewell to the Emperor,
he then descended to the islet.
The Emperor could only weep bitterly in response,
and said nothing more.
The Emperor sent the monk Huìlín to see him.
Yìkāng asked:
"Does your disciple have any chance of returning?"
Huìlín replied:
"It is regrettable that you did not read several hundred volumes of books!"
Earlier,
the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, Xiè Shù,
was the younger brother of Xiè Yù.
Xiè Yù appears in scroll 115 of the *History of the Jin Dynasty*, in the fifth year of Yìxī of Emperor Ān of Jin.
He often offered admonitions and advice;
he died early.
When Yìkāng governed Jiānglíng,
Shù served as Chief Clerk of the General of Agile Cavalry and Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
When Yìkāng entered the capital as Prime Minister,
Shù again became Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education.
Shù,
is pronounced suǒ jiǎo.
He was about to be transferred south from Jiànkāng to Yùzhāng.
"In the past, only Xiè Shù urged me to withdraw,
while Liú Bān urged me to advance.
Now Bān survives and Shù is dead—
my downfall is only fitting!"
The Emperor also said:
"If Xiè Shù were alive,
Yìkāng would certainly not have come to this."
The Emperor appointed the Army Commander of the Campaign Against Barbarians, Xiāo Bǐn, as Advisory Army Officer for Yìkāng,
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
Matters great and small
were all entrusted to him.
Bǐn
was the son of Mózhi.
Xiāo Mózhi appears in the previous scroll, year twelve.
Those among Yìkāng's attendants who were cherished and remembered
were all permitted to accompany him.
His provisions and support were generous,
and gifts and allowances followed one after another.
Major affairs of the court were all reported and shown to him.
After some time,
the Emperor attended a banquet gathering with Princess Kuàijī,
and it was very joyful.
The Princess rose,
bowed twice and kowtowed,
overcome with grief.
The Emperor did not understand her meaning,
and rose to help her up.
The Princess said:
"Chēzi, in his later years, will surely not be tolerated by Your Majesty.
I now specifically beg for his life."
Yìkāng
had the childhood name Chēzi.
The Emperor also shed tears,
and pointing to Jiǎngshān, said:
"There will certainly be no such concern.
If I violate this oath today,
it would be to betray Chūnínglíng."
Emperor Gāozǔ was buried at Chūnínglíng,
located at Jiǎngshān.
He also wrote:
"Sister Kuàijī, while drinking at a banquet, remembered her younger brother.
The remaining wine is now sealed and sent."
Thus, for the rest of the Princess's life,
Yìkāng remained unharmed.
Your subject, Guāng, remarks: Emperor Wén's affection for Yìkāng,
the feelings of brotherly love,
were not initially lacking in depth.
Yet in the end, they lost the harmony of brothers,
and damaged the righteousness between ruler and minister.
Tracing the origin of the disorder,
it was precisely due to Liú Zhàn's insatiable heart for power and profit.
The *Book of Songs* says:
"The greedy man ruins his kind."
This is from Ruì Liángfū's poem "Sāngróu."
Ruin,
is pronounced bǔ mài.
16. The Emperor summoned the General of the Southern Campaign Against Barbarians and Prince of Jiāngxià, Liú Yìgōng, to serve as Minister of Education and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
On the wùyín day,
he appointed the Prince of Línchuān, Liú Yìqìng, as Governor of Yānzhōu.
Yīn Jǐngrén was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu,
remaining as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Minister of Personnel.
Yìgōng, taking warning from the failure at Péngchéng,
although he held overall responsibility,
merely carried out documents,
and the Emperor was thus put at ease.
Péngchéng
refers to Yìkāng.
Other matters were similar to this.
However, Yìgōng was by nature extravagant,
and his expenses were often insufficient.
The Emperor additionally gave him money,
amounting to tens of millions each year.
17. In the eleventh month,
on the dīnghài day,
the Wei Emperor went north of the mountains.
18. After Yīn Jǐngrén was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu,
his chronic illness grew severe.
The Emperor issued an order that no carriage noise be allowed on the roads of the Western District.
On the guǐchǒu day,
he died.
In the twelfth month,
on the guǐhài day,
the Emperor appointed the Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, Wáng Qiú, as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
On the wùchén day,
he appointed the Prince of Shǐxīng, Liú Jùn, as Governor of Yángzhōu.
At that time, Jùn was still young,
and the affairs of the province were all entrusted to the Rear Army Chief Clerk, Fàn Yè, and the Registrar, Shěn Pú.
Yè
was the son of Tài.
Pú
was the son of Línzǐ.
Fàn Tài was appreciated and loved by Emperor Gāozǔ.
Línzǐ followed Emperor Gāozǔ as a general and achieved merit.
The Emperor appointed the Gentleman of Personnel, Shěn Yǎnzhī, as General of the Right Guard,
jointly in charge of the imperial guard troops.
He also appointed Yǔ Bǐngzhī as Gentleman of Personnel,
and both participated in confidential matters.
Yǎnzhī
was the great-grandson of Jìn.
Shěn Jìn defended Luòyáng to the death,
to atone for his father Chōng's crime of rebellion.
Yè had outstanding talent,
but was shallow in emotion and conduct,
repeatedly violating moral teachings,
and was despised by the scholarly class.
He was by nature impatient and competitive,
and believed his talents were not fully utilized,
often feeling discontented and frustrated.
This sets the stage for Fàn Yè's later plot to rebel.
"Fàn Yè's aspirations and tendencies are abnormal.
I request that he be sent out to serve as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
If he remains within and trouble arises,
we will have no choice but to apply the axe of execution.
Frequent use of the executioner's axe
is not a good thing for the state."
The Emperor said:
"We have just executed Liú Zhàn,
and now we are transferring Fàn Yè.
People will say that you and others cannot tolerate talent,
and that I believe and accept slanderous words.
As long as we all know he is like this,
he cannot do any harm."
19. This year,
the Wei General of Pacifying the South, Wáng Huìlóng, died.
Lǚ Xuánbó guarded his tomb,
and never left for the rest of his life.
Huìlóng did not kill Xuánbó;
see the previous scroll, year eight.
20. The Wei emperor intended to appoint Yī Bá as Minister of Works and
enfeoff him as Duke of a Commandery.
Yī Bá declined, saying:
"The duties of the Minister of Works are heavy,
and the rank of Duke is of the utmost importance.
These are not positions that a young and foolish person like myself should presume to accept."
The emperor asked him what he desired instead.
He replied:
"The Central Secretariat and the Imperial Library both have many literary scholars.
(Central and Imperial Library refer to the Central Secretariat and the Imperial Library.)
I beg to be allowed to join their ranks."
The emperor approved of this
and appointed him as General of the Central Protector Army and Supervisor of the Imperial Library.
21. The Great King of Qin, Yáng Nándāng, resumed the title of King of Wǔdū.
(In the thirteenth year, Yáng Nándāng had proclaimed himself Great King of Qin.)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Wei appointed Jǔqú Wúhuì as Great General Who Conquers the West, Governor of Liáng Province, and King of Jiǔquán.
2. Prince Yìkāng of Péngchéng arrived at Yùzhāng.
He declined the post of Regional Inspector (he declined the post of Regional Inspector of Jiāng Province).
On the Jiǎchén day,
Yìkāng was appointed Commander of the military affairs of Jiāng, Jiāo, and Guǎng provinces.
The former Assistant to the Dragon-Soaring General, Fú Lìngyù of Bādōng, went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the past, Yuán Àng admonished Emperor Wén of Hàn, saying: 'If the King of Huáinán were to die from exposure to frost and dew on the road,
Your Majesty would bear the reputation of having killed your brother.'
Emperor Wén did not heed this advice and later regretted it endlessly.
(See the sixth year of Emperor Wén's reign, scroll 14.)
The beloved son of the previous dynasty,
Your Majesty's younger brother,
if he has committed errors and transgressions,
you should properly admonish him with good and evil,
guide him with righteousness and principle.
How can you, believing in doubtful suspicions,
suddenly demote and strip him of rank,
sending him far to the southern border!
Even the common people in the wilds
all ache for Your Majesty over this.
The past affair concerning Lúlíng
is sufficient to serve as a mirror.
(See the first year, scroll 120.)
If he were to perish suddenly in the south,
although I am lowly and insignificant,
I would secretly feel shame for Your Majesty.
Your Majesty only knows that an offending branch should be cut off,
but do you not know that cutting the branch injures the tree!
I humbly hope that you will urgently summon Yìkāng back to the capital region.
If brothers are harmonious
and ruler and ministers are amicable,
then the hopes of the realm will be blocked,
and the path of many words will be cut off.
Why must one be Minister Over the Masses and Governor of Yáng Province before one can establish Prince Péngchéng?
If what I have said is wrong for the state,
I beg to suffer severe punishment to apologize to Your Majesty."
When the memorial was presented,
he was immediately arrested and handed over to the Jiànkāng prison,
where he was ordered to commit suicide.
Commentary by Péi Zǐyě: When those above do good,
it is like clouds moving and rain falling;
all things receive their bounty.
When they do evil,
it is like the heavens splitting and the earth quaking;
all things are startled and terrified.
Who does not know of it?
Who does not see it?
How can killing one person's body
or gagging one man's mouth
allow one to evade
or extinguish it?
These are all cases of being unable to overcome anger and thereby increasing the ailment.
With Tàizǔ's magnanimity and tolerance,
he still covered his ears regarding the execution of Péngchéng.
From that time onward,
who dared to speak freely?
(Zhèng Xuán said: Yóu means 'to use'. Yì is pronounced with the 'chì' tone.)
Rarely do we hear of honest and sincere remonstrance.
Is it that the spirit of outspokenness
has made customs ashamed before the ancients?
Or is it the penal administration of the rulers of the time that has made it so?
Zhāng Yuē perished due to powerful ministers.
(The event is seen in the first year, scroll 120.)
The cauldrons of Sòng—
alas,
how fearsome!
3. The Prince of Xīnxīng of Wei, Jùn, was dissolute and lawless.
In the third month,
on the Gēngxū day,
he was demoted in rank to Duke.
Jùn's mother had previously been convicted and executed.
Jùn harbored resentment and discontent,
and plotted rebellion.
When the affair was discovered,
he was ordered to commit suicide.
4. On the Xīnhài day,
Wei granted Yùjiǔlǘ Qǐlièguī the title of King of Shuòfāng,
and Jǔqú Wànnián the title of King of Zhāngyē.
(In the sixteenth year, Wei captured Qǐlièguī. Jǔqú Wànnián also surrendered Gūzāng to Wei that year.)
5. In summer,
the fourth month,
Jǔqú Táng'ér rebelled against Jǔqú Wúhuì.
Wúhuì left his cousin Tiānzhōu to guard Jiǔquán
and led troops with his brother Yídé to attack Táng'ér.
Táng'ér was defeated and died.
Wei, considering that Wúhuì would ultimately be a border trouble,
on the Gēngchén day,
dispatched General Who Guards the South, Xī Juàn, to attack Jiǔquán.
6. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Wei sent the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Zhāng Wěi, to pay a courtesy visit.
7. In the ninth month,
on the Wùxū day,
the Prince of Yǒngchāng of Wei, Jiàn, died.
8. In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the Wùzǐ day,
Wáng Qiú died.
On the Jǐhài day,
Mèng Yǐ, the Governor of Dānyáng, was appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
9. In Jiǔquán city, the food was exhausted.
Over ten thousand people starved to death.
Jǔqú Tiānzhōu killed his wife to feed the soldiers.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Wei's Xī Juàn captured Jiǔquán,
captured Tiānzhōu,
sent him to Píngchéng,
and executed him.
Jǔqú Wúhuì, lacking food and fearing the strength of the Wei army,
planned to cross the shifting sands to the west.
He sent his brother Ānzhōu to attack Shànshàn to the west.
The King of Shànshàn intended to surrender,
but it happened that a Wei envoy arrived
and urged him to resist and hold out.
Ānzhōu could not overcome them
and retreated to defend the eastern city.
(The eastern city of the state of Shànshàn.)
10. The Dí king, Yáng Nándāng, mobilized his entire state to invade,
planning to seize the lands of Shǔ.
He sent his General Who Establishes Loyalty, Fú Chōng, to emerge from Dōngluò to resist the Liáng Province troops.

(Wǔdài Zhì: Jǐnggǔ County of Yìchéng Commandery was formerly Báishuǐ County. Later, Zhōu abolished Dōngluò Commandery and merged it. According to my investigation, Báishuǐ County belonged to Guǎnghàn in Hàn times, to Zǐtóng in Jìn times, and at this time belonged to Jìnshòu. Thus, Dōngluò was within the boundaries of Jìnshòu.)
Zhēndào was the son of Huáijìng. (Liú Huáijìng appears in the third year of Lóng'ān of Jìn Āndì, scroll 111.)
They captured the Administrator of Jìnshòu, Shēn Tǎn,
and then besieged Fúchéng.
The Administrators of Bāxī and Zǐtóng commanderies, Liú Dàoxī, defended the city and held firm.
Nándāng attacked for over ten days
but could not capture it,
and then withdrew.
Dàoxī was the younger brother of Dàochǎn.
In the twelfth month,
on the Guǐhài day,
an edict ordered the Dragon-Soaring General Péi Fāngmíng and others to lead three thousand armored soldiers,
and also mobilized troops from Jīng and Yōng provinces to attack Nándāng,
all under the command of Liú Zhēndào.

(Péi Fāngmíng was an excellent general of Yì Province. During the rebellions of Chéng Dàoyǎng and Zhào Guǎng, he repeatedly had military achievements, hence he was employed. This sets the stage for the pacification of Chóuchí the following year. Xiāng is pronounced 'sī jiāng fān'. Shuài is read as 'shuài'. Yōng is pronounced 'yú yòng fān'.)
Textual analysis note: The Dí-Hú biography says
"in the first month of the nineteenth year, Fāngmíng and others were dispatched."
Here we follow the Imperial Annals.
11. The Administrator of Jìnníng, Cuàn Sōngzǐ, rebelled.
The Regional Inspector of Níng Province, Xú Xún, attacked and pacified him.
(In the second year of Yǒng'ān of Jìn Huìdì, the seven western counties of Jiànníng were separated to form Yì Province Commandery. By the time of Huáidì, it was renamed Jìnníng Commandery.)
The Tiānmén barbarians Tián Xiàngqiú and others rebelled,
and overran Lóuzhōng.
Shěn Yuē said: Lóuzhōng County,
did not exist during the two Hàn dynasties,
but appears in the Jìn Tàikāng geographical records.
It is suspected to have been established during Wú,
and belonged to Tiānmén Commandery.
Lóu,
pronounced láng hóu fān.
13 Kòu Qiānzhī of Wèi spoke to the Wèi sovereign, saying:
"Now Your Majesty rules the world as a True Sovereign,
and has established the method of the Tranquil Wheel Celestial Palace.
Since ancient times,
there has never been such a thing.
You should ascend and receive the talismanic texts to manifest your sagely virtue."
The Emperor complied.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ proofread
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Student Tiān Tái
Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì Zhōng Zhī Zhōng
Yuánjiā 19th Year (Rénwǔ, 442)
1 Spring,
first month,
Jiǎshēn,
the Wèi sovereign prepared the imperial carriage,
went to the Daoist altar to receive the talismanic registers,
and all the banners were blue.
From then on, every emperor upon ascending the throne received the registers.
What was received here
is what present-day Daoists call the "method registers."
The Suīshū records: The method for a Daoist to receive the Way,
first receive the Five Thousand Character Register,
next receive the Three Caverns Register,
next receive the Cavern Mystery Register,
next receive the Supreme Clarity Register.
The registers are all written on plain silk,
recording the names of the celestial officials, subordinates, and assistants.
There are also various talismans interspersed among them,
the writing is strange and bizarre,
not recognized by the world.
Lù,
pronounced lóng yù fān.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Tranquil Wheel Palace is northeast of the Daoist altar,
the Daoist altar is east of Píngchéng on the left bank of the Lěi River.
It was intended to connect with the heavenly spirits above.
Cuī Hào urged the Emperor to build it,
the labor and expense amounted to tens of thousands,
and after a year it was still not completed.
The Crown Prince Huǎng admonished, saying:
"The Way of Heaven and the way of man are different,
the lowly and the lofty are fixed in their stations,
they cannot connect,
this principle is inevitable.
Now we are depleting the treasury in vain,
exhausting the common people,
for a useless endeavor,
what purpose will it serve!
If it must be as Qiānzhī says,
I request we use the ten-thousand-ren height of the Eastern Mountains,
referring to the Eastern Mountains of Píngchéng.
The Emperor did not listen.
2 Summer,
fourth month,
Jǔqú Wúhuì led over ten thousand households,
abandoned Dūnhuáng and went west to join Jǔqú Ānzhōu.
Before arriving,
the King of Shànshàn, Bǐlóng, fearing him,
led his people and fled to Qiěmò,
and his heir apparent surrendered to Ānzhōu.
Wúhuì then occupied Shànshàn,
and more than half of his soldiers died of thirst crossing the Liúshā desert.
Lǐ Bǎo from Yīwú led two thousand men and occupied Dūnhuáng,
repaired the city walls and government offices,
and settled the former inhabitants.
When Jǔqú Mùjiān perished,
see the previous scroll, year 16.
Jiān,
pronounced jū yán fān.
He proclaimed himself Grand Administrator.
Táng Qì was pressured by the Róurán,
gathered his followers and hurried west towards Gāochāng,
intending to seize its territory.
The Róurán sent their general Āruò to pursue and attack him,
Qì was defeated and died.
In the first year of Yíngyáng Wáng Jǐngpíng,
Qì fled to Yīwú together with Lǐ Bǎo.
At that time, Jǔqú Ānzhōu was stationed at Héngjié City,
Hé attacked and captured it,
and also captured the two cities of Gāoníng and Báilì.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The state of Gāochāng had forty-six garrisons,
Jiāohé, Tiándì, Gāoníng,
Báirèn, Héngjié, etc.;
the rest are not fully recorded.
"Báilì",
should be
"Báirèn".
3 Jiǎxū,
the Emperor, because his illness had recovered,
issued a great amnesty.
4 Fifth month,
Péi Fāngmíng and others arrived at Hànzhōng,
and together with Liú Zhēndào and others divided their forces to attack Wǔxīng, Xiàbiàn, and Báishuǐ,
capturing them all.
"Xiàbiàn",
the Hànshū writes as
"Xiàbiàn".
Bìng,
pronounced pí xiàn fān.
The Yuánfēng Jiǔyù Zhì: Jiānglì County in Jiē Prefecture had the Lángāo Garrison.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì,
Jiānglì County
was Shímén County of Wǔxīng Commandery during the Later Wèi.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Northwest of Wǔxīng is the Lángāo Garrison,
two hundred lǐ from Qiúchí.
"Fú",
I fear should be
"Fú";
the Yáng clan and the Fú clan,
were both of the Dī ethnicity.
Fāngmíng fought Hóngzǔ at Zhuóshuǐ,
Zhuóshuǐ City was southeast of Shànglù County,
northwest of Wǔjiē City.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Zhuóshuǐ is Báishuǐ.
Wǔjiē City was the former seat of Xiàbiàn County.
Hóngzǔ was beheaded;
Hé retreated and fled,
they pursued him to Chìtíng,
and again defeated him.
Nándāng fled to Shàngguī;
they captured Nándāng's nephew, the Jianjie General Bǎochì.
Nándāng had appointed his son Hǔ as Governor of Yì Province,
guarding Yīnpíng.
Hearing that Nándāng had fled,
Hǔ led his troops back,
arriving at Xiàbiàn;
Fāngmíng sent his son Sùzhī to intercept and attack him,
captured Hǔ,
sent him to Jiànkāng,
and executed him;
Qiúchí was pacified.
They appointed the Assistant Commander of the State, Hú Chóngzhī, as Governor of Northern Qín Province,
to guard the area;
established Yáng Bǎochì as the successor to Yáng Xuán,
and had him guard Qiúchí.
Yáng Nándāng deposed Xuán's son Bǎozōng and established himself,
see scroll 121, year 6.
Autumn, seventh month,
they appointed Liú Zhēndào as Governor of Yōng Province,
Péi Fāngmíng as Governor of Liáng and Southern Qín Provinces;
Fāngmíng declined and did not accept the appointment.
Examination of discrepancies: The biography of Zhēndào,
places this event after Hú Chóngzhī's defeat;
the biography of the Dī and Hú,
places Chóngzhī's defeat in the second month of the following year;
thus the biography of Zhēndào is mistaken.
Bǐngyín,
the Wèi sovereign sent the General of Pacifying the West, Gǔ Bì
Examination of discrepancies: The Sòng biography of the Suǒlú writes
"Tǔxī Ài Bì",
the biography of the Dī and Hú writes
"Tǔxī Bì",
probably his original surname.
Now follow the Later Wèi Shū.
and the King of Wǔdū, Yáng Bǎozōng, to enter from the south of Qíshān,
Bǎozōng fled to Wèi, see the previous scroll, year 16.
and to join forces at Qiúchí.
He also sent the Prince of Qiáo, Sīmǎ Wénsī, to supervise the armies of Luò and Yù and head south towards Xiāngyáng,
in the second year of Yíngyáng Wáng Jǐngpíng,
Wèi took Hénán,
established Luò Province at Luòyáng,
and Yù Province at Hǔláo.
Qū,
pronounced qī yù fān;
same below.

Actions,

Words with the prestigious competition,

Shāo,

A grievance for a hundred generations?

In the end,

Yè was still hesitant and undecided.

Yè's household lacked inner conduct,

Yè remained silent,

Yè and Shěn Yǎnzhī were both known by the emperor,

Xiè Zòng and his father Shù,

Dānyáng Yǐn Xú Zhànzhī,

Taoist Fǎ Luè and the nun Fǎ Jìng,

Names and reasons were detailed,

The North Star is the celestial pole,

Seal,

Ribbon,

That night,

Examination of Discrepancies states: The Annals of Emperor Wén of Sòng record:

It seems Sòng and Wei each recorded the month when the reports arrived.

"The invaders plundered Tàiyuán,

Probably the Wei people exaggerated the numbers,

The Emperor was worried about the Wei incursions,

Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Hé Chéngtiān submitted a memorial,

"All strategies for defending against the Xiōngnú [Wei]
fall into just two categories: military men exhaust plans for conquest,

If we now wish to follow in the footsteps of Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbīng,
unless we extensively cultivate fields in the Huái and Sì regions,
and internally enrich Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu,

to sweep them away in one stroke,

in retaliation for their invasions and violence,
then they will certainly flee swiftly on light cavalry,
unwilling to engage in battle;
we would only incur enormous expense,
without harming them,
and retaliatory campaigns
would then never cease.
This is the most inferior of strategies.
Securing the borders and holding firm in defense
is the better plan.
I consider that when Cáo and Sūn held hegemony,
their talents were equal and their wisdom matched.
Between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
they did not occupy territory within several hundred *li* of each other.
Cáo and Sūn refer to Cáo Cāo and Sūn Quán.
The borderlands where scouts operated
were not areas for farming or herding.
Therefore, they strengthened their defenses, cleared the fields, and awaited the enemy's arrival,
kept their armor in order and their weapons repaired to exploit their weakness;
protecting the people and preserving the entire territory
does not depart from this path.
To summarize and conclude,
the strategy has four points: First is moving those far away closer.
Now the original people of Qīng and Yǎn, and the newly attached of Jìzhōu,
who are at the border, number over thirty thousand households.
They can all be relocated and settled south of the Dàxiàn Mountains,

Second is building many walled towns to house the newly relocated families,

so they farm and herd in spring and summer,

When the invaders arrive,
with one town of a thousand households,
the men fit for battle
will be no fewer than two thousand.
The remaining weak and elderly
can still mount the walls and raise a clamor,
sufficient to resist thirty thousand enemy troops.
Third is assembling paired oxen and carts to transport grain and equipment.
Assembling means
gathering together.
With no fewer than five hundred pairs of oxen,

The various generals wanted to send them to Píngchéng,

"Cháng'ān is strategically secure and fortified,

If we do not behead Wú now,

Wú himself is hiding in flight;

If we halt a hundred thousand troops to pursue one man,

It would be better to secretly promise Wú's uncles,
spare their wives and children,
and have them pursue Wú themselves.
They will certainly capture him."
The various generals all said:
"Now the bandit's followers have already scattered,

What can he possibly accomplish?"
Sì said:
"Have you gentlemen not seen a venomous snake!
If you do not cut off its head,

If he escapes now,

The generals said:
"What you say is right.

and instead send him away,

Sì said:

The Prince of Gāoliáng, Nà, also considered Sì's plan sound,

*Textual Analysis* says: The Wèi Imperial Annals state:

These are all boastful words from Wèi history;
