The various armies took advantage of the situation to attack,
and Yìxuān’s troops also collapsed.
Yìxuān fled alone in a small boat,
shutting the door and weeping,
with over a hundred boats from Jīngzhōu still following him.
Zhì wanted to meet Yìxuān to discuss matters,
but Yìxuān had already left.
Zhì did not know what to do,
so he also fled.
His followers all surrendered or scattered.
On the jǐwèi day,
the state of emergency was lifted.
9 On the guǐhài day,
Liú Yánsūn, the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, was appointed as the Right Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
10 In the sixth month,
on the bǐngyín day,
the Wei Emperor went to Yīnshān.
11 Zāng Zhì reached Xúnyáng,
burned down the government buildings,
and fled westward with his singing girls and concubines.
He ordered his favorite attendant Hé Wénjìng to lead the remaining troops ahead,
reaching Xīyáng.
The Grand Administrator of Xīyáng, Lǔ Fāngpíng, deceived Wénjìng, saying:
“The imperial decree only seeks to capture the chief culprit;
the rest will not be pursued.
It would be better for you to flee.”
Wénjìng abandoned his troops and fled.
Zhì had previously appointed his brother-in-law Yáng Chōng as the Grand Administrator of Wǔchāng Commandery.
According to the Jìn Dynasty Records of Daily Life: In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, Jiāngxià was renamed Wǔchāng Commandery.
Also, according to the Jìn Dynasty Records,
the Wu ruler Sūn Quán established Wǔchāng Commandery in Dōng’è.
This is now Shòuchāng Army.
Chōng had already been killed by the Commandery Assistant Hú Pìzhī,
so Zhì had nowhere to go.
He then fled to Nán Lake.
Nán Lake is now located eight lǐ east of Wǔchāng County in Shòuchāng Army.
When the pursuing troops arrived,
he covered his head with lotus leaves,
submerged himself in the water,
and exposed only his nose.
On the wùchén day,
the army commander Zhèng Jù’ér spotted him,
shot an arrow,
hitting the center of his body.
Soldiers swarmed in with blades,
and his intestines tangled with water plants.
His head was cut off and sent to Jiànkāng.
His sons and grandsons were all executed in the marketplace,
and his associates, including the Grand Administrator of Lè’ān
Rén Huìzhī,
the Interior Historian of Línchuān Liú Huáizhī, and the Grand Administrator of Póyáng Dù Zhòngrú, were also executed.
Zhòngrú
was the nephew of Dù Jì.
Dù Jì
served as the Inspector of Qīngzhōu during the Yuánjiā era.
The Chancellor Liú Yìxuān fled to Jiāngxià.
Hearing that there were troops at Bālíng,
the troops at Bālíng
were likely Wéi Sōng's soldiers;
some said they were the troops of Liú Zūnkǎo, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ fān.
His followers scattered and were nearly all gone.
With about ten attendants on foot,
his feet were sore and he could not proceed.
He hired a civilian's open cart to carry himself,
begging for food along the way.
Upon reaching the outskirts of Jiānglíng,
he sent someone to inform Zhú Chāomín.
Chāomín prepared ceremonial guards and troops to welcome him.
At that time, Jīngzhōu still had over ten thousand armored soldiers.
His attendant Zhái Língbǎo advised Yìxuān to comfort his generals and officers,
saying:
"Zāng Zhì violated the proper directives,
leading to our defeat.
Now we should train troops and repair armor,
and plan for the future.
In the past, Hàn Gāozǔ suffered a hundred defeats,
yet ultimately achieved great success..."
But Yìxuān forgot Língbǎo's words,
mistakenly saying
"Xiàng Yǔ suffered a thousand defeats,"
causing everyone to cover their mouths.
Covering their mouths to laugh.
Yìxuān was confused and dispirited,
no longer maintaining his composure.
He entered his quarters and did not come out again.
His close attendants and confidants gradually deserted him.
Lǔ Xiù fled north.
Examination of discrepancies says: Sòng Lüè states:
"Xiù retreated after defeat at Xiāngyáng,
and as he approached Jiānglíng,
hearing of the defeat, he fled north."
Now follow the Sòng Shū.
Wishing to follow Xiù,
he took his son Tāo
(son,
meaning child)
dressed in men's clothing to accompany him.
The city was in turmoil,
with blades crossing everywhere.
Yìxuān was afraid,
fell from his horse,
and proceeded on foot.
Zhú Chāomín escorted him outside the city,
gave him another horse,
then returned to guard the city.
Yìxuān could not find Xiù,
and his attendants all abandoned him.
At night,
he returned to the empty office of Nánjùn;
the office of the Governor of Nánjùn,
likely located outside Jiānglíng city.
Xiè,
read as gǔ ài fān.
Chāomín arrested and sent him to the Cìjiān.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
government offices have had Cìjiān officials.
Sitting on the ground, he sighed:
"That old slave Zāng Zhì misled me!"
His five concubines were soon sent away.
Yìxuān wept and wailed,
saying to the prison officer:
"Ordinary days were not bitter,
but today's separation is truly bitter."
Lǔ Xiù's followers scattered,
and he could not leave.
Returning toward Jiānglíng,
people on the city walls shot at him.
Xiù threw himself into the water and died.
They retrieved his head.
An edict ordered the Right Deputy Liú Xiào
Sūn to go to Jīng and Jiāng provinces,
to distinguish right from wrong,
and carry out executions and rewards accordingly;
also to divide the lands of the two provinces,
discussing the establishment of a new province.
Thus, lands from Jīng, Xiāng, Jiāng, and Yù were divided to establish Yǐngzhōu.
Initially,
when the Jìn moved south,
they made Yángzhōu the capital region,
from which grain and cloth were supplied;
they made Jīng and Jiāng important garrisons,
where all armored troops were concentrated;
often placing great generals there.
The population of these three provinces
accounted for half of Jiāngnán.
The Emperor disliked their strength,
so he wished to divide them.
On Guǐwèi,
five eastern Zhèjiāng counties of Yángzhōu were separated to establish Dōngyángzhōu,
with its seat at Kuàijī;
the five counties: Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Yǒngjiā, Línhǎi, Xīn'ān.
Kuài,
read as gōng wài fān.
Governing Jiāngxià;
dividing Jīngzhōu's Jiāngxià, Jìnglíng, Suí, Wǔlíng, Tiānmén, Xiāngzhōu's Bālíng, Jiāngzhōu's Wǔchāng, and Yùzhōu's Xīyáng, totaling eight counties.
According to Yǒngchū Jùnguózhì and Hé Chéngtiān's records,
the Governor of Jiāngxià originally governed from Ānlù,
but after this moved to govern Xiàkǒu;
now Èzhōu governs Jiāngxià County, which is that location.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ fān;
the following Xiàkǒu is the same.
Their camp was moved to Jiànkāng.
Jìn Wǔdì established the Protector of the Southern Mán Colonel at Xiāngyáng,
abolished early in Jiāngzuǒ,
but soon reestablished at Jiānglíng.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Southern Mán Colonel's office was at Fāngchéng;
from Yóukǒu eastward,
camps were connected,
all being garrisons of the Southern Mán office.
Xiào,
read as hù jiào fān.
The Minister Hé Shàngzhī said:
"Xiàkǒu is in the middle of Jīng and Jiāng,
directly facing Miǎnkǒu,
connecting to Yōng and Liáng,
truly a crucial crossing.
From Xiàkǒu entering the Miǎn River,
going upstream,
to Xiāngyáng,
and further upstream to Hànzhōng,
hence it connects to Yōng and Liáng.
Yōng,
read as yú yòng fān.
Its foundation is not easy to change,
Xiàkǒu has been an important garrison since Wú times.
The harbor is large enough for ships,
which is convenient for affairs."
For defending the river,
ships are most urgent,
hence a large harbor for ships is convenient.
Fǎng,
read as fǔ wàng fān.
Subsequently, Jīng and Yáng became depleted.
Shàngzhī requested to reunite the two provinces,
but the Emperor did not allow it.
12 On Wùzǐ,
the office of Lù Shàngshū Shì was abolished.
The Emperor disliked the strength of the imperial clan,
not wanting power in subjects' hands;
the Grand Tutor Liú Yìgōng knew his intention,
hence requested its abolition.
13 The Emperor had dukes, ministers, and the eight high officials write to the Governor of Jīngzhōu, Zhū Xiūzhī,
Jìn Zhì says: The five department heads, one deputy, and two ministers are the eight high officials.
Sòng likely had two deputies,
one minister.
Before the letter arrived,
on Gēngyín,
Xiūzhī entered Jiānglíng,
killed Yìxuān,
and also executed his sixteen sons,
along with accomplices Zhú Chāomín, Attendant Officer Cài Chāo, Consultant Cānjūn Yán Lèzhī, etc.
Chāomín's brothers should have been executed as well,
but Hé Shàngzhī memorialized:
"Once the rebels fled,
one man could capture them.
If Chāomín were duplicitous and greedy,
he would have seized them,
not only avoiding blame,
but also gaining unrighteous rewards.
Yet Chāomín had no such intention,
slightly showing that observing faults reveals benevolence.
Hé Shàngzhī said this to intercede for Zhú Chāomín's brothers.
Yāo,
read as yī yáo fān.
He carefully guarded the treasury,
sitting calmly awaiting arrest.
Now executing his brothers
would make them no different from other rebels,
which is excessive in affairs."
The Emperor then pardoned them.
14 Autumn,
seventh month,
on Bǐngshēn, first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 On Gēngzǐ,
the Wèi prince Hóng was born;
on Xīnchǒu,
a great amnesty was declared,
changing the era name to Xīngguāng.
16 On Bǐngchén,
a great amnesty was declared.
17 Eighth month,
on Jiǎxū,
the Wèi Prince of Zhào, Shēn, died.
18 On Yǐhài,
the Wèi sovereign returned to Píngchéng.
This year in summer,
it records the Wèi sovereign going to Yīnshān.
In the winter of the 19th year,
in the eleventh month,
on the Wùxū day,
the Wei ruler went to Zhōngshān,
and then proceeded to Xìndū;
in the twelfth month,
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
he returned,
visiting Língqiū,
Língqiū County had belonged to Dài Commandery since the Hàn dynasty,
and in the Táng dynasty it became Yùzhōu.
On the Gēngchén day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
1 In the spring,
in the first month,
the Wei Chariot and Horse General Yuèpíng Wáng Bá was ordered to commit suicide for his crimes.
2 The Great General Who Guards the North and Governor of Nányǎn, Shěn Qìngzhī, requested retirement due to old age;
in the second month,
on the Bǐngyín day,
he was appointed as Left Brilliantly Virtuous Grand Master and granted the privilege of establishing a personal administrative office.
Qìngzhī firmly declined,
submitting dozens of memorials,
and personally pleading in audience,
even to the point of kowtowing and weeping.
The Emperor could not force him,
so he allowed him to retire to his residence as the Duke of Shǐxīng,
with generous provisions.
Shortly after,
the Emperor again wanted to employ Qìngzhī,
sending Hé Shàngzhī to persuade him to return.
Shàngzhī repeatedly conveyed the Emperor's intentions,
but Qìngzhī laughed and said:
"Shěn does not imitate Hé,
who goes and returns again."
Shàngzhī could not persist,
see volume 126, the 28th year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign.
On the Xīnsì day,
Shàngshū Right Deputy Liú Yánsūn was appointed as Governor of Nányǎn.
3 In the summer,
in the fifth month,
on the Wùxū day,
Liú Zūnkǎo, Governor of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed as Shàngshū Right Deputy.
4 In the sixth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Wei changed its era name to Tài'ān.
5 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
6 On the Jiǎshēn day,
the Wei ruler returned to Píngchéng.
The history also does not record the places he visited.
7 In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Guǐsì day,
the Emperor's younger brother Xiūyòu was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shānyáng,
Xiūmào as the Prince of Hǎilíng,
and Xiūyè as the Prince of Póyáng.
8 On the Bǐngchén day,
the Wei ruler went to Héxī.
9 The Governor of Yōngzhōu, Prince of Wǔchāng Hún
(after Zhū Xiūzhī had already gone to Jiānglíng,
and Liǔ Yuánjǐng remained in Jiànkāng,
Hún was appointed as Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Yōng,
pronounced as yòng.
) proclaimed himself Prince of Chǔ,
changed the era name to Yǒngguāng,
established a full set of officials,
treating it as a joke.
Chief Clerk Wáng Yìzhī sealed and presented his handwritten documents.
In the eighth month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
Hún was deposed as a commoner,
and exiled to Shǐ'ān Commandery.
The Emperor sent the Extraordinary Attendant Gentleman Dài Míngbǎo of Dōnghǎi to interrogate and reprimand Hún,
sǎn,
pronounced as sǎn.
qí,
pronounced as qí.
jié,
pronounced as jié.
He was seventeen years old at the time.
10 On the Dīnghài day,
the Wei ruler returned to Píngchéng.
11 An edict was issued to sacrifice at the suburban altars and ancestral temple,
initially setting up ceremonial music,
following the proposal of the former Palace Central Section Gentleman Xún Wànqiū.
After the Jìn dynasty moved south and was newly established,
the two suburban sacrifices had no music;
although the ancestral temple had songs for ascending,
it also lacked the two dances.
After defeating Fú Jiān,
obtaining musicians,
they began to have metal and stone music.
In the 22nd year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign,
at the southern suburban sacrifice,
they first set up songs for ascending.
What is called ceremonial music here,
is not the ability to prepare elegant music,
but the secular music since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties.
In the second year of Emperor Shùn's Shēngmíng reign,
Wáng Sēngqián said
"the court's rituals and music often violate the old codes,"
probably referring to this kind.
12 The Emperor wanted to weaken the kings and marquises.
In the winter,
in the tenth month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Prince of Jiāngxià Yìgōng and Prince of Jìnglíng Dàn memorialized to reduce
the regulations for kings' and marquises' carriages, clothing, utensils, and music and dance,
totaling nine items;
the Emperor then hinted to the officials to memorialize to expand them to twenty-four articles:
In the audience hall,
they may not sit facing south,
nor set up curtains and screens.
Officials of vassal states, in the first and winter months, may not go barefoot to ascend the state hall or serve alongside the state tutor,
transmit orders, or carry oiled halberds.
Princesses may not transmit orders in red clothing.
Carriages may not have double crossbars.
Screens may not have pheasant tails.
Lance tassels may not be made of peacock feathers or white otter fur.
Escort teams may not wear crimson jackets.
Ordinary riding horses may not exceed two.
Barbarian performers may not wear colorful clothes.
Female dancers in the first and winter months must wear formal robes,
and may not wear makeup or cover flowers.
In the first and winter month gatherings, sword dances and cup tray dances are not allowed.
Long stilts performances, throwing balls and swords, Bóshān performances, climbing large poles performances, and five table performances,
unless performed at the first and winter month gatherings, dance music may not be played.
Various lords may not wear embroidered belts.
Signal banners,
unless for officials of the central departments, must all be crimson.
Commandery and county administrators, chancellors, and officials within the fief,
regarding their enfeoffed lord,
since they are not among the three (heaven, earth, and ruler),
after leaving office they need not continue to show respect;
they should not be called subjects,
but only show official respect from superior to subordinate.
Various garrison commanders' regular traveling carriages,
the escort before and after may not exceed six teams,
white-clad escorts alongside the carriage are not included in this limit;
swords may not have silver or copper decorations.
Daughters of various kings enfeoffed as county mistresses,
sons and grandsons of various kings inheriting fiefs,
wives of kings and enfeoffed marquises,
in processions may not have honor guards.
Sons of various kings succeeding as kings,
in weddings and funerals, auspicious and inauspicious events,
must all follow the rituals of dukes and marquises of states,
and may not be the same as the Emperor's younger brothers and sons.
Carriages other than light carriages may not have oiled canopies.
Ordinary boats must be flat at both ends,
shaped like an exposed flat surface,
and may not imitate dragon boats.
None may have red oiled curtains.
Inlays may not be made in five-flower or vertical bamboo shoot shapes.
Swords may not be shaped like pulley wheels;
Jìn Zhuó said: ancient long swords,
had jade heads shaped like well pulleys.
They may not be called subjects,
after leaving office they need not continue to show respect.
The edict approved.
13 On the Gēngwǔ day,
Wei appointed Liáoxī Wáng Chángyīng as Grand Steward.
14 On the Rénwǔ day,
Grand Tutor Yìgōng was appointed to concurrently serve as Governor of Yángzhōu,
Prince of Jìnglíng Dàn as Minister of Works and concurrently Governor of Nánxúzhōu,
and Prince of Jiànpíng Hóng as Shàngshū Ling.
15 In this year,
the son of the former Dí king Yáng Bǎozōng, Yuánhé, was appointed as General Who Conquers Barbarians,
and Yáng Tóu as General Who Supports the State.
Tóu,
was a cousin of Wéndé.
Although Yuánhé was the legitimate heir of the Yáng clan,
the court considered him young and weak in talent,
and did not formally grant him the title;
the tribe had no fixed leader.
Tóu had previously garrisoned Jiālú,
his mother, wife, children, and younger brothers were all captured by Wei,
in the 20th year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign,
when Wei captured Chóuchí,
Yáng Wéndé was defeated and fled;
Tóu's mother, wife, children, and younger brothers were captured by Wei,
which should have been in that year.
In the 27th year,
Tóu was first sent to garrison Jiālú.
The Governor of Yōngzhōu, Wáng Xuánmó, memorialized:
"Request to appoint Tóu as Acting Jie, Governor of Xīqínzhōu,
to pacify and settle his people.
After several years,
when Yuánhé has grown somewhat,
let him inherit the former domain.
If Yuánhé's talent is not suitable,
then it should be returned to Tóu.
Tóu can defend the Hàn River region,
preventing barbarian troubles,
those four thousand households in a remote province are hardly worth regretting.
If Jiālú is not held,
the Hàn River region will also have no basis for existence."
The Emperor did not follow this advice.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Gēngyín day,
the Emperor’s younger brother Xiūfàn was enfeoffed as Prince of Shùnyáng,
and Xiūruò as Prince of Bālíng.
On the Wùxū day,
the Emperor’s son Zǐshàng was enfeoffed as Prince of Xīyáng.
2. On the Rénzǐ day,
the daughter of Right Guard General Hé Yǔ was taken as consort for the Crown Prince.
Yǔ
was the great-grandson of Hé Chéng.
On the Jiǎyín day,
a general amnesty was declared.
3. On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Wei ruler elevated his concubine, Lady Féng, to Empress.
The Empress
was the daughter of Féng Lǎng, Duke of Liáoxī Commandery;
Féng Lǎng’s surrender to Wei is recorded in the 122nd scroll, in the ninth year of Emperor Wén’s Yuánjiā era.
He was executed for involvement in an affair,
and as a result, the Empress was taken into the palace.
This laid the groundwork for Empress Féng’s monopolization of Wei’s government.
4. In the second month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the Wei ruler established his son Hóng as Crown Prince,
first having his mother, Concubine Lǐ, write down a list of her entrusted brothers,
and then, following precedent, ordering her to commit suicide.
5. On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Zōng Què, Governor of Guǎngzhōu, was appointed Governor of Yùzhōu.
According to precedent,
when matters were discussed within a commandery or province,
a summary of the matters discussed was written on a slip beforehand,
and a Diǎnqiān was appointed to oversee it.
In the Sòng dynasty, many of the imperial princes appointed as regional commanders were young,
so the reigning sovereigns often had close attendants serve as Diǎnqiān,
and the authority of the Diǎnqiān gradually increased.
By this time,
even when adult princes governed frontier regions
or common clans were sent out as commanders,
the Diǎnqiān handled the issuance and reception of orders,
holding the pivotal authority,
and the Regional Inspector could not exercise his duties independently.
When Què became Governor of Yùzhōu,
Wú Xǐ of Lín’ān served as Diǎnqiān.
Wú divided Yúháng to establish Línshuǐ County,
and in the first year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Lín’ān,
belonging to Wúxīng Commandery.
Xǐ frequently disobeyed and contested decisions,
and Què became greatly enraged,
saying:
“Zōng Què is nearly sixty years old,
and has exhausted his life for the state,
yet I have only obtained a province as small as a dou measure.
alternatively written as
Xǐ kowtowed until his forehead bled,
and only then did Què relent.
6. Several thousand families of Dīnglíng hid in the Jǐngxíng Mountains and became bandits.
The Wei Minister of Personnel, Lù Zhēn
(Chūxuéjì: Emperor Chéng of Hàn established four Departmental Ministers,
one of them being the Regular Attendant Department;
Emperor Guāngwǔ renamed the Regular Attendant Department as the Ministry of Personnel,
responsible for appointments;
Emperor Líng renamed the Ministry of Personnel as the Ministry of Selections.)
In early Northern Wei, there were five Ministers: Palace, Music, Carriages, Southern, and Northern;
the Minister of Selections was likely established around this time.
7. In the intercalary month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Liú Zūnkǎo, Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed Governor of Dānyáng.
8. On the Guǐyǒu day,
Prince of Póyáng, the Mourned, Xiūyè, passed away.
9. The Grand Tutor, Yìgōng, because Xīyáng Prince Zǐshàng, Governor of Nányǎnzhōu, was favored,
intended to avoid him,
and thus resigned from Yángzhōu.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yìgōng was relieved of Yángzhōu;
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Zǐshàng was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
At that time, Mars remained in the Southern Dipper,
and the Emperor abandoned the old offices in Xīzhōu,
having Zǐshàng move his administration to the eastern city to counteract it.
Shěn Huáiwén, Assistant to the Governor of Yángzhōu, said:
“Heavenly phenomena show changes,
and we should respond with virtue.
Now, even if we empty Xīzhōu,
I fear it will be of no benefit.”
He was not heeded.
Huáiwén
was the elder brother of Huáiyuǎn.
10. In the eighth month,
the Wei General Who Pacifies the West, Yùjuàn, Duke of Yúyáng, attacked Yīwú,
captured its city,
and returned with great spoils.
Lǐ Bǎo surrendered Yīwú and Dūnhuáng to Wei.
After Bǎo entered the court,
Yīwú rebelled again,
hence the attack.
(Yù,
pronounced yūwù.)
(Huán,
pronounced xuān,
or as usual.)
11. In the ninth month,
on the Rénxū day,
Liú Zūnkǎo, Governor of Dānyáng, was appointed Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
12. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
the Wei ruler returned to Píngchéng.
(Also, the place he went to is not recorded.)
13. On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Grand Tutor, Yìgōng, was promoted to Grand Steward,
concurrently serving as Minister of Education.
14. In the eleventh month,
Wei appointed Yuán Hè, Minister of the Western Pacification, as Governor of Jìzhōu,
and further enfeoffed him as Prince of Lǒngxī.
Hè memorialized:
“Now the northern barbarians roam like ghosts,
and the southern bandits rely on their strongholds,
so on the borders,
defense garrisons are still necessary.
In my humble opinion,
except for those guilty of great treason or bare-handed murder,
those sentenced to death for corruption, theft, or accidental offenses
could all be pardoned,
and exiled to guard the frontiers;
then those with severed bodies would receive the grace of rebirth,
and families burdened by corvée would enjoy the benefit of respite.”
Emperor Gāozōng of Wei followed this.
After some time,
he said to his ministers:
“By adopting Hè’s suggestion,
many lives have been spared in a year,
and the garrison troops have also increased.
If each of you were like Hè,
what would I have to worry about!”
It happened that Shí Huá of Wǔyì accused Hè of plotting rebellion.
(Wǔyì County,
in the Western Hàn belonged to Xìndū,
in the Eastern Hàn to Ānpíng,
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn separately established Wǔyì Commandery,
and by Suí and Táng times, it comprised the three counties of Wǔyì, Wǔqiáng, and Héngshuǐ.)
The Emperor said:
“Hè has served the state with utmost loyalty,
and I guarantee to you all
that there is no such thing,
it is clear.”
He ordered a thorough investigation;
Huá indeed admitted to false accusation,
confessing his crime of false accusation.
The Emperor then said to his attendants:
“Even with Hè’s loyalty,
he still could not avoid slander;
those inferior to Hè—can they not be cautious!”
15. In the twelfth month,
the Administrators of Púyáng, Jiāng Lóngjū, and of Xīnpíng, Yáng Zìlún, abandoned
their commanderies and fled to Wei.
(According to Shěn Yuē’s records: Púyáng and Xīnpíng both belonged to Yǎnzhōu, but their seats are not recorded,
likely being émigré commanderies.
Xīnpíng Commandery,
also established in the seventh year of Emperor Míng’s Tàishǐ era,
should be examined.
Also according to Wǔdài Zhì: Juànchéng County formerly established Púyáng Commandery.
Pú,
pronounced bómù.)
16. The Emperor intended to move the combined garrison of Qīng and Jì Provinces to Lìchéng,
but many in the discussions disagreed.
Yuán Hùzhī, Governor of Qīng and Jì Provinces, said:
“To the north of Qīng Province are the Yellow River and Jì River,
and there are many marshes,
which are not routes favored by the barbarians;
whenever they come to raid,
they must pass through Lìchéng.
Combining the two provinces into one garrison
is a far-sighted strategy.
Moreover, it is close to the river in the north,
making it easy for those who submit to return.
In the near term, it relieves the people’s distress,
and in the long term, it extends the royal prestige—
this is the best plan for securing the border.”
Thus, it was decided.
(Qīng Province originally administered Dōngyáng,
Jì Province administered Lìchéng,
now they were combined into one garrison.)
In the Yuánjiā era (424–453),
the government minted four-zhū coins,
with rims and outer edges,
their shape and specifications being the same as the five-zhū coins.
However, the cost of minting was unprofitable,
meaning the expense of casting one coin was exactly equal to the value of one coin,
leaving no profit margin.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he also minted the Xiàojiàn four-zhū coins,
which were thin, small in form,
and lacked proper rims and edges.
(A coin:
the outer circle is the rim,
the inner square is the edge.)
They were adulterated with lead and tin;
people clipped and filed down old coins,
causing coins to become increasingly thin and small.
Local officials were unable to prohibit this,
and those sentenced to death or dismissed from office followed one another.
Counterfeiting grew even more severe,
commodity prices soared,
and the imperial court was troubled by this.
Last spring,
an edict was issued that thin, small coins without rims or edges could not circulate,
causing great disturbance among the people.
That year,
the Duke of Shǐxīng Commandery, Shěn Qìngzhī, proposed,
suggesting that
"It would be appropriate to allow the people to mint coins,
establishing coin offices in the commanderies and counties,
where families willing to mint coins would all reside within the offices,
standardizing their models and specifications,
and eliminating adulteration and counterfeiting.
The new coins prohibited last spring
should be permitted for use for a time,
and all current minting should follow this standard.
A tax of three thousand per ten thousand [coins minted] should be levied,
and counterfeiting should be strictly inspected."
(Jiǎn:
to bind,
to investigate.)
It was also suggested that
"The weight of the five-zhū coin,
established during the Hàn dynasty,
(Emperor Wǔ of Hàn implemented the five-zhū coin in the fifth year of the Yuánshòu era.)
cannot be altered;
truly, because goods and currency were already balanced,
changing them would give rise to counterfeiting.
Now it is said that the coins prohibited last spring should be permitted for use for a time;
if coins of all sizes are allowed to circulate without following official minting,
the profits for individuals would be too great,
and fraud would know no bounds,
private minting and clipping would become completely unstoppable,
wealth and goods would not be sufficient,
large coins would be exhausted,
and within a few years,
they would all turn to dust.
Now that the new prohibition has just been implemented,
the standards and forms are not yet unified,
and the disturbance will cease of its own accord in a short while,
it is not worth causing Your Majesty concern;
only the emptiness of the government treasury
is truly a grave worry.
Even if small coins are allowed to circulate now,
it is unreasonable for the government to increase taxes;
although the common people may become prosperous,
it will not relieve the government's shortage.
Only by reducing expenses and eliminating extravagance,
focusing solely on frugality,
can the way to sufficiency be found;
nothing is more important than this."
Others in the discussion suggested that
"Copper is increasingly difficult to obtain,
so we should mint two-zhū coins."
Yán Jùn said:
"Those in the discussion believe the government treasury is empty,
so the coinage should be changed;
copper is scarce in the empire,
so the coin standard should be reduced to remedy both crises.
(The government treasury is empty,
with no coins to meet expenses,
and copper is scarce in the empire,
so there is nothing to mint coins with—
these are both crises.)
Those in the discussion therefore wish to mint smaller coins to remedy this.
(Shǎo:
pronounced as in the poem Zhǎo.)
Zhèn:
to enrich,
also to relieve or rescue.)
Shū:
to relax,
to ease.)
Zhèn:
pronounced jīn rěn.)
If we now mint two-zhū coins,
allowing new, small coins to circulate freely,
it will not relieve the government's shortage,
but will greatly encourage fraud and craftiness among the people;
the goods of the empire will be ground to dust and utterly exhausted.
Merely establishing strict prohibitions in vain,
while the profits are deep and difficult to stop,
within a year or two,
the harm will be beyond remedy.
(Meaning the harm will become severe before a year or two have passed.)
Fù:
pronounced fú yòu.)
Moreover, fearing the recent new prohibitions,
in the markets and streets,
disputes and disturbances are bound to arise.
Long-term benefits are not yet seen,
but immediate troubles are heaped upon us;
wealthy merchants will have their way,
while the poor will be trapped in hardship—
all of these are extremely unacceptable."
The proposal was then abandoned.
18. The Governor of Dìng Province of Wèi, Xǔ Zōngzhī of Gāoyáng, was unrestrained in his demands and exactions.
Mǎ Chāo, a commoner of Shēnzé, spoke ill and slandered Zōngzhī.
(Shēnzé County:
during the Former Hàn, it belonged to Zhuō Commandery;
during the Later Hàn, it belonged to Ānpíng;
from the Jìn onward, it belonged to Bólíng Commandery.
Later, Wèi's Bólíng Commandery belonged to Dìng Province.
The Táng changed Bólíng Commandery to Dìng Province,
later dividing Dìng Province to establish Qí Province,
with Shēnzé County belonging to it.)
Fearing that Mǎ Chāo's family would file a complaint,
Zōngzhī accused Chāo of defaming and slandering the court's governance.
Emperor Gāozōng of Wèi said:
"This must be false.
(The character 'Wèi' is redundant.)
What grudge could he have against Chāo to say such things?
Surely Zōngzhī, fearing punishment, falsely accused Chāo."
Upon investigation,
it was indeed so.
Zōngzhī was executed south of the capital.
19. The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Yán Yánzhī, passed away.
Yánzhī's son, Jùn, was noble and influential.
For all the provisions and supplies [Jùn offered],
Yánzhī accepted none of them,
remaining in coarse clothes and a thatched hut,
living in simplicity as before.
He often rode a weak ox in a crude cart,
and when he encountered Jùn's procession,
he would immediately move aside to the edge of the road.
(The order of guides and attendants is called a procession.)
Bǐng:
pronounced bìng yǐng.)
"In my life, I have never liked to see important people;
now, unfortunately, I have seen you!"
When Jùn built a mansion,
Yánzhī said to him:
"Do it well,
so that later generations do not laugh at your clumsiness."
Once, Yánzhī went early to visit Jùn
and saw the gate filled with guests,
while Jùn had not yet risen.
Yánzhī angrily said:
"You rose from the dirt
to the heights of the clouds and mist,
yet you are so swiftly arrogant like this—
how can it last long!"
Things fear being full to the brim.
The calamity that befell Yán Jùn
was known by his father.
Dīng:
to match;
Guō Pú said: to be worth.)
[Jùn] was appointed as General of the Right,
while remaining Governor of Dānyáng as before.
Jùn firmly declined,
submitting ten memorials;
(Shàng:
pronounced shí zhǎng.)
but the Emperor did not permit it,
sending the Palace Secretary Dài Míngbǎo to carry Jùn into the carriage,
and transporting him to the commandery residence.
(Zhī:
to go to.)
The commandery residence
was the office of the Governor of Dānyáng.)
They wrapped him in colorful silk,
and sent the Master of Clothing to dress him.
(The Master of Clothing
was in charge of the Emperor's clothing,
equivalent to the Táng position of the Director of the Palace Clothing Service.)
Jiù yī:
pronounced yú jì.)
The first year of the Dàmíng era (Dīngyǒu, 457)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day of the month, Xīnhài,
the era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
2 On the Rénxū day,
the Wei sovereign hunted at Guō Mountain.
Guō Mountain is located in Guō County, Yànmén Commandery.
Guō,
is pronounced in the ancient manner as "bó".
On the Wùchén day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
3 Wei appointed Yùyáng King Wèi Juàn as Grand Commandant and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
4 In the second month,
Wei forces invaded Yǎnzhōu,
heading towards Wúyán,
and defeated Liú Hú, the Administrator of Dōngpíng and a native of Nányáng.
Wúyán County
has belonged to Dōngpíng Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
Defeated,
is pronounced "bài" with the tone "mài".
Shěn Fǎxì, the Administrator of Dōngyáng, led the naval forces
towards Péngchéng to resist them,
and both were placed under the command of Shēn Tǎn, the Governor of Xúzhōu.
By the time they arrived,
the Wei troops had already withdrawn.
Prior to this,
bandits had gathered in the brambles and thickets of Rénchéng,
causing trouble for generations,
and were called the "Rén Thickets".
Shēn Tǎn requested to turn the army back to suppress them.
The Emperor approved.
When the Rén Thickets heard of this,
they all fled and scattered.
At the time, there was a drought,
and both men and horses suffered from thirst and exhaustion,
so they returned without achieving anything.
Āndū and Fǎxì were punished by being stripped of their official ranks but allowed to retain their duties.
Shēn Tǎn deserved execution,
and many ministers pleaded for him,
but none succeeded.
Shěn Qìngzhī held Tǎn and wept in the marketplace, saying:
"You died without guilt.
I weep for you in the marketplace,
and soon I will join you!"
The officials reported this,
and the Emperor then pardoned him.
5 In the third month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
the Wei sovereign hunted at Sōng Mountain;
on the Jǐsì day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
6 The Wei sovereign enfeoffed his younger brother Xīnchéng as the Yángpíng King.
7 After the Emperor had completed the mourning period and resumed normal activities,
the three-year mourning period had ended, and he returned to normal life.
he undertook many construction projects.
Yán Jùn, the Governor of Dānyáng, as an old minister from the Emperor's princely court,
when the Emperor was still a prince,
Jùn served as his assistant,
thus he was an old minister from the princely court.
Between the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
a commandery was called a "commandery court",
a prefecture was called a "prefectural court",
and a princely establishment was called a "princely court".
When Emperor Wǔ of Sòng was the King of Sòng,
and Emperor Gāo of Qí was the King of Qí,
it was called the "hegemon court".
Court,
is pronounced "zhāo" with the tone "yáo";
the same below.
Jùn did not avoid taboos in his remonstrances,
and the Emperor gradually became displeased.
Jùn believed himself talented enough to manage affairs of the time,
and that no one could compare to him in terms of the Emperor's old favor,
thinking he should remain in the central government and permanently hold power.
However, most of his proposals were not accepted,
so he suspected the Emperor intended to distance him,
and requested an external posting to gauge the Emperor's intention.
In summer,
the sixth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
an edict appointed Jùn as the Governor of Dōngyángzhōu,
and Jùn began to feel great fear.
This sets the stage for the Emperor's later execution of Jùn.
8 On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Wei sovereign went to Yīn Mountain.
9 The area under Yōngzhōu's jurisdiction contained many immigrant commanderies and counties,
and Governor Wáng Xuánmó memorialized:
"The immigrant commanderies and counties lack defined territories,
causing confusion between old and new jurisdictions,
and tax collection is irregular.
I request that they all be locally registered."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
an edict merged three commanderies and sixteen counties in Yōngzhōu into one commandery.
The migrant people in the commanderies and counties were unwilling to be registered locally,
meaning to be registered as permanent residents.
At the time, Liǔ Yuánjǐng's clan was powerful,
and many of his cousins served as two-thousand-bushel officials in the Yōng region.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng
was from Xiè County, Hédōng,
who moved south,
and resided as an immigrant in the Yōng region.
Cousins,
refers to paternal cousins.
From,
is pronounced "cóng" with the tone "yòng".
Xuánmó ensured internal and external peace to dispel public confusion,
sent a swift messenger to report to the Emperor,
and fully explained the situation.
The Emperor knew it was unfounded,
and sent the Secretariat Director Wú Xǐ to console him,
Secretariat Director,
was a position held by a Clerk under the Imperial Secretary in the Later Hàn.
The Hàn Imperial Secretariat had twenty-one Secretariat Clerks;
since the Eastern Jin,
the Central Secretariat had a Secretariat Director.
saying, "A seventy-year-old man,
what else could he be seeking!
Between ruler and minister,
there is enough to ensure mutual security.
This is just a jest,
to ease your furrowed brow."
Xuánmó was by nature stern,
and never laughed frivolously,
so the Emperor teased him with this.
10 In the eighth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
the Wei sovereign returned to Píngchéng.
11 On the Jiǎchén day,
the Minister of Works and Governor of Nánxúzhōu, Jìnglíng King Liú Dàn, was transferred to be Governor of Nányǎnzhōu,
and the Crown Prince's Household Manager Liú Yánsūn was appointed Governor of Nánxúzhōu.
Initially,
Emperor Gāozǔ's testamentary edict stated
that Jīngkǒu was a crucial location,
close to Jiànkāng,
and unless it was a close relative of the imperial clan,
no one should be stationed there.
Although Yánsūn's ancestors shared the same origin as Emperor Gāozǔ,
Emperor Gāozǔ belonged to Péngchéng,
while Yánsūn belonged to Jǔ County.
The "History of the Southern Dynasties" biography of Yánsūn says
"Lǚ County".
Lǚ County belonged to Péngchéng Commandery,
while Jǔ County belonged to Dōngguǎn Commandery.
Upon detailed examination,
Lǚ County is correct.
Péngchéng and Lǚ counties both belonged to Péngchéng Commandery,
so Yánsūn and the imperial family shared the same origin and commandery,
only differing in county.
After the Emperor appointed Yánsūn to guard Jīngkǒu,
he issued an edict to combine clans with Yánsūn,
making all the princes rank by age.
The Emperor behaved improperly within the palace,
not distinguishing between close and distant relatives, or between noble and humble,
and rumors spread among the people,
reaching everywhere.
Dàn was generous and courteous,
and had rendered great merit in suppressing Crown Prince Shào and Chancellor Yìxuān,
both being major achievements.
Dàn raising troops to suppress Shào is recorded in the thirtieth year of Emperor Wén's Yuánjiā reign in the previous scroll;
his advice to stop the Emperor from welcoming Yìxuān is mentioned above.
Dàn gathered many talented and capable men,
and stockpiled fine armor and sharp weapons,
so the Emperor feared and resented him,
not wanting Dàn to remain in the capital,
and sent him to guard Jīngkǒu;
still feeling he was too close,
he further transferred him to Guǎnglíng.
Nányǎnzhōu was then administered from Guǎnglíng.
He stationed him at Jīngkǒu to guard against him.
This sets the stage for the Emperor's later campaign against Dàn.
12 The Wei sovereign planned an eastern tour,
and in winter,
the tenth month,
he ordered Grand Steward Cháng Yīng to construct a traveling palace at Huáng Mountain in Liáoxī.
According to Wèi Shōu's "Treatise on Geography",
Huáng Mountain is in Féirú County, Liáoxī Commandery.
13 In the twelfth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
Shùnyáng King Xiūfàn was renamed as Guìyáng King.
Xiūfàn
was enfeoffed as Shùnyáng King in the third year of the Xiàojìàn reign.
Renamed,
is pronounced "gēng" with the tone "héng".
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day, Jǐngwǔ,
the Wei state established a prohibition on alcohol.
Brewing, selling, and drinking alcohol were all punishable by beheading;
brewers, sellers, and drinkers were all beheaded.
Permission was granted to lift the prohibition,
with a set duration.
The Wei ruler believed that many officials and commoners engaged in fights and discussed state affairs due to alcohol,
hence the prohibition.
Additional internal and external surveillance officials were appointed,
to spy on various departments, provinces, and garrisons.
The Wei state had surveillance officials since Emperor Dàowǔ,
and now their numbers were increased.
Sì,
means to observe officials.
To seek out the faults of all officials,
the authorities thoroughly investigated,
interrogating and torturing to obtain confessions;
officials found guilty of corruption amounting to two zhàng were all beheaded.
Additionally, seventy-nine new laws were added.
2. On Yǐmǎo,
the Wei ruler went to the Wēnquán Palace in Guǎngníng,
then toured Píngzhōu;
the territory of Wei’s Píngzhōu
consisted only of the two commanderies of Liáoxī and Běipíng.
On Gēngwǔ,
he arrived at the Huángshān Palace;
in the second month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
he ascended the Jiéshí Mountain,
to gaze upon the vast sea;
on Wùyín,
he went south to Xìndū,
and hunted in Guǎngchuān.
Guǎngchuān County,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to the Guǎngchuān Kingdom,
during the Later Hàn, to the Qīnghé Commandery,
during the Jìn, to the Bóhǎi Commandery,
according to Wèi Shōu’s *Treatise on Geography*, it belonged to the Chánglè Commandery,
Chánglè being Xìndū.
The *Wǔdài Zhì* states: In the Northern Qí, Guǎngchuān was abolished and merged into Zǎoqiáng.
Liú Xù said: In the Suí, a new county was established eighty lǐ east of the old county,
later renamed Chánghé County,
belonging to Dézhōu.
3. On Yǐyǒu,
Chǔ Zhànzhī was appointed as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, with the title of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
4. On Bǐngxū,
Jiànpíng Xuānjiǎn Wáng Hóng resigned as Director of the Imperial Secretariat due to illness;
in the third month,
on Dīngwèi,
he died.
5. On Bǐngchén,
Emperor Gāozōng of Wei returned to Píngchéng,
and began construction of the Tàihuá Hall.
Lì Dàoyuán said: In the sixteenth year of the Tàihé era of Wei,
the Tàihuá, Ānchāng, and other halls were demolished,
and the Tàijí Hall, its eastern and western wings, and the audience hall were built.
The Attendant Official Guō Shànmíng,
cunning by nature,
persuaded the emperor to extensively build palaces.
The Vice Director of the Central Secretariat, Gāo Yǔn, remonstrated:
“When Tàizǔ first established the capital,
all constructions
were undertaken during agricultural off-seasons.
Moreover, the state has long been established,
the front hall of Yǒng’ān is sufficient for court assemblies,
the western hall and warm chambers are sufficient for rest and banquets,
and the purple tower is sufficient for viewing;
even if expansion is needed,
it should be done gradually,
as the *Yìjīng* says: Gradually attain the way.
Xiàng Xiù said: Xún means to follow.
Chéng Yí said: Xún means to habituate,
to habituate and gradually reach abundance.
Xún,
pronounced similarly to zūn.
Now, the estimated labor force required is twenty thousand men,
with the elderly and weak providing supplies doubling that number,
and the project is expected to be completed in half a year.
If one man does not farm,
someone may suffer hunger,
let alone the labor and expense of forty thousand men—
how can it be justified!
This is something Your Majesty should carefully consider.”
The emperor accepted his advice.
Yǔn was fond of blunt remonstrance.
Whenever there were improper matters in the court,
Yǔn would request an audience,
and the emperor would often dismiss his attendants to wait for him.
Sometimes from morning till evening,
or for several days without leaving;
the courtiers did not know what they discussed.
Sometimes his words were painfully blunt,
to the point where the emperor could not bear to hear them,
and he would order attendants to escort him out,
yet he always treated him well.
At times, some submitted memorials that were provocative and accusatory.
The emperor reviewed them
and said to his courtiers:
“The ruler and father are one.
If a father has faults,
why would a son not write a letter to admonish him in public?
But to admonish in private, secluded places—
píng means to conceal.
Píngchù means a hidden place.
Píng,
pronounced bìng.
When it comes to serving the ruler,
why should it be any different?
If the ruler has faults,
one cannot state them face-to-face,
but instead submits a memorial openly admonishing,
wishing to expose the ruler’s shortcomings
and display one’s own righteousness—
is this what a loyal minister does!
Someone like Gāo Yǔn
is
a loyal minister.
When I have faults,
he never fails to speak directly to me,
even to the point where I cannot bear to hear it,
yet Yǔn avoids nothing.
I know my faults, but the world does not—
can this not be called loyalty!”
Among those who were summoned together with Yǔn, such as Yóu Yǎ and others,
(the summoning of Yǔn and others is recorded in the 122nd volume of Emperor Wén’s Yuánjiā eighth year.)
were enfeoffed as marquises,
and dozens to hundreds of their subordinates became governors or officials with salaries of two thousand dàn.
Subordinate officials refer to
those who served under Yǔn in the Central Secretariat.
For twenty-seven years, he was not promoted.
In the fourth year of the Shénjiā era of Emperor Shìzǔ of Wei,
Yǔn was summoned and appointed as a Doctor of the Central Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Director of the Bureau of Historiography,
and by this year, it had been twenty-five years.
“Although you all hold bows and swords by my side,
you merely stand there,
meaning you can only stand in attendance but cannot offer admonition.
You only wait for moments when I am pleased
to beg for offices and titles,
and now you have all reached the ranks of princes and dukes without merit.
Yǔn has wielded the brush to assist our state for decades,
contributing greatly,
yet he remains merely a court gentleman.
Do you not feel ashamed!”
Then he appointed Yǔn as Director of the Central Secretariat.
The earlier mention of twenty-seven years without promotion
suggests that Yǔn’s appointment as Director of the Central Secretariat did not occur in this year.
At that time, Wei officials received no salaries,
so Yǔn often had his sons gather firewood to support themselves.
The Minister over the Masses, Lù Lì, said to the emperor:
“Although Gāo Yǔn receives Your Majesty’s favor,
his family is poor,
and his wife and children lack establishment.”
Lì means to achieve,
to establish,
to set up,
to build;
meaning he cannot build a family estate.
“Why did you not speak earlier?
Now that you see I have employed him,
you mention his poverty!”
That same day,
the emperor went to Yǔn’s residence,
where there were only a few thatched huts,
cotton quilts,
and coarse hemp robes.
Kǒng Ānguó said: Yùn means coarse hemp padding.
Meaning the robes were padded with mixed hemp.
The *Book of Rites* says: Yùn makes a robe.
Zhèng Kāngchéng annotated: Yùn means old wadding,
or tangled hemp.
Yùn,
pronounced yùn.
The emperor sighed,
bestowed five hundred bolts of silk,
a thousand hú of grain,
and appointed his eldest son, Yuè,
as the governor of Chánglè.
Yǔn firmly declined,
but the emperor did not permit it.
The emperor esteemed Yǔn,
often calling him Lìnggōng instead of by his name.
You Yǎ often said:
"Previous histories praise the character of Zhuō Zǐkāng and Liú Wénráo.
Zhuō Mào,
courtesy name Zǐkāng.
Liú Kuān,
courtesy name Wénráo.
I have associated with Master Gāo for forty years,
yet have never seen a look of joy or anger on his face.
Only now do I know that the ancients did not speak falsely.
Master Gāo is cultivated within and gentle and compliant without.
His speech is halting, as if words cannot leave his mouth.
Formerly, Minister Cuī once said to me: 'Master Gāo is richly talented and broadly learned,
an excellent scholar of his generation.
What he lacks
is a heroic, upright air and integrity.'
I also thought this was so.
When the Minister incurred guilt,
arising from a trivial matter,
and the imperial edict pointed directly at him, holding him responsible,
the Minister's voice grew hoarse and his legs trembled,
nearly unable to speak;
from Zōng Qīn downward,
all prostrated themselves on the ground, sweating profusely,
their faces drained of color.
Only Master Gāo alone laid out the facts and principles of the matter,
explained and clarified right and wrong,
his arguments clear and articulate,
his tone lofty and resonant.
The sovereign was moved by this,
and none of the listeners failed to be stirred in spirit.
The event is recorded in scroll 125, the 27th year of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén.
wéi,
read as yú wèi fān.
Zōng Ài was then in power,
his might shaking the land.
He once summoned all officials to the Dūzuò hall.
The Wèi had the Dūzuò Dàguān.
The Wèi's Dūzuò
is like the Táng dynasty's court hall.
Some say Dūzuò Shàngshū.
Dūzuò is the Táng's Zhèngshì Hall.
zuò,
read as cú wò fān.

Gùnzhī,

"Běi Yīnpíng".

pronounced chǔjiā.
Ānguó set off,
carrying two days' worth of pre-cooked food;
when food ran out,
with no sign of Shūbǎo,
the soldiers wished to turn back,
Ānguó said,
"You have already eaten once today.
Tonight, the rice carts must surely arrive;
if not,
it will still not be too late to retreat by night."
Shūbǎo did indeed arrive;
they used the rice carts as a makeshift barricade,
Shūbǎo prepared a mobile force outside.
Battalion Commander Yáng Zhònghuái led 500 men ahead,
Ānguó and Huí attacked and beheaded them,
including all their soldiers.
When Shūbǎo arrived,
Huí wished to seize the moment to attack,
but Ānguó said,
"They will retreat on their own,
no need to pursue further."
They withdrew 30 lǐ,
rested for the night,
sending scouts to survey,
Shūbǎo did indeed abandon the rice carts and fled.
Ānguó returned at night to burn the rice carts,
driving over 2,000 oxen back.
In May,
on the night of dīnghài,
Liú Shùn's forces were defeated,
fleeing to Huáixī to join Cháng Zhēnqí.
Cháng Zhēnqí held Xuánhù, located west of the Huái River.
Flee,
pronounced zòu.
They advanced towards Shòuyáng.
Shūbǎo gathered the residents and scattered soldiers,
and fortified the city for defense,
Miǎn and other armies set camps outside the city.
Shānyáng Wáng Xiūyòu wrote to Yīn Yǎn,
explaining the benefits and harms,
the emperor also sent Imperial Censor Wáng Dàolóng with a decree to pardon Yǎn's crimes.
Miǎn wrote to Yǎn,
enclosing a letter from Yǎn's brother Yuàn and nephew Miǎo.
Yǎn, along with Shūbǎo and others, intended to surrender,
but the people's hearts were not united,
and thus they reinforced the city to defend it.
The Lìng of the western mountains of Yíyáng, Tián Yìzhī, rose in arms to support Jiànkāng,
the emperor decreed Yìzhī as General who Supports the State,
overseeing the affairs of the western Yíyáng Lìng.
On rénchén,
Shěn Yōuzhī was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǒngzhōu.
On dīngwèi,
Minister of the Left Wáng Jǐngwén was appointed Central Army General.
On gēngxū,
General Níngshuò Liú Chéngmín was appointed Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu.
Shěn Yōuzhī was previously in the southern army,
intending to replace Yuán Yí;
Liú Chéngmín was at Línjì,
and thus was appointed to Jìzhōu.
On jiǎyín,
Empress Dowager Zhāo was buried at Xiūníng Mausoleum.
Empress Dowager Lù was posthumously named Zhāo;
Xiūníng Mausoleum is southeast of Xiàowǔ Mausoleum.
31. Zhāng Yǒng, Xiāo Dàochéng, and others engaged in battle with Xuē Suǒ'ér,
inflicting a major defeat upon him.
Suǒ'ér retreated to defend Shíliáng.
(Nowadays, in Liùhé County of Yángzhōu, there is the Shíliáng River.
During the Jiangzuo period, the Shíliáng Commandery was established.
Between the Suí and Táng dynasties, Shíliáng County was established.)
He then fled towards Lèpíng.
(Lèpíng County,
in the Former Hàn was called Qīng,
belonging to Dōng Commandery.
Emperor Zhāng of the Later Hàn renamed it Lèpíng.
During the Jiangzuo period, displaced people from Lèpíng County
had a separate Lèpíng County established for them within the boundaries of Zhōnglí Commandery.)
Shēn Xiàoshū avenged his father's enemy.
He went to Péi Jìzhī to surrender.
Fù Língyuè fled to Huáixī.
Wǔwèi General Wáng Guǎngzhī of Pèi Commandery captured him alive
and sent him to Liú Miǎn.
Miǎn interrogated him about his rebellion.
Língyuè said:
"The call to righteousness resounded across the Nine Provinces;
how could it be my doing alone!
Lord Xuē was incapable of properly employing the wise and the brave,
instead entrusting matters to his sons and nephews.
This is the reason for his defeat.
A man's life ends in death;
I truly have no face to beg for my life."
Miǎn sent him to Jiànkāng.
The Emperor wished to pardon him,
but Língyuè's words remained unyielding to the end,
so he was executed.
32. Dèng Wǎn, because Liú Hú and Shěn Yōuzhī and others were locked in a stalemate with no resolution,
added Yuán Yǐ to oversee all military affairs of the expedition.
In the sixth month,
on the jiǎxū day,
Yǐ led a thousand tower ships
and twenty thousand soldiers
to enter Quèwěi.
Yǐ originally had no military strategy,
and his nature was also timid and weak.
In the army, he never wore military attire,
his speech never touched upon battle formations,
he only composed poetry and discussed principles,
and he did not further console or connect with the various generals.
Whenever Liú Hú discussed matters,
Yǐ's responses were very brief.
Because of this, he greatly lost the hearts of the men.
Hú often gnashed his teeth in anger and resentment.
Hú, because the grain shipments from the south had not arrived,
and the soldiers were lacking supplies,
went to Yǐ to borrow the funds from Xiāngyáng.
Yǐ refused,
saying:
"My two residences in the capital are not yet completed;
I should be managing their construction."
When two enemies face each other,
the decision of victory or defeat,
survival or destruction, hangs upon it.
Yuán Yǐ actually wanted to keep the funds from Xiāngyáng to manage his private residences.
Once Zǐxūn was defeated,
would those two capital residences still belong to Yǐ!
It is said
"The price of rice in Jiànkāng is expensive,
reaching several hundred per dǒu,"
and he believed the enemy would collapse without being attacked,
so he held onto his armor and waited for it.
(Holding onto armor
is like saying holding onto troops.)
33. Tián Yìzhī led over ten thousand Mán followers to besiege Yìyáng.
(Sòng Bái said: Yìyáng was originally the land of the Yìyáng township of Píngshì County in the Hàn.
During the Huángchū era of Wèi,
Píngshì was divided, belonging to Yìyáng Commandery and Yìyáng County.)
Yìzhī was defeated and fled without engaging in battle.
34. Ānchéng Grand Administrator Liú Xí
and Shǐ'ān Neishǐ Wáng Shízhī
(Textual Discrepancy Note: The Sòng Shū writes
"Wáng Zhízhī."
Here we follow the Sòng Lüè.)
both raised their commanderies and came to surrender.
Xí
was the grandson of Dàolián.
Dàolián
was the younger brother of Emperor Wǔ.
35. Xiāo Dàochéng's heir, Zé, was the magistrate of Nánkāng Gàn.
Dèng Wǎn sent an envoy to arrest and imprison him.
A retainer, Huán Kāng of Lánlíng, carried Zé's wife, Péi, and his sons Chángmào and Zǐliáng, fleeing into the mountains.
Together with Zé's clansman Xiāo Xīnzǔ and others, they gathered followers, obtaining over a hundred men.
They attacked the commandery,
broke into the prison, and rescued Zé.
Nánkāng Xiàng Shěn Sùzhī led officers and clerks in pursuit of Zé.
Zé fought them,
and captured him.
Zé proclaimed himself Níngshuò General,
occupied the commandery and raised troops,
responding in concert with Liú Xí and others.
Wǎn appointed Zhōnghùjūn Yīn Fú as Yùzhāng Grand Administrator,
to oversee the five upper commanderies
(Yùzhāng, Lúlíng, Línchuān, Ānchéng, and Nánkāng—these five commanderies
were all in the upper reaches of the Nánjiāng.)
36. Héngyáng Neishǐ Wáng Yìngzhī raised troops in response to Jiànkāng,
and attacked Héngzhōu Xíngshì Hé Huìwén in Chángshā.
Yìngzhī and Huìwén abandoned their armies and fought personally.
Yìngzhī hacked Huìwén, inflicting eight wounds.
Huìwén hacked Yìngzhī, severing his foot,
and killed him.
37. Shǐxīng man Liú Sìzǔ and others occupied their commandery and raised troops in response to Jiànkāng.
Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Tànyuǎn sent his general Lǐ Wànzhōu and others to suppress them.
Sìzǔ deceived Wànzhōu, saying
"Xúnyáng has already been pacified."
Wànzhōu returned and attacked Pānyú,
captured Tànyuǎn,
and beheaded him.
The Emperor appointed Wànzhōu to act as administrator of Guǎngzhōu.
38. Earlier,
the King of Wǔdū, Yáng Yuánhé, governed Báishuǐ.
(According to the Běi Shǐ,
this is the Báishuǐ of Wǔdū.)
(Note: According to the Wǔdài Zhì: The old Báishuǐ Commandery was established in Jiànwēi County of Wǔchāng.
Jiànwēi
was abolished in the Táng and incorporated into Jiānglì County of Jiē Prefecture.)
He abandoned his state and fled to Wèi.
Yuánhé's cousin Sēngsì re-established himself,
stationing at Jiālú.
Fèi Xīnshòu reached Bādōng.
Bādōng man Rèn Shū'ér occupied Báidì,
proclaiming himself Fǔguó General.
He attacked Xīnshòu,
and beheaded him.
(Xiāo Huìkāi had sent Xīnshòu eastward;
see above, first month.)
The Jiāng River flows from Bādōng to Yílíng.
In between are the Guǎngxī Gorge, Wū Gorge, and Xīlíng Gorge,
called the Three Gorges.
One says
the Three Gorges
are Xī Gorge, Guī Gorge, and Wū Gorge.
For seven hundred lǐ,
the mountains on both banks are continuous,
with almost no gaps.
They obscure the sky and block the sun.
Unless it is midday or midnight,
one cannot see the sun or moon.
Yáng Sēngsì led the Dí to cut off the road,
and sent a secret messenger to report this.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the dīngyǒu day,
Sēngsì was appointed as Běiqínzhōu Cìshǐ and King of Wǔdū.
39. The various armies faced Yuán Yǐ at Nónghú,
with no resolution for a long time.
Lóngxiāng General Zhāng Xīngshì suggested:
"The bandits occupy the upper reaches;
their troops are strong and their position advantageous.
Although we can hold our ground, we lack the means to control them.
If we secretly send several thousand surprise troops above them,
fortify ourselves according to the terrain,
and act when advantage appears,
we can make them anxious from head to tail,
hesitant and obstructed in advance and retreat.
Once the middle reaches are blocked,
their grain transport will naturally become difficult.
This is an extraordinary strategy to control the bandits.
The Qiánxī riverbank is the narrowest.
(The Xīn Tángshū Dìlǐ Zhì: Nánlíng County of Xuān Prefecture had a Méigēn Supervisor of coin officials.
Below it says: Chén Qìng reached Qiánxī,
and camped at Méigēn.
This is likely today's Méigēn Harbor.
Because there was a coin minting supervisor,
it was called Qiánxī.)
It overlooks swirling eddies and submerged currents.
(A swirling flow is called 'huí';
a submerged flow is called 'fú'.)
There is also a Hèngpǔ where ships can be hidden.
With a thousand men guarding the strategic point,
ten thousand could not pass.
Among crucial strategic locations,
none surpasses this."
Shěn Yōuzhī and Wú Xǐ both approved his plan.
At that time, Páng Mèngqiú led troops to aid Yīn Yǎn.
(Páng Mèngqiú came from Yìyáng to reinforce Shòuyáng.)
Prince of Jiàn'ān, Xiūrén, wished to send Xīngshì to rescue him.
Shěn Yōuzhī said:
"Mèngqiú is a gathering of ants;
he certainly cannot accomplish anything.
Sending another general with several thousand infantry and cavalry
is sufficient to handle him.
Xīngshì's mission
is a crucial opportunity for our safety or peril;
it absolutely must not be halted."
So he sent Duàn Fóróng to lead troops to rescue Miǎn,
and selected seven thousand warriors and two hundred light boats to assign to Xīngshì.
Xìng Shì led his troops upstream for a while,
but soon withdrew.
This continued for several days.
Liú Hú heard the news,
and laughed, saying:
"I dare not cross the river to seize Yángzhōu,
Yángzhōu,
refers to Jiànkāng.
How could they lightly hold my territory upstream!"
He took no precautions.
One night,
at the fourth watch,
with a favorable wind,
Xìng Shì set sail straight ahead,
crossing Hú and Bái,
passing Quèwěi.
Once Hú found out,
he dispatched his general Hú Língxiù with troops to the eastern shore,
advancing in formation.
On the evening of Wùxū,
Xìng Shì camped at Jǐnghóngpǔ,
where Língxiù also stayed.
Xìng Shì secretly dispatched his general Huáng Dàobiāo with seventy ships directly towards Qiánxī,
setting up a camp;
on Jǐhài,
Xìng Shì led the soldiers to seize it,
Língxiù could not stop him.
On Gēngzǐ,
Liú Hú led twenty-six units of infantry and cavalry to attack Qiánxī.
A note of discrepancy says: Sòng Lüè states:
"Hú advanced his troops to Quètóu,
sending his general Chén Qìng with 300 ships to threaten Qiánxī."
We now follow the Sòng Shū.
Xìng Shì restrained them, saying:
"The enemy is still far away,
their spirits high and arrows frequent;
when they become frequent, they easily run out,
meaning arrows easily run out.
Easily,
means translating with 'fǔ' and 'fān';
the same below.
It is better to wait."
He ordered the soldiers to repair the city as before.
Soon Hú approached closer,
their boats entered the whirlpool;
Xìng Shì ordered Shòu Jìzhī and Rèn Nóngfū to lead several hundred strong men to attack,
the main army followed one after another,
Hú was defeated and fled,
severing several hundred heads,
Hú gathered his troops and retreated.
At that time, Xìng Shì's fortification was not yet secure,
Jiàn'ān Wang Xiūrén was concerned that Yuán Yǐ might join forces to attack Qiánxī again,
wishing to divide their power.
On Xīchǒu,
he ordered Shěn Yōuzhī, Wú Xǐ, and others to attack Nóng Hú with leather-covered ships,
covering the ships with cowhide to defend against arrows and rocks,
hence they were called leather-covered ships.
Ships,
translated as 'hù àn fān'.
On that day,
Liú Hú led 20,000 infantry and 1,000 iron cavalry,
intending to attack Xìng Shì again.
Not yet reaching Qiánxī several tens of li away,
Yuán Yǐ due to the urgency at Nóng Hú,
hastily recalled them,
thus the Qiánxī fortification was secured.
Hú sent someone to spread false news,
"Qiánxī is at peace,"
which frightened the troops,
Shěn Yōuzhī said:
"It is not so.
If Qiánxī were truly defeated,
among ten thousand there would be one who escaped,
surely they lost the battle,
spreading false words to deceive the troops."
He restrained the army from acting rashly;
restrained,
means to strictly command.
Yōuzhī showed the ears and noses of the Hú troops sent from Qiánxī to Nóng Hú,
alarming Yuán Yǐ.
Yōuzhī returned at nightfall.
General Lóngxiāng Liú Dàofú attacked Shānyáng,
Chéng Tiānzuò surrendered.
Chéng Tiānzuò's son, Xūn,
see above in the first month.
Páng Mèngqiú advanced to Yìyáng,
Liú Miǎn sent Lǚ Ānguó and others to intercept at Liǎotán,
according to Hànzhì,
Liùànguó had Liǎo County,
in Jìn it belonged to Ānfēng Prefecture.
The Commentary on the Waterways: The cut-off water flows past the east of the ancient city of Liǎo County,
where it joins the irrigation water.
The so-called Liǎotán,
should be in this place.
Mèngqiú fled to Yìyáng.
Wáng Xuánmó's son, Tánshàn, raised an army to occupy Yìyáng in support of Jiànkāng,
Mèngqiú fled and died among the barbarians.
Liú Hú sent General Fǔguó Xuē Dàobiāo to surprise Héféi,
killing the Governor of Rǔyīn Péi Jìzhī,
Péi Jìzhī surrendered Héféi to Liú Miǎn,
see above in February.
Hóng,
younger brother of Láng;
Yuán Láng appears in volume one hundred and twenty-nine, second year of Xiàowǔ Dì's Dàmíng.
He is the son of Āndū.
Huáixī native Zhèng Shūjǔ raised an army to attack Cháng Zhēnqí in support of Zhèng Hēi;
on Xīnhài,
Shūjǔ was appointed as Prefect of North Yùzhōu.
Cuī Dàogù was attacked by locals,
closing the doors and defending himself.
Cuī Dàogù responded to Xúnyáng from Lìchéng,
see above in the first month.
Dàogù sought to surrender.
On Jiǎyín,
Dàogù was restored as the Prefect of Xūzhōu.
Dàogù was originally an inspector of Jìzhōu.
Restored,
means to 'fŭ yòu fān';
similar words below.
In August,
Huángfǔ Dàoliè and others heard of Páng Mèngqiú's defeat,
opening the gates to surrender.
The Tiger Slayer's division collapsed,
Huángfǔ Dàoliè fled back to Shòuyáng.
Having seized Qiánxī,
Xìng Shì's troops lacked food at Nóng Hú.
Dèng Wǎn sent provisions in abundance,
fearing Xìng Shì,
and dared not advance.
Liú Hú commanded 400 light ships,
through the inner route from Quètóu to attack Qiánxī,
Quèzhōu is in the middle of the river;
the river waters divide,
hence there is an inner route and an outer route.
Ships,
pronounced 'gǔ wǒ fān'.
"Since my youth, I have been skilled in land battles,
not familiar with water warfare.
In land battles,
one is always among thousands;
in water battles one is on a single boat,
each boat moves independently,
no longer interdependent,
only among thirty people,
this is not a safe plan,
I will not do it."
Hence he feigned illness,
staying at Quètóu without advancing,
sending General Lóngxiāng Chén Qìng with 300 ships toward Qiánxī,
instructing Qìng not to fight:
"I know Xìng Shì well,
he will flee on his own."
Chén Qìng reached Qiánxī,
setting camp at Méigēn.
Hú sent another general Wáng Qǐ with a hundred ships to attack Xìng Shì,
Xìng Shì attacked Qǐ,
defeating him greatly.
Hú led the remaining ships back,
telling Yǐ:
"Xìng Shì's camp has been established,
it cannot be attacked suddenly;
yesterday's skirmish,
did no significant damage.
Chén Qìng has joined the Nánlíng and Dàléi forces to block their upper route,
the main army is here,
the Quètóu generals have also cut off their downstream;
surrounded,
there is no need to worry."
Yǐ was angry at Hú for not fighting,
asking:
"With the grain transport blockaded,
what can we do?"
"Blocked" implies like a fishbone stuck in the throat.
pronounced 'xī sī fān'.
"They can still ascend against the current,
why can't our transport descend with the current past them?"
So he sent Sīmǎ Shěn Zhòngyù of the North An Command with a thousand men to Nánlíng to receive the grain.
Zhòngyù reached Nánlíng,
loaded 300,000 bushels of rice,
several tens of boats with money and cloth,
setting up a flag as a fortress,
intending to break through.
Upon reaching Guìkǒu,
he dared not advance,
according to the Commentary on the Waterways: "The river enters from the east of Shíchéng becoming Guìkǒu."
Now, the pool at Chízhōu Guìchí County is Guìkǒu.
Zhāng Shùnmín stated: "From Tónglíng, traveling by boat for about sixty miles reaches Méigēngǒng,
and another fifty miles to Guìchíkǒu."
Ordered to send a reinforcement army.
Xìng Shì sent Shòu Jìzhī, Rèn Nóngfū, and others with 3,000 troops to Guìkǒu to attack,
Zhòngyù fled back to Yǐ's camp,
capturing all their supplies;
Hú's troops were terrified,
Hú's general Zhāng Xǐ came to surrender.
The Eastern Garrison’s Central Army Officer Liú Liàng advanced his troops and pressed close to Hú’s camp,
and Hú was unable to control the situation.
Yuán Yǐ, terrified, said:
“The rebels have penetrated into our very livers and spleens—
how can we possibly survive!”
Hú secretly plotted to flee.
On the jǐmǎo day,
he deceived Yǐ, saying:
“I intend to lead another twenty thousand infantry and cavalry
upstream to capture Qiánxī,
and at the same time go down to Dàléi to bring back the remaining supplies.”
He ordered Yǐ to select all the horses and assign them to him.
That same day,
Hú abandoned Yǐ and left,
heading straight for Méigēn.
He had earlier ordered Xuē Chángbǎo to prepare boats,
and now he mobilized all the troops at Nánlíng,
set fire to the various forts at Dàléi, and fled.
Only when night fell
did Yǐ learn of this.
Furious,
he cursed, saying:
“This year I have been ruined by that little brat!”
He called for his usual excellent horse,
“Flying Swallow,”
and said to his followers:
“I shall pursue him myself!”
And with that he too fled.
On the gēngchén day,
Prince of Jiàn’ān Liú Xiūrén led his troops into Yǐ’s camp,
accepting the surrender of a hundred thousand soldiers,
and sent Shěn Yōuzhī and others to pursue Yǐ.
Yǐ fled as far as Quètóu,
where he joined the garrison commander Xuē Bózhēn and the several thousand men under his command, and together they left,
intending to go to Xúnyáng.
At night,
they stopped in the mountains.
Yǐ had horses killed to reward the officers and men,
then turned to Bózhēn and said:
“It is not that I cannot die;
but I wish first to reach Xúnyáng,
confess my crime to the sovereign,
and then cut my own throat.”
Thereupon, with passionate indignation, he shouted to his attendants to fetch his official tally,
but none responded.
At dawn,
Bózhēn requested a private word,
and then cut off Yǐ’s head.
The Southern History states: Yǐ fled to Qīnglín Mountain, where he was killed.
The master of Xiāngyáng, Yú Zhànzhī,
then beheaded Bózhēn,
and sent both heads as his own achievement.
Liú Hú led twenty thousand men toward Xúnyáng,
falsely reporting to Prince of Jìn’ān Liú Zǐxūn:
“Yuán Yǐ has surrendered,
his army has all scattered,
only I have led my own troops back alone;
you must quickly decide,
and provide resources for one final battle.
I shall halt and hold Péngchéng,
vowing to die without turning traitor.”
Then, by night, he headed for Miǎnkǒu along the outer river route.
In the river there were islets and shoals at intervals,
boats traveling close to the southern bank were said to take the inner route,
those close to the northern bank the outer route.
Dèng Wǎn, hearing that Hú had left,
was anxious and panicked, at a loss what to do.
He summoned the Palace Secretariat Receptionist Chǔ Língsì and others to discuss the situation,
but none knew what to do.
Zhāng Yuè feigned illness,
summoned Wǎn to discuss matters,
and had armed men hidden behind the tent curtains,
instructing them:
“If you hear me call for wine,
come out at once.”
When Wǎn arrived,
Yuè said:
“You were the first to propose this plan;
now the situation is critical,
what scheme do you propose?”
Wǎn said:
“We should just execute the Prince of Jìn’ān,
seal the storehouses,
and confess our crime.”
Yuè said:
“How could we sell out His Highness today to save our own lives!”
Thereupon he called for wine.
Zǐ Xún came out with a sword and beheaded Wǎn.
Xún
was Yuè’s son.
He then led troops and arrived.
Yuè sent someone to tell him:
“Dèng Wǎn plotted rebellion,
and has now been executed.”
Xīnzhī then turned back.
They seized Wǎn’s sons,
and killed them as well.
Yuè then took a single boat, carrying Wǎn’s head, and raced downstream,
going to Prince of Jiàn’ān Liú Xiūrén to surrender.
Xúnyáng fell into chaos.
Without a ruler,
chaos ensued.
The Workshop Section,
in charge of manufacturing weapons,
was located outside Xúnyáng’s walls.
They seized Zǐxūn,
and imprisoned him.
When Shěn Yōuzhī and the other armies reached Xúnyáng,
they beheaded the Prince of Jìn’ān Liú Zǐxūn,
and sent his head to Jiànkāng.
He was eleven years old at the time.
The Prince of Jìn’ān’s raising of troops
was in fact a righteous act.
Dèng Wǎn is not worth mentioning,
but as for Yuán Yǐ and Kǒng Jì, can one say they did not meet their deserved end?
The world should not judge them by success or failure.
Earlier,
Dèng Wǎn had sent the Neishi of Línchuān, Zhāng Yān, from Póyáng via the mountain path into Sānwú,
stationing his army at Shàngráo.
The Jìn Tàikāng Geographical Treatise states: Póyáng Commandery had a Shàngráo County,
but the Jìn Shū does not record it,
so it was likely established during Wú.
Today it is Xìnzhōu,
with a road connecting to Póyáng.
Sòng Bái states: Xìnzhōu’s Shàngráo County
originally lay within the boundaries of Qín’s Pó County,
under Hàn it was Póyáng County;
the present prefecture’s ancient city ruins
are the ancient Shàngráo abolished during the Suí’s Kāihuáng era.
The so-called Shàngráo
was named thus because it lay above Ráozhōu.

First year of Yuánhuī (Guǐchǒu, 473)
1st, in spring,
in the first month,
on the Wùyín day, the first day of the month,

Returning from the campaign against the Rouran.
4th, on the Guǐchǒu day,
Wei issued an edict ordering commandery administrators and county magistrates to encourage and supervise agricultural work.
Within the same district,
the rich and poor should assist each other,
and households with multiple oxen
should lend to those without;
if they disobeyed the edict,
the entire family would be barred from holding office for life.
5th, on the Wùwǔ day,
the Wei Retired Emperor arrived at Píngchéng.
From Yúnzhōng to Píngchéng.
6th, on the Jiǎxū day,
Wei issued an edict:
"If a county magistrate can pacify banditry in one county,
he shall concurrently administer two counties,
and receive the corresponding salary;
if he can pacify two counties,
he shall concurrently administer three counties,
and after three years be promoted to commandery administrator.
If a commandery administrator of two thousand piculs rank can pacify two commanderies up to three commanderies, the same applies,
and after three years he shall be promoted to provincial inspector."
7. Guìyáng King Liú Xiūfàn
was by nature mediocre and inarticulate,

“Mediocre” means ordinary and common;

His rank

All of the emperor’s uncles were executed,

The imperial court, aware of his rebellious intentions,

Xiāo Dàochéng returned triumphantly to Jiànkāng,

On the day of dīngyǒu,

In year 5, Róurán sent envoys to establish relations.

From this, Dàochéng gained power.

We now follow the Sòng Shū.

zealously serving the king,

In year 8, on the day of yǐmǎo,
the Wèi edict declared:
"The common people are violent,
showing no regard for kin,
one person's wrongdoing,
brings disaster to the whole family.
As the father and mother of the people,
I deeply grieve for them.
From now on, except for rebellion and treason,
punishment shall be limited to the individual."
Thus, they began to eliminate the penalty of clan extermination.
'Clan extermination' referred to executing one’s entire clan;
'house extermination'
referred to executing all of one’s household.
At the time, in Héběi, the great families like the Cuī and the Lǐ,

The Wèi Emperor Xianzu was diligent in governance,
with strict and clear rewards and punishments,
carefully selecting local administrators,
advancing the honest and dismissing the corrupt.
Matters in the offices often required consultation for decisions,
previously many petitions were submitted,
and orders were verbal,
which occasionally led to mistakes.
The emperor commanded that all matters, regardless of size,
be judged by the law,
and uncertain petitions were not allowed;
those complying were approved,
those defying were scrutinized,
all executed with written edicts,
'approved' meaning
a personal edict was granted for what was requested.
'Scrutinized'
means to investigate thoroughly.
'Complying,'

'Defying,'
signifies against the law.
'Scrutinized,'

Special emphasis was placed on penalties,
frequently reviewing major cases.
Major offenses
referred to capital crimes.
Some ministers suggested against it,
the emperor said:
"Delay in justice is not good governance,
but is it not better than rashness and injustice!
When people are in distress, they reflect on their wrongs,
thus the wise see imprisonment as reform,
I particularly grieve their plight,
hoping they reform through compassion and leniency."
Thus, although imprisonments lingered,
the penalties were often appropriate.
Also, with pardons leading to further wrongdoing,
since Yánxīng began,

to the west,

the Róurán.

(Note: Wèi is pronounced as 'wèi.')

The assembled ministers deliberated,
