why wait for the fortress at Shítóu!
On the road, encountering their younger brother Yùn,
Yùn opened the carriage asking:
"Today's affairs,
should they belong to brother?"
Bǐng said:
"We have already yielded to the Commander."
Yùn clasped his chest, saying:
"How can a brother have blood in his flesh!
This year, the family is ruined!"
The matters of Sòng are gone,
everyone below knows this.
On this day,
by the Empress Dowager's command,
the crimes of the Prince of Cāngwú were enumerated,
saying:
"I secretly ordered General Xiāo to subtly operate with clarity.
Prince Ānchéng Zhǔn,
should preside over the Myriad Kingdoms."
Posthumously enfeoffing Yù as the Prince of Cāngwú.
The ceremony and guard reached the Eastern Provincial Gate,
where Prince Ānchéng ordered the gatekeeper not to open,
waiting for Minister Yuán to arrive.
When Càn arrived,
the Prince then entered the hall.
History recounts Yuán Càn being esteemed at the time.
"Court,"
pronounced "zhí yáo fān."
On the day of Rénchén,
the Prince ascended the throne as Emperor,
eleven years old at the time,
establishing a new era,
and granting a great amnesty.
Established the new era of Shēngmíng.
The southern suburban altar was located south of the Imperial City,
in the third year of Shìzǔ, Dàmíng,
the southern suburban altar was moved to Niútóu Mountain to correct the position of yang.
In the fifth year, Prince Jīngzhào of Wèi, Wang Zǐtuī, passed away.
In the sixth year of Jiǎwǔ,
Xiāo Dàochéng left to station in the Eastern Garrison.
In the year of Bǐngshēn,
Dàochéng was appointed as Sīkōng, Chancellor in charge of governmental affairs, and General-in-Chief of the Cuirassiers.
Yuán Càn was promoted to Director of the Secretariat,
and Chǔ Yuān was given the additional title of Head of the Three Departments.
Liú Bǐng was promoted to Chief Secretary,
with the added title of Commandant of the Central Guards.
Jìn Xī Wáng Xiè was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Initially, Liú Bǐng held the belief that the myriad affairs should be managed by the court,
so that no upheavals would occur in the world;
however, Xiāo Dàochéng soon took over military and state responsibilities,
deploying his trusted confidantes,
independently making decisions.
Chǔ Yuān had always depended on him.
Bǐng and Yuán Càn deferred to him completely.
To defer means
to be complacent in position without accomplishment,
like hands held as if clasped together.
To defer [means] to bend to his will.
Xīnchóu
appointed Shàngshū Right Servant Wáng Sēngqián as Servant.
Bǐngwǔ,
designated Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn as Inspector of Yǐngzhōu;
Xiāo Dàochéng was reassigned to Inspector of Southern Xúzhōu.
In the seventh month,
Rénzǐ,
the Wèi issued a great amnesty.
Guǐhài,
ordered Yuán Càn to station at Shítóu.
Yuán Càn was naturally calm and serene,
and whenever there was an imperial command,
he would usually decline;
when he couldn't refuse due to insistent pressures,
he eventually assumed the position.
Upon realizing Xiāo Dàochéng's ambition for disloyalty,
he secretly plotted,
then obediently accepted the order;
it was to set the base for his commitment at Shítóu.
Originally,
the Tàizōng commanded Chén Zhāohuá's mother to care for Shùn Dì;
Wùchén,
giving the title of Empress Dowager to Zhāohuá.
The Míng Emperor of Wèi appointed Zhāohuá,
and the Emperor Wǔ of Jìn regulated that Shū, Shūyuàn, Shūyí, Xiùhuá, Xiùróng, Xiùyí, Jiépó, Chōnghuá, and Rónghuá became the nine concubines,
and the title Zhāohuá ceased to exist.
During the reign of Sòng Xiàowǔ, Zhāoyí, Zhāoróng, Zhāohuá replaced Xiùhuá, Xiùyí, Xiùróng.
On the fourth of the twelfth month,
the Wèi decree stated:
"Artisans and commoners,
each has their role;
yet the officials are indulgent and corrupt,
some become mere followers of trends.
From now on, anyone involved in labor within households,
will be ultimately responsible only to the original official.
‘Flow of Trends’
in the Northern Histories is written as
‘Clear Flow’.
This was because officials appointed at that time did not distinguish between ranks and positions,
hence the decree that all households involved in labor
would only be overseen by the original official.
Do not breach this regulation."
Xiāo Dàochéng repeatedly declined the title of Sīkōng;
Gēngchén,
was made General-in-Chief of the Cuirassiers, Head of the Three Departments.
In the ninth month,
Yǐyǒu,
Wèi revised the laws and regulations.
Wùshēn,
conferred the title of Marquis, Count, Viscount, and Barons on Yáng Yùfū and twenty-four others.
In the winter,
in the tenth month,
Dī chieftain Yáng Wéndù sent his brother Wénhóng to attack Wèi at Chóuchí,
capturing it.
Initially,
Wèi's Xuzhou Inspector Lǐ Xīn,
served Xiǎnzǔ as Shàngshū of the Department of Granaries,
during the reign of the Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, Granaries Department Officials were first appointed,
under the Minister of Revenue;
the title Shàngshū of the Department of Granaries was set up by the Later Wei,
equivalent to the previous Grand Granaries Minister.
Xīn,
pronounced as "xīn."
Xīn's brother, Left General Yīng, advised:
Historical discrepancies note: Diǎn of Wèi:
"biāo" appears as
"piāo";
"Yīng" appears as
"Pú".
Now follows the Wèi Shū.
I considered Biǎo and Piāo to be the same;
pronounced "piāo."
Yīng,
pronounced "yīng."
"Piāo deceives others with appearance,
gives generously to buy influence,
values power over virtue;
pleasing words but treacherous actions,
not severing ties early,
will lead to later regret."
Xīn did not heed,
entrusted heart matters entirely to Biǎo.
Shàngshū Zhào Hēi,
and Xīn were favored by Xiǎnzǔ,
jointly managed the Selection Department.
Xīn privately nominated people for Provincial roles;
in ancient times, eight provinces and eight leaders were known as the "Fāng",
later generations equated provincial inspector with "Fāngzhōu".
Subsequently, a rift developed.
After a while,
Xīn exposed Hēi’s earlier misconduct as a Treasury Overseer,
misappropriating state resources.
Hēi was demoted to doorkeeper.
Hēi resented it,
his appetite diminished with distress;
over a year later,
he was reinstated as Chamberlain, Shàngshū Left Servant,
in charge of selection.
After Xiǎnzǔ died,
Hēi accused the regent Empress Dowager Féng,
claiming Xīn’s tyranny,
ordering his removal to Xuzhou.
Fàn Biǎo knew the Empress Dowager’s resentment towards Xīn,
and informed Lǐ Fū of it; the event appears in Volume 132, Tàishǐ's sixth year;
Xīn serving as Grand Granaries Minister is also in this year.
The Empress Dowager summoned Xīn to Píngchéng for questioning,
Xīn denied the allegations,
the Empress Dowager brought Biǎo as a witness.
Xīn told Biǎo: "You now falsely accuse me,
what can I say!
You received such great kindness from me,
yet have no qualms about doing this?"
Biǎo said: "The kindness I received from you,
how was it greater than what you received from Lǐ Fū?
Since you had no qualms in dealing with Fū,
why should I have qualms about dealing with you?"
Xīn sighed ruefully: "My failure to heed Yīng's advice,
what regrets can suffice now!"
Zhào Hēi further schemed his guilt,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Xīn and his sons Lìnghé and Lìngdù were executed;
only then did Hēi return to normal life.
In the eleventh month,
Guǐwèi,
Wèi's Commander of the Western forces Pí Huānxǐ and three other generals, led forty thousand troops to attack Yáng Wénhóng.
Dīnghài,
Wèi's Huáizhōu native Yíqí Gǒu claimed to be a descendant of Yáo,
Yáo,
of the Yíqí Clan,
hence saying so.
The Zhòng Mountains,
were north of Gòng County.
Zhòng,
pronounced "chóng."
Empress Dowager Féng intended to execute all the citizens of the city,
Yōngzhōu’s Inspector Zhāng Bǎizé advised:
"The main culprits and traitors,
have already been completely dealt with;
Yōngzhōu of Wèi governed districts like Jīngzhào, Fúfēng, Féngyì, Xiányáng, Northern Territories, Píngqín, Wǔdū, and others.
To kill all without distinguishing innocent from guilty,
how can this be justified!"
So it was halted.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi's Pí Huānxǐ's forces reached Jiàn'ān,
Shuǐjīng Annotation: Yáng Dìng relocated from Lǒngyòu to manage Lìchéng,
one hundred twenty miles from Chóuchí.
Lìchéng was later renamed Jiàn'ān City.
Historical discrepancies: this year,
Wèi set an intercalary month in the eleventh month,
which corresponds to the twelfth month of Sòng.
19. Initially,
Shěn Yōuzhī and Xiāo Dàochéng had served together in the palace departments during the Dàmíng and Jǐnghé eras,
and were deeply close and friendly.
Dàochéng's daughter was married to Yōuzhī's son, the Secretariat Gentleman Wénhé.
While Yōuzhī was in Jīngzhōu,
the Palace Guard General Gāo Dàoqìng,
whose family home was in Huáróng,
(Huáróng County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Nánjùn.
According to the *Jiǔyù Zhì*: the present-day Jiànníng town in Shíshǒu County, Jiānglíng Prefecture, is its location.
Sòng Bái states: Jiānlì County, Jiānglíng Prefecture,
was originally the territory of the Hàn-era Huáróng County.)
passed through Jiānglíng,
and got into a competitive lance game with Yōuzhī.
He galloped back to Jiànkāng,
reporting that Yōuzhī's signs of rebellion were complete,
and requested to attack him with three thousand men.
The ruling ministers all considered this inadvisable,
and Dàochéng still vouched for him, saying it was not so.
Yáng Yùnzhǎng and others, who hated Yōuzhī,
secretly plotted with Dàoqìng to send an assassin to kill Yōuzhī,
but did not succeed.
It happened that the Cāngwú Prince was assassinated,
and the Registrar Zōng Yǎnzhī and the Merit Official Zāng Yín urged Yōuzhī to raise troops on this pretext.
Yōuzhī, because his eldest son Yuányǎn was in Jiànkāng serving as Vice Director of the Left of the Minister of Education,
therefore did not act.
Yín
was the son of Zāng Níngzhī.
(Zāng Níngzhī appears in the 127th scroll, in the 30th year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén of Sòng.)
At that time, Yáng Yùnzhǎng and others were no longer in the inner court,
(having already been sent out as external officials,
and were not within the departments.)
Yōuzhī felt that Dàochéng's fame and rank had always been beneath his own,
yet he had suddenly monopolized the court's power,
and was discontented.
He said to Yuányǎn:
"I would rather die like Wáng Líng,
than live like Jiǎ Chōng."
(The affairs of Wáng Líng and Jiǎ Chōng
both appear in the Wèi Annals.)
He then submitted a memorial offering congratulations,
and detained Yuányǎn there.
The Governor of Yōngzhōu, Zhāng Jìng'ér,
had always been on good terms with Yōuzhī's Marshal Liú Rǎngbīng.
Suspecting Yōuzhī was about to start trouble,
he secretly inquired of Rǎngbīng.
Rǎngbīng said nothing,
but sent Jìng'ér a single stirrup.
Jìng'ér then made preparations.
Yōuzhī had a plain letter of several dozen lines,
which he often concealed in the corner of his liǎngdāng.
(*Bóyǎ* states: Liǎngdāng
is called the bǎifù.
Liǎng,
read as lǐ yǎng.
Dāng,
read as dū láng.)
When Yōuzhī was about to raise troops,
his concubine Cuī shì admonished him:
"Master, you are already old,
why not consider the hundred mouths [of your household]!"
(Between the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
from personal followers to maids and servants,
they generally called their master 'guān'.)
He then claimed an envoy from the Empress Dowager had arrived,
bestowing something upon Yōuzhī.
He cut open the candle,
and obtained a handwritten order from the Empress Dowager which said:
"All matters of the state,
I entrust entirely to you."
Thereupon, he marshaled his troops, issued a proclamation,

and sent envoys to solicit Zhāng Jìng'ér, the Governor of Yùzhōu Liú Huáizhēn, the Governor of Liángzhōu Fàn Bǎinián of Zǐtóng, the Governor of Sīzhōu Yáo Dàohé, and the Acting Governor of Xiāngzhōu Yǔ Pèiyù.
(The Prince of Nányáng had not yet arrived,
therefore Yǔ Pèiyù was acting as Governor.) Jìng'ér, Huáizhēn, and Wénhé all beheaded his envoys,
and swiftly submitted memorials to inform the court;
Wénhé soon abandoned his province and fled to Xiàkǒu.
(Bālíng
was not a province;
"province"
should be
"commander".
Xià,
read as hù yǎ.)
Dàohé
was the grandson of the Later Qín's Gāozǔ.
(The Later Qín ruler Yáo Xīng
had the temple name Gāozǔ.)
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Yōuzhī sent the Auxiliary General Sūn Tóng and others eastward in succession.
Yōuzhī sent a letter to Dàochéng,
stating:
"The Young Emperor was insane and tyrannical;
you should have secretly deliberated with the various lords,
jointly reported to the Empress Dowager,
and ordered his deposition.
How could you collude with his attendants,
and personally carry out regicide?
To the extent that he was not encoffined,
and maggots crawled at the door?
Among all your subjects,
who would not be shocked and indignant!
Furthermore,
you replaced the old court officials,
(old court officials refers to the veteran court ministers.)
and the keys to the palace gates
are all controlled by your family members.
I wonder if the bequeathed instructions of Zǐmèng and Kǒngmíng were truly like this!
(Huò Guāng,
styled Zǐmèng;
Zhūgě Liàng,
styled Kǒngmíng.)
How dare I abandon the integrity of Bāoxū!"
(Shēn Bāoxū begged for Qín troops to preserve Chǔ,
the affair is seen in the *Zuǒzhuàn*.)
[Dàochéng] was alarmed and fearful.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
Dàochéng entered and took guard of the court hall,
ordering the Palace Attendant Xiāo Yí to replace him in guarding the Eastern Headquarters,
and the Army Pacification Acting Army Adviser Xiāo Yìng to guard Jīngkǒu.
Yìng
was Yí's younger brother.
On the Wùchén day,
strict security measures were enforced inside and outside.
On the Jǐsì day,
the Prince of Wǔlíng, Zàn, Governor of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed Governor of Jīngzhōu.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
the General of the Right Guard Huáng Huí was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
to command the various vanguard armies to attack Yōuzhī.
Initially,
Dào Chéng appointed his heir Zé as the Chief Clerk to Prince Xiāo of Jìnxī,
acting as the administrator of Yǐng Province,
and had him repair and prepare weapons and equipment in preparation for Yǒu Zhī.
After Dào Chéng suppressed the rebellion of Guìyáng,
he was promoted to the rank of County Duke,
and appointed Zé as his heir.
Zé,
(pronounced) shì gé fān.
Zhì,
(pronounced) zhí zhī fān.
He appointed Zé as General of the Left Guard,
and sent him downriver together with Xiāo.
Liú Huáizhēn said to Dào Chéng:
"Xiàkǒu is a crucial strategic point,
we must have the right person in charge."
Dào Chéng wrote a letter to Zé, saying:
"Since you are entering the court,
you must entrust the subsequent affairs to someone who is both civilly and militarily capable and whose intentions align with yours."
Zé then recommended Liǔ Shìlóng, the Marshal of Xiāo, to replace himself.
Dào Chéng appointed Shìlóng as the Chief Clerk to Prince Zàn of Wǔlíng,
acting as the administrator of Yǐng Province.
As Zé was about to depart,
he said to Shìlóng:
"If Yǒu Zhī suddenly revolts,
burns the ships at Xiàkǒu,
and advances eastward along the river,
he will be uncontrollable.
If we can make Yǒu Zhī stay and attack Yǐng City,
he will certainly not be able to capture it quickly.
You will be on the inside,
I will be on the outside,
and we will surely defeat him."
When Yǒu Zhī raised his troops,
Zé had reached Xúnyáng,
but had not yet received instructions from the court.
The troops wanted to double their speed and rush to Jiànkāng,
but Zé said:
"Xúnyáng is located in the middle of the river,
close to the capital region.
If we station ourselves at Pénkǒu,
we can protect the court internally,
and provide external support to Xiàshǒu,
Xiàshǒu,
which is Xiàkǒu.
We can control the southwest,
and our gathering here today
is arranged by Heaven."
Some thought that Pénkǒu City was too small and difficult to defend,
but General of the Left Central Guard Zhōu Shāntú said:
"Now we hold the middle of the river,
providing support to all directions,
we cannot be deterred by minor difficulties;
if the troops are united in heart,
the rivers and mountains themselves become our walls and moats."
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Zé escorted Xiāo to garrison Pénkǒu;
Zé entrusted all matters to Shāntú.
Shāntú commandeered planks from passing ships to build watchtowers,
erected water barriers,
and completed everything within ten days.
When Dào Chéng heard this,
he joyfully said:
"Zé is truly my son!"
He appointed Zé as the Commander of the Western Campaign,
and Zé recommended Shāntú as his deputy.
At that time, the Inspector of Jiāng Province, Prince Yǒu of Shàolíng, was stationed at Xúnyáng.
Zé believed that Xúnyáng City was not sufficiently defensible,
and petitioned to have Yǒu move to garrison Pénkǒu together.
Xúnyáng was then administered from Cháisāng,
now Cháisāng Mountain is located ninety lǐ southwest of Déhuà in Jiāng Province.
Pénkǒu is one lǐ west of Déhuà County.
Jiāng Province was administered from Déhuà,
likely near the ancient city of Pénkǒu.
The Inspector of Xiāng Province, Wáng Yùn, was dismissed and returned home due to his mother's mourning,
and when he reached Bālíng,
he formed a deep alliance with Shěn Yǒu Zhī.
Bālíng is over four hundred lǐ from Jiānglíng,
so it seems that messengers were sent back and forth,
forming a deep alliance.
When Yùn passed through Yǐng Province,
he wanted to take advantage of Xiāo Zé's attendance at a funeral to stage a rebellion,
and seize Yǐng City.
Zé learned of this,
and did not go out.
Upon returning,
when he reached the Eastern Prefecture,
he again wanted to take advantage of Xiāo Dào Chéng's attendance at a funeral to stage a rebellion,
but Dào Chéng also did not go out.
"Staging a rebellion" means
wanting to kill him.
Nàn,
(pronounced) nǎi dàn fān.
Generals Huáng Huí, Rén Hóubó, Sūn Tánguàn, Wáng Yíxīng, Bǔ Bóxīng, and others were all involved in the conspiracy.
Bóxīng
was the son of Tiānyǔ.
Bǔ Tiānyǔ died in the rebellion of the vicious Shào.
When Dào Chéng first heard about Yǒu Zhī's uprising,
he personally went to visit Yuān,
but Yuān refused to see him.
The Attendant Gentleman Yuán Dá said to Yuān,
"You should not show disagreement or alignment,"
Attendant Gentleman,
is the Gentleman Cavalier Attendant.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established the Extraordinary Gentleman Cavalier Attendant,
and in the second year of Tàixīng of Emperor Yuán,
he assigned two people to serve together with the Gentleman Cavalier Attendant,
hence they were called Gentleman Cavalier Attendants.
"If he uses the young age of the sovereign and the difficult times,
which are no different from the time of Guìyáng,
referring to the rebellion of Prince Xiūfàn of Guìyáng.
How can I refuse him!
Once we are together,
how can we differ!"
Dào Chéng then summoned Chǔ Yuān,
and shared a seat with him,
consulting him on every matter.
It turned out just as Yuán Cài had anticipated.
He entered duty at the Chancellery;
Commentary on Discrepancies: In the Book of Southern Qí,
"Yùn"
is written as
"Tāo",
but now we follow the Book of Sòng and the History of the Southern Dynasties.
Huáng Huí and other generals all went out to garrison Xīntíng.
Initially,
when Chǔ Yuān was General of the Guard,
he left his post due to his mother's mourning,
and despite the court's urging,
he did not return.
Cài had long enjoyed a great reputation,
and personally went to persuade him,
persuade,
meaning to advise and explain.
Shuō,
(pronounced) shū ruì fān.
When Cài became the President of the Imperial Secretariat,
and encountered his mother's mourning,
Yuān earnestly persuaded him,
and Cài consequently did not return to duty,
which caused Yuān to resent him.
Yuān resented Cài
because he forced him to abandon his own intentions and made him fail in his duty as a son.
Yet by killing Cài to overthrow Sòng,
he also failed in his duty as a subject.
In terms of loyalty and filial piety,
Yuān failed in both.
Dào Chéng discussed it with Yuān.
Yuān said:
"The turmoil in the western region,
will certainly not succeed,
you should first prepare internally."
Meaning to prepare against Yuán Cài and others.
They were about to inform Yuān;
the others said that since Yuān and Dào Chéng had long been close,
they should not inform him.
Cài said:
"Although Yuān is close to him,
how could he allow major differences!
If we do not inform him now,
once the matter is settled, we should eliminate him."
So they informed Yuān of the plan,
Yuán Cài still treated Chǔ Yuān according to past sentiments.
Dào Chéng had also heard of their plan beforehand,
and sent Army Commanders Sū Liè, Xuē Yuān, and Tàiyuán Wáng Tiānshēng to lead troops to help Cài defend Shítóu.
Xuē Yuān firmly declined,
but Dào Chéng forced him,
and Yuān had no choice,
tearfully bidding farewell.
Dào Chéng said:
"You will be near Shítóu,
coming and going day and night,
why are you so sad,
and what is your reason for declining?"
Yuān said:
"I am not sure if you can guarantee that you and Yuán will remain as one family?
Now if I go,
if I side with him, I betray you;
if I do not side with him, I will immediately suffer disaster—
how can I not be sad!"
Dào Chéng said:
"The reason I am sending you
is precisely because you can handle situations appropriately,
so that I have no worries from the west.
Shítóu is west of the palace city,
hence the expression.
Wèi,
(pronounced) yú wèi fān.
Say no more."
Yuān
was the nephew of Āndū.
Dào Chéng also appointed the General of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry Wáng Jìngzé as the Palace Attendant,
to jointly command the imperial guards with Bóxīng.
Yuán Càn plotted to forge an order from the Empress Dowager,
ordering Yuán Wěn and Bó Xìng to lead the palace guard troops to attack Xiāo Dàochéng at the court hall,
while Huí and others would lead their own troops in response.
Liú Bǐng, Rén Hóubó, and others all headed for Shítóu,
originally planning to launch the attack on the night of Rénshēn.
Bǐng was panicked and confused, not knowing what to do,
and after the afternoon meal, he packed his belongings;
just before leaving,
he drank some soup,
which spilled onto his chest,
and his hands trembled uncontrollably.
Before dark,
he loaded his womenfolk,
and with his entire household fled to Shítóu,
accompanied by several hundred retainers,
creating a grand spectacle along the road.
Upon arrival,
he saw Càn,
who exclaimed in shock:
"Why have you come so hastily?
Now we are doomed!"
Bǐng's flight to Shítóu
meant the plot was fully exposed,
hence Càn said they were certainly doomed.
"To see you, my lord,
even ten thousand deaths would be no regret!"
Sūn Tánguàn, hearing of this,
also fled to Shítóu.
The Deputy of Dānyáng, Wáng Xùn, and others rushed to inform Dàochéng,
and the affair was thus fully exposed.
Xùn
was the son of Wáng Sēngchuò.
Wáng Sēngchuò held power at the end of the Yuánjiā era.
Dàochéng secretly sent someone to inform Wáng Jìngzé.
At that time, the palace gates were already closed,
and Jìngzé wanted to open them to exit,
but Bǔ Bóxīng had troops strictly on guard.
Jìngzé then sawed through the wall of the room he was in to get out,
and went to the Secretariat to arrest Wěn.
Wěn had already completed his preparations,
"preparations"
meaning outfitted;
"completed preparations"
means his gear was already arranged,
awaiting the time to launch.
Seeing Jìngzé suddenly arrive,
he rose in shock to greet him,
saying:
"Brother, what brings you here at night?"
Jìngzé rebuked him:
"How dare you, scoundrel, commit treason!"
Wěn embraced Jìngzé,
who punched him in the face, knocking him to the ground, and killed him.
He also killed Bóxīng.
Bǔ Bóxīng and his son both died in the disaster of the Liú clan.
He then held the granary city to resist Càn.

An examination of discrepancies says:

He replied to Jìng'ér's letter with the words: 'A word or two spoken casually,'
and placed a few items like chicken feathers and peach wood ears in the envelope.
Jìng'ér's envoy for winter congratulations immediately rode post-haste to report to the Duke.
On the twelfth day, Rénchén,
Yōuzhī sent Sūn Tóng and others ahead.
On the seventeenth day, Dīngyǒu,

On the eighteenth day, Wùxū,
the Duke led his troops into the court to guard it.
On the fourteenth day of the intercalary month, Guǐsì,
Yōuzhī arrived at Xiàkǒu."
According to the Sòng calendar of that year, the intercalary month began on Gēngchén,
while the Wèi calendar had the intercalary month beginning on Gēngxū.
Thus, the winter solstice must have been at the end of the eleventh month.
If Yōuzhī was still secretive when speaking to Jìng'ér's envoy offering winter congratulations,
how could he have already sent troops eastward on the twelfth day?
Moreover,
if Yōuzhī had raised troops in Jiānglíng on the twelfth day,
how could it take over sixty days to reach Xiàkǒu?
Also, the Annals of Emperor Shùn of Sòng state:

Yōuzhī rebelled.
On Dīngmǎo,
the Prince of Qí entered to guard the court."
Dīngmǎo was the eighteenth day of the twelfth month.
"On Guǐsì of the intercalary month,

The Biography of Yōuzhī states:
"He rebelled in the eleventh month.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month,

The Annals of Emperor Gāo of Southern Qí states:

The various records generally correspond,

having joined him in this great undertaking,
if in a moment of crisis
I were to change my fundamental loyalty,
I could not do it."
When the city fell,
soldiers captured him and brought him before Jìng'ér.
Jìng'ér said:
"Lord Biān, why did you not come earlier!"
Róng replied:
"Lord Shěn appointed me to guard the city;
I could not bear to abandon it.
I never sought to live."
("Qí"
means to seek,
to request.)
Jìng'ér said:
"Death is not hard to obtain!"
And ordered him executed.
Róng went to his death laughing joyfully.
Róng's guest, Chéng Yōngzhī of Tàishān, embraced Róng and said:
"I have traveled and associated with Lord Biān;
I cannot bear to see Lord Biān die.
I beg to be killed first."
The soldiers could not proceed with the execution,
and reported it to Jìng'ér.
Jìng'ér said:
"To seek death is very easy;
why should it not be allowed!"
He had Yōngzhī killed first,
and then executed Róng.
None among the soldiers failed to shed tears.
Sūn Tóng, Zōng Yǎnzhī, and others were all executed.
(Zōng Yǎnzhī and Zāng Yín had urged Yǒuzhī to raise troops,
and Sūn Tóng served as the vanguard commander.)
On Bǐngzǐ,
the state of emergency was lifted.
The Attendant-in-Chief Liǔ Shìlóng was appointed Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Xiāo Dàochéng returned to garrison Dōngfǔ.
On Dīngchǒu,
the Right
Guard General Xiāo Zé was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and the Attendant-in-Chief Xiāo Yí was appointed Central Army Commander.
In the second month,
on Gēngchén,
the Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Wáng Sēngqián was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and the Right Vice Director Wáng Yánzhī was appointed Left Vice Director.
On Guǐwèi,
Xiāo Dàochéng was additionally appointed Grand Commandant and Commander of the Various Military Affairs of Sixteen Provinces including Nánxú.
(Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū lists: Commander of Nánxú, Nányǎn, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, Sī, Yù, Jīng, Yōng, Xiāng, Yè, Liáng, Yì, Guǎng, and Yuè—sixteen provinces.)
Dàochéng submitted a memorial returning the Yellow Battle-Ax.
(As the upper reaches were now pacified, he memorialized to return the Yellow Battle-Ax.)
The Ministry of Personnel Gentleman Wáng Jiǎn,
son of Sēngchuò,
possessed profound and expansive spirit and bearing.
He loved learning and was widely knowledgeable,
and from a young age harbored the ambition to become Chancellor.
Contemporary opinion also praised and esteemed him.
Dàochéng appointed Jiǎn as Right Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant.
(The Grand Commandant's office at that time established Left and Right Chief Clerks.)
"Hào"
is pronounced "hū dào fān".
"Shǎo",
is pronounced "shī zhào fān".
"Xiàng",
is pronounced "xī liàng fān".
He entrusted all matters, great and small, exclusively to him.
2 On the Dīnghài day,
the Wei sovereign went to the Dài hot springs;
these are the hot springs of the Wei capital at Dài;
referring to them as the Dài hot springs
distinguishes them from the hot springs at Qiáoshān in Xiàluò County.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states: ninety lǐ north of Dài City is Sānggān City,
crossing the Sānggān River west of the city,
ten lǐ from the city,
there are hot springs,
effective in treating illnesses.
Also, forty lǐ southwest of Xiàluò County is Qiáoshān,
below which are hot springs.
On the Guǐmǎo day
he returned.
3 Dàngchāng King Míjī had recently ascended.
In the third month, on the Bǐngzǐ day,
Wei sent an envoy to appoint Míjī as General Who Conquers the South, Governor of Liáng and Yì Provinces, Duke of Hénán, and King of Dàngchāng.
4 Huáng Huí was unhappy being in Yǐng Province,
and persistently sought Nányǎn,
so he led his troops and returned without authorization;
on the Xīn
mǎo day,
he was changed to Commander of Military Affairs of the Five Provinces Including Nányǎn and Governor of Nányǎn.
Huáng Huí,
with the blade at his neck,
yet he returned east without authorization,
this was courting death.
5 Earlier,
when Wáng Yùn left Xiāng Province,
Xiāng Province Governor Nányáng Prince Huì had not yet taken up his post,
Chángshā Internal Clerk Yǔ Pèiyù acted as prefectural administrator.
Huì first sent Central Army Adjutant Hán Yòuzōng to lead troops to garrison Xiāng Province,
and he did not get along with Pèiyù.
When Shěn Yōuzhī rebelled,
the two became suspicious of each other,
and Pèiyù attacked and killed Yòuzōng.
When Huáng Huí reached Yǐng Province,
he sent Auxiliary General Rén Hóubó to act as administrator of Xiāng Province;
Hóubó then killed Pèiyù without authorization,
hoping to exonerate himself.
Rén Hóubó and Huáng Huí were both co-conspirators with Yuán and Liú.
Rén,
pronounced rén.
Xiāo Dàochéng sent Ānguó to execute Hóubó.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
the Wei sovereign went to Guōshān;
on the Dīnghài day,
he returned.
7 Xiāo Dàochéng believed Huáng Huí would ultimately cause calamity and disorder;
Huí had several thousand troops,
and Dàochéng wanted to send someone to arrest him,
but feared it would cause rebellion.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
he summoned Huí to the Eastern Prefecture.
Upon arrival,
Huí was detained in the outer quarters,
and Dàochéng had Huán Kāng lead several dozen men,
enumerate Huí’s crimes, and kill him,
along with his son, Jìnglíng Chancellor Sēngniàn.
Dàochéng eliminated his adversaries,
and by this point it was complete.
Shǔ,
pronounced shǔ.
Xiàng,
pronounced xiàng.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
Xiāo Dàochéng appointed Huáinán and Xuānchéng Commandery Administrator Xiāo Yìng to act as administrator of Nányǎn Province,
and still had his younger brother Xiāo Huǎng replace him.
Huáinán and Xuānchéng were close to the capital,
so Dàochéng did not entrust them to others.
8 In the fifth month,
Wei prohibited imperial clansmen, nobles, and families of officials and commoners from disregarding clan status,
and marrying beneath their class;
violators would be punished for violating regulations.
9 The Wei sovereign and the Empress Dowager visited the tiger enclosure,
and a tiger escaped,
climbed onto the elevated walkway,
nearly reaching the imperial seat,
the guards were all startled and scattered;
Minister of Personnel Wáng Ruì seized a halberd and defended against it,
the Empress Dowager praised him as loyal,
and trusted and employed him even more.
The historian states that Empress Féng used public righteousness to serve her private interests.
10 In the sixth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
Auxiliary General Yáng Wénhóng was appointed Governor of Northern Qín Province and King of Wǔdū.
11 On the Gēngzǐ day,
the Wei imperial uncle Ruò died.
12 Xiāo Dàochéng believed that since the Dàmíng era,
both public and private extravagance had been rampant,
so in autumn,
the eighth month,
he petitioned to abolish the Imperial Workshop,
the position of Imperial Workshop Director,
had existed since the Hàn,
under the Shàofǔ in Hàn,
under the Guānglùxūn in Jìn.
According to the Sòng Jì,
in the fourth year of Emperor Shìzǔ’s Dàmíng era,
the Director of the Fine Works Office was changed to Left and Right Imperial Workshop Directors.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
he also petitioned to ban extravagant and counterfeit miscellaneous items among the people,
totaling seventeen articles.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn’s Qí Shū,
the petition banned: using gold and silver as foil;
horse trappings must not be gilded with gold and silver;
embroidered skirts must not be woven;
brocade shoes must not be worn on the roads;
red color must not be used for banners, canopies, or clothing;
colored silk must not be cut into miscellaneous flowers;
damask silk must not be used for miscellaneous ornaments;
brocade with deer patterns and beds with carved legs of tamarisk or cypress,
boxes, baskets, and miscellaneous items;
colored silk for screens;
brocade-edged mats;
private manufacture of weapons;
seven treasures adorning musical instruments;
also, miscellaneous decorative items must not have gold and silver flowers and animals;
unauthorized casting of gold and copper into images: all were promulgated by imperial decree,
totaling seventeen articles.
13 On the Yǐwèi day,
Xiāo Zé was appointed General of the Central Army,
and Xiāo Yí was appointed Governor of Jiāng Province.
14 In the ninth month,
on the Yǐsì day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 Xiāo Dàochéng wanted to recruit contemporary worthies to assist in his great enterprise,
at night,
he summoned the Chief Clerk of the Cavalry General Xiè Fěi,
dismissed others and spoke with him,
for a long time,
Fěi said nothing;
only two children held candles,
Dàochéng worried Fěi found it difficult,
so he took the candles and sent the children away,
Fěi still said nothing;
Dàochéng then called his attendants.
Fěi,
was the son of Zhuāng.
The Right Chief Clerk of the Grand Commandant Wáng Jiǎn understood his intention,
another day,
he requested a private audience with Dàochéng and said:
"Merit too great to be rewarded,
this is not unique in ancient or modern times.
With your current position and status,
if you wish to remain a subject forever,
is it possible?"
Dàochéng sternly rebuked him,
but his expression softened inwardly.
Jiǎn then said:
"Jiǎn has received your special regard,
hence I speak what is difficult to speak;
why do you reject it so deeply!
The Sòng house has lost virtue,
without you, how could peace be restored!
But human sentiment is fickle,
and cannot last long;
if you hesitate even slightly,
then people’s hopes will fade.
Not only will the great enterprise be lost forever,
but even your own life may not be preserved."
Seven chǐ,
refers to the seven-chǐ body.
"What you say is not without reason."
Jiǎn said:
"Your current fame and position,
indeed make you the regular chancellor,
you should establish rituals surpassing all others,
subtly indicating change.
You should first let Chǔ Gōng know,
Jiǎn requests to carry out this mission."
Dàochéng said:
"I will go myself."
After a few days,
Dàochéng personally visited Chǔ Yuān,
and they conversed cordially for a long time.
Then he said:
"I dreamed that I should receive an official post."
Yuān said:
"You have just been appointed now,
referring to the recent addition of Grand Commandant and Commander.
Moreover, auspicious dreams may not come true immediately."
Dàochéng returned,
and told Jiǎn.
Jiǎn said:
"Chǔ simply does not understand the principle."
Jiǎn then proposed to add Dàochéng as Grand Tutor,
with the authority of the Yellow Axe,
and had the Secretariat Drafter Yú Zhěng draft the edict.
Dào Chéng's trusted confidant Xiá said:
"This is a major matter,
we should report it to Lord Chǔ."
Dào Chéng said:
"What if Lord Chǔ does not comply?"
Xiá said:
"Yànhuí cherishes his life and protects his wife and children,
he does not possess extraordinary talent or exceptional integrity;
I can control him."
Yuān indeed offered no opposition.
Chǔ Yuān,
styled Yànhuí.
History states regarding Chǔ Yuān's character,
that everyone could insult and belittle him.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
an edict was issued to promote Dào Chéng to Acting Commander with the Yellow Axe, Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without, Grand Tutor, and concurrently Governor of Yángzhōu,
permitted to wear his sword and shoes when ascending the palace hall,
not required to hasten his steps when entering court,
not required to announce his name when paying homage,
while retaining his previous positions of Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand Commandant, General of Agile Cavalry, Chief of the Imperial Secretariat, and Governor of Southern Xúzhōu.
Dào Chéng firmly declined the special honors.
Wearing sword and shoes when ascending the hall, not hastening steps when entering court, and not announcing name when paying homage,
were all special honors.
16. Appointed the Governor of Yángzhōu, Prince Xi of Jìnxī, as Minister over the Masses.
17. On the wùshēn day,
Grand Tutor Dào Chéng appointed Xiāo Yìng as Governor of Southern Yǎnzhōu.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the dīngchǒu day,
appointed Xiāo Huǎng as Governor of Yùzhōu.
18. On the jǐmǎo day,
Sūn Tánguàn was captured,
and executed.
During the calamity at Shítóu,
Tánguàn had fled.
Tán,
pronounced as "tán".
19. Wèi's Gentleman Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Zhèng Xī, came on a diplomatic mission.
20. On the rényín day,
Lady Xiè was established as Empress.
The Empress,
was the granddaughter of Zhuāng.
21. In the eleventh month,
on the guǐhài day,
Marquis of Línlǐ, Liú Huǎng, was implicated in plotting rebellion,
and he along with his accomplices were all executed.
Huǎng,
was the nephew of Bǐng.
Shěn Yuē's records state: Línlǐ County,
was established in the fourth year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
belonging to Tiānmén Commandery.
Lǐ,
pronounced as "lǐ".
22. On the jiǎzǐ day,
Prince Huī of Nányáng was transferred to become Prince of Suí Commandery.
23. The Wèi Empress Dowager Féng harbored jealousy towards the Governor of Qīngzhōu, Prince of Nán Commandery, Lǐ Huì,
(because) Emperor Gāozǔ's mother,
was Huì's daughter,
hence the jealousy.
In the twelfth month,
on the guǐsì day,
Huì, his wife, and his sons and younger brothers were executed.
The Empress Dowager, due to suspicion and resentment, exterminated over ten families,
yet Huì had implemented benevolent governance wherever he served,
so the people of Wèi particularly felt wronged and pitied him.
24. The Minister over the Masses, Wáng Sēngqián, submitted a memorial stating:
"The court's rituals and music,
largely deviate from the orthodox standards.
During the Dàmíng period, the palace ensemble was already combined with the pí and fú dances;
the Jìn records state: The origin of the pí dance is unclear,
but it was already performed at banquets and feasts during the Hàn dynasty;
the fu written by Fù Yì and Zhāng Héng,
all describe it.
The old melodies consisted of five pieces: First,
'In Guāndōng There is a Worthy Woman';
second,
'In the Second Year of Zhānghé';
third,
'Long-lasting Joy';
fourth,
'The Sovereign of the Four Directions';
fifth,
'Before the Hall Grows a Cassia Tree': their lyrics are all lost.
Wèi composed five new songs.
During the Tàishǐ period, new songs were separately composed again,
all changing their tune names.
The fú dance originated from Jiāngzuǒ,
formerly said to be a Wú dance;
examining its songs,
they are not Wú lyrics;
it was also performed in the palace halls.
Yáng Hóng's preface states: Since arriving south of the river, I have seen the White Talisman dance,
some call it the White Waterfowl dance,
said to have existed for several decades.
Examining its lyrical intent,
it was actually that the people of Wú, suffering under Sūn Hào's tyrannical rule,
longed to belong to Jìn.
Its tunes include: 'White Dove', 'Abundant', 'Solitary Deer', 'Jiéshí', and 'Prince of Huáinán', five pieces.
In my view, their lyrics are far superior to those of the various gentlemen of Wèi and Jìn,
but they suffer from being mournful and bitter,
not the music of a well-governed era.
Xuán,
read as 'xuán'.
Pí,
is the same as 'pí'.
I fear it violates the elegant style.
Furthermore,
the present qīngshāng music,
indeed originates from the Bronze Sparrow Terrace,
the refined legacy of the Three Ancestors,
their lingering sounds fill the ears,
esteemed between Cháng'ān and Luòyáng,
even more prized in Jiāngzuǒ;
Wèi Tàizǔ built the Bronze Sparrow Terrace in Yè,
personally composing yuèfǔ poems,
set to wind and string instruments,
later establishing the Office of Qīngshāng to manage it,
under the Chamberlain for Attendants.
The Three Ancestors,
refer to Wèi Tàizǔ, Gāozǔ, and Lièzǔ.
The Táng Huìyào states: Since Jìn's relocation,
ancient music gradually dispersed and was lost.
Fú Jiān destroyed Liáng,
and first obtained the Hàn and Wèi qīngshāng music,
transmitting it to the Former and Later Qín;
when Sòng Wǔ pacified Guānzhōng,
he collected it and brought it south of the river;
Suí, upon conquering Chén, acquired it,
Emperor Wén of Suí said:
'This is the orthodox sound of Huáxià.'
Then he established the Qīngshāng Office,
collectively called qīng music.
Nothing comes closer to this.
Yet with changing tastes and shifting listening habits,
it gradually declined again,
within a decade or so,
nearly half was lost,
while among the people there is fierce competition to create new tunes and miscellaneous songs,
excessively wanton and boundless,
it is appropriate to order the relevant officials to comprehensively repair and supplement them."
The court followed his suggestion.
25. This year,
Wèi's Governor of Huáizhōu, Gāo Yǔn, due to old age and illness, requested to return to his hometown,
soon after he was again summoned to Píngchéng in a comfortable carriage,
appointed as General Who Guards the Army and Supervisor of the Central Secretariat;
he firmly declined,
but it was not permitted.
He rode in a carriage into the palace hall,
and when paying court congratulations, he did not perform the bow.
Niè Chóngqí punctuated, Wáng Chóngwǔ proofread.
